title: Saint Nicholas’s Collegiate Church
summary: Officially, Saint Nicholas’s was built in the early 1300s but this is almost certainly incorrect.
heading: All Tribes: Saint Nicholas’S Collegiate Church.
paras: Officially, Saint Nicholas’s was built in the early 1300s but this is almost certainly incorrect. The origins of Galway as an urban settlement date to the 1120s and settlements always had attendant churches. A contemporary annal states that in 1132 the Mhic Carthaig of Munster “demolished the castle of Bun Gaillmne and plundered and burned the town.” The castle and town were attacked several times over the next hundred years before its capture by Richard de Burgh fitz William and his allies in the 1230s.

Situated on what is almost the highest ground within the medieval city, the church of Saint Nicholas was visible to seafarers far out into Loch Lurgan, alias Galway Bay. Patron saint Its earliest surviving inscribed graveslab, wrongly termed the ‘Crusader’s Tomb, dates to the 1200s and is in the Chapel of Christ. Its inscription is in Norman-French and translated, reads: Here likes Adam Bure. May God have mercy on his soul. Whoever will pray for his soul will have twenty days indulgence.”

The earliest known cleric of Saint Nicholas’s was named in a mandate of January 1458 from Pope Callixtus III: Richard Obare, priest, of the diocese of Tuam, who is to be summoned and removed, has wrongfully detained [the perpetual vicarage of Saint Nicholas's, Galway] for more than a year but less than two years without any canonical title.” The surname Obare alias Ó Bérra alias Berry is now generally found in Conamara.

In the south transept is a flamboyant walled tomb plus a tomb associated with wrongly associated with Mayor James Lynch fitz Stephen. The first dates from around the late 15th or early 16th century but because it was defaced by English Commonwealth troops in the 1650s it is difficult to say which family it belonged That which is supposed to be that of James fitz Stephen features the arms of Lynch, Athy and possibly French families as well as merchant marks. Above it is an empty frame which also features merchant marks plus the Lynch and Athy arms.

Dated 1566 is a headstone in the south transept to Elen Lynch and her husband John Robert fitz Tadhg. It contains either a mason’s mark or a merchant’s mark, denoting the occupation of Elen’s husband.
Particularly impressive is an elaborate graveslab dated Anno Domini 1580 which commemorates Muirchertach Ó Tighernaigh and his wife Cáit and his brother Tadhg, coopers in the town.

During the visit of Lord Deputy of Ireland Sir Henry Sydney town authorities were told in no uncertain terms to turn Saint Nicholas’s to the Church of Ireland. In the Lynch aisle a memorial dated 1635 memorialises Richard Browne and his wife Cate Browne plus their son Mathew Browne and his wife Mary Tierney plus their children.

Galway town rebelled against the English parliament in March 1642 and the following year Saint Nicholas’s was brought back into Catholic worship. One window in the church frames an altar tomb of the Lynch family which bears an inscription in Latin. Translated, it reads: “Stephen Lynch, of illustrious lineage, the darling of his soldiers and the terror of the enemies, in years still a young man but old in valour, of whom the world was not worthy, was exalted to heave the 14th of March A.D. 1644.”

Besides the war outside the walls there was sometimes conflict within. During March 1642 a number of Protestants were killed by Catholics before civic authorities and town priests put an end to it. During 1648 Marcus Darcy fought in a sword fight within the church, killed Patrick French. After a nine-month siege, Galway surrendered in April 1652 to English Commonwealth forces. Consequences included the destruction of many of the memorials and tombs in the church.

In 1688 Saint Nicholas’s again came back into Catholic worship under Warden Bodkin. Several baptisms survive for the year 1690 from a parish register but on 26 July 1691, after the battle of Aughrim, Saint Nicholas’s was returned to Church of Ireland worship. Nevertheless several members of the Tribes and other families were permitted to be buried in it. Among them was Warden Bodkin, who died about 1711. Another was Catholic Archbishop of Armagh Robert Blake.
He died at Carrowbrowne in 1787 and directed that he be buried in Browne’s Aisle in Saint Nicholas’s. It is presumed he was buried there but no memorial exists.

Mary Browne died during 1827, aged thirty-seven. Founder of Saint Nicholas’s Church Sunday School, she was mother-in-law of the then Warden Daly and was widow of Thomas Browne esquire who died in 1813 aged fortyone. Browne had been barrack master of the town plus Sheriff of Galway in 1793-94, 1800-01 and 1812-13.

A memorial to Reverend John Darcy states he was Rector of Galway for fiftyfive years, that he died aged eighty-two on 2 September 1875, his memorial placed by his widow and children. Reverend Darcy helped build the Claddagh
Basin, brought weavers and industry into the town and was secretary of the Harbour Commissioners.

A brass plaque placed by their siblings commemorates siblings Major John Denis Kirwan of the Royal Artillery and Agnes Kirwan, both of who died in June 1891 and were children of Richard Kirwan esquire of Baunmore.
The latest memorial concerning any of the Tribes is the Lynch-Athy memorial, which commemorates Charles Crofts of Renville who died 21 April 1946 and his wife Murial Lynch Athy.

title: Saint Nicholas’s College
street: Church Lane, by the Saturday Market
summary: On the 1662 Pictorial Map called “The college of the Priests and Pastors”, this was a three-way building with an enclosed courtyard in front of the main doorway of Saint Nicholas’s church.
heading: All Tribes: Saint Nicholas’S College.
paras: On the 1662 Pictorial Map called “The college of the Priests and Pastors”, this was a three-way building with an enclosed courtyard in front of the main doorway of Saint Nicholas’s church. Called the College House, it was the residence of the Warden of Galway, a bishop in all but name. The office was created by Archbishop of Tuam Donncha Ó Muireadhaigh (himself vicar of Saint Nicholas’s in 1446) to solve jurisdictional issues between the town, the diocese of Annaghdown and archdiocese of Tuam. Archbishop Ó Muireadhaigh raised the church of Saint Nicholas to the status of a college ruled by a Warden and staffed by eight priests or vicars. Most unusually, Ó Muireadhaigh gave their appointments not to himself or his successors but to the Corporation of Galway, who were not clerics but secular men.

Part of the College was built by John Lynch fitz Edmond while Mayor during 1494-95 but it was evidently not finished as John Lynch fitz John saw it necessary in 1496 to finance its completion. It may not have been finished even then as Dominick Dubh Lynch fitz John, who did not die until 1508, was another credited among its founders.

Because they were elected annually, there was as high a turnover among the Wardens as there were with the Mayors. Earliest now known was Sior Énrí Ó Brannagáin alias Sir Henry Brannagain, Warden in 1497. Seán Mac Feorais alias John Bermingham was Warden in 1514 while a document dated 27 March 1522 named Sior Tadhg Ó Casaide alias Sir Thady Cahisy as Warden. Others were Énrí Ó Curraoin in 1525; Seán Ó Diarmada around 1527; Thomas French in 1540; John Bermingham in 1545; 20 August 1549. Diarmaid Ó Nún, 1549; Patrick Blake, April 1551; Sir Tadhg Ó Diarmada, October 1551; Patrick Blake between 1561 and 1563. An order for Blake’s arrest of Blake came in October 1563 because the post had been split into Catholic and Protestant Wardenships. It began on 27 April 1551 when the king, a zealous Protestant, authorised that Patrick Blake become Warden while the vicars choral should be
Patrick Kirwan, Thomas French, Darby Ó Hession, John Talman, Darby O’Rowan, John Dermot, John O’Branagan and Edmund O’Flaherty.

Thus the succession became confused for the rest of the century. Because the English government were now Protestant in denomination, opposing Catholic and Protestant wardens were created. Catholics regained the College and church in June 1643 but their jurisdiction ended with the surrender of the town in April 1652 to the English Commonwealth army under Sir Charles Coote with Colonels Sadlier and Stubbers.

During those years the College House housed a scholar from County Sligo named Dubhaltach Mac Fhirbhisigh. Why precisely remains unknown as he was not in any holy order. It is possible that he was attached to it as a teacher in some capacity. At any rate Mac Fhirbhisigh was in Galway by April 1645 and completed a transcription of SeanchasSílÍr from LeborUa Maine. His transcript of its seventy pages became very useful because the original has since lost four of its fourteen folios. On 8 December 1647 he noted he completed the translation from English into Gaeilge of the Rule of Saint Clare, commissioned by Mother Mary Bonaventure Browne, then Abbess of the Poor Clares of Galway. He gave his place of writing as the College of Galway. Sometime between then and 13 April 1649 Mac Fhirbhisigh began work on his monumental work, LeabharnanGenealach, a massive compilation of Irish genealogies, both Gaeil and Gaill. He completed the section titled RéimRíoghraide Éireann on 8 August 1649, the same week as the inhabitants of Blake’s Castle on the quays became infected with the bubonic plague, an epidemic which over nine months would killed almost four thousand in the town. Mac Fhirbhisigh finished the book’s index on 28 December 1650. Sometime in those years he left the College; in January 1671 he was murdered during a pub brawl in his native county.

An unofficial Catholic wardenship became official in March 1686 with the assent of King James VII and II. Henry Brown was elected Warden, his vicars being Henry Joyce (absent), Michael Lynch, James Fallon, John Rodin, Jerome Martin, Nicholas Nolan and Thomas Lynch – but the church was withheld from them by the Protestant Warden, Doctor Vesey. They seem to have gained it by 1690, when a register suggests Catholic baptisms were once again held within the church – but the army of Queen Mary II and King William III of Orange entered Galway on 26 July 1691 and took possession of the church and college from the then Warden, Reverend John Bodkin.

His successor was Edmund Lynch, who sent the moveable property of the church and college to France for safekeeping. These were converted into money which was regularly sent back to Galway to support its once again unofficial Warden and vicars, carrying out their duties in secret. Only in 1725

was a Catholic chapel openly built on Middle Street under the supervision of Warden Patrick Bermingham. He was succeeded by Hyacinth Bodkin who died in 1749. Bodkin was succeeded by Marcus Kirwan, who was replaced during 1750 by Anthony Blake who in that year rebuilt the chapel on Middle Street into Saint Augustine’s Church. After him were Francis Kirwan, John Joyce to 1783, Valentine Kirwan to 1791, succeeded by John Joyce.

Made around 1792, a list of clergy in the Wardenship named Reverend John Joyce as Warden while priests in Rahoon were Denis and Malachy Mannion. for Saint Nicholas parish were fathers John Joyce and T. Walsh. Saint Francis’s parish, alias Wood Quay, had fathers Bodkin and McHugh while in Saint Augustine Street were James Kirwan and Thomas Tierney. Out in the West which is now the Dominick Street-Henry Street area were fathers Bartholomew Burke and John Fallon. Several other priests were named in the several other parishes of the Wardenship.

Far more documentation exists from the 18th to 19th centuries, showing the positive result gradual relaxing of the Penal Laws was having on the preservation of Catholic parish registers and diocesan records. One document date 16 May 1796 was from Sam Ruxton in Parsonstown, King’s County, complaining to Warden John Joyce about the conducted of Miss O’Shaughnessy of Abbeygate Street because she had jilted him. Another written in Baltimore, Maryland on 5 December 1797 was by Bishop John Carroll of Baltimore, who was at the time the only Catholic bishop in the USA. Bishop Carroll wrote to Warden John Joyces saying that he had received the Warden’s letter by his kinswoman Miss Joyce; that Carroll had married her to a Mr. McDermott; that the couple were now living in Philadelphia. One from around 1800 stated that some Catholics had left local Freemason lodges, that disputes between the clergy and lay patrons were now mostly peaceful, and that the Charity School now had sixty boy pupils.

Warden Joyce was the centre of a case of apparent character assassination early in the 19th century. Catherine O’Brien alleged the Warden had “criminal intercourse” with her in 1785, was illegally elected Warden and other allegations. Among his character witnesses in 1801 was Catherine Blake who had served him for fourteen years as housekeeper. Blake vindicated Joyce’s character and refuted charges brought against by Catherine O’Brien nee Liddane who, claimed Blake, “was a drunken, quarrelsome and importunate slum-dweller.”
Valentine Bodkin was Warden in 1805 and the last Warden, Edmund French, died in 1831. In that year the Pope created a Bishop of Galway, Doctor George Brown.

The Wardenship of Galway had lasted three hundred and forty-seven years. The College House lasted a little longer, completely demolished in 1836. Nothing above ground survives of it, the place where it once stood now taken by Galway’s Saturday Market.

title: Franciscan Abbey and graveyard
summary: In his will of 19 August 1772, James Darcy of New Forest house in Kilkerrin parish bequeathed his ‘soul to Almighty God’ and requested that his ‘body to be interred in my family Vault in the Francisca…
heading: All Tribes: Franciscan Abbey And Graveyard, Saint Francis Street.
paras: In his will of 19 August 1772, James Darcy of New Forest house in Kilkerrin parish bequeathed his ‘soul to Almighty God’ and requested that his ‘body to be interred in my family Vault in the Franciscan Abbey of Galway.’ This reflects a long-established practice among the old merchant families for interment in the graveyards of Galway.

Saint Francis’s Abbey was founded in 1296 by Sir William Laith de Burgh on Saint Stephen’s island outside the town walls. It was a place of burial for several prominent members of the de Burgh lineage in south and north Connacht. But due to its proximity to the town, it was locals who formed its clergy, parishioners and interments.

Among the earliest locals known to be buried in it was William Blake fitz Geoffrey fitz Walter, a great-grandson of Richard Cadel alias Blake the founder of the family in Galway. William fitz Geoffrey died in 1458 and was ancestor of the Blakes of Kiltullagh, Ballinafad and Ardfry.

Andrew Lynch fitz Stephen died in 1523 and was interred in Saint Francis’s. He was Mayor 1498-99 and had died while imprisoned at Dublin by the 8th Earl of Ormond in a trade dispute between Galway town and the earl. One of several notables from outside the town interred were Archbishops of Tuam Donncha Ó Muraigh (died 1485), Muiris Ó Fitcheallaigh (died 1513) and Tomás Ó Maoilalaidh (died 1536). The latter was survived by his children including son Isóg, ancestor to the Counts of Toldendal.

Less exalted clergy included David O’Crissain, who died in February 1523 and was described as a man of great devotion and contemplation. His surname may now be Clesham. Another was Doctor Donncha Ó Nialláin who died in July 1558 and was acclaimed for his skill in medicine. He was buried in the vault of Henry Joyce and his family.

Mayor during 1526-27 and 1535-37, Richard Martyn seems to have been buried there while Seán an tSalainn French, Mayor 1538-39, had a chapel built on the abbey’s south side. And despite the reformation the Franciscans remained present; the 1568 will of Nicholas Blake, made provisions for the friars in case they were removed.

But like Saint Nicholas’s the visit in 1567 of Lord Deputy Sir Henry Sydney marked its handover to the Church of Ireland; thus on 9 March 1569 a lease of the abbey and all its belonings was made to Mayor Gyven Font and the citizens of Galway. Besides the abbey itself, it possessed twelve gardens, two parts of a water mill, the ninth part of tithes of Gortnekalle beside the town and customs of one salmon every Friday plus eels. But Mayor Font, his successors and the citizens were in no hurry to expel the friars, who were still present in October 1572. In his will of 27 December 1583, Edmund Skerrett directed his body be buried where his mother was buried in Saint Francis’s abbey, demonstrating that though formally owned by the town and Protestant, it was still run by the friars.

On 21 February 1604 the lease to the town was withdrawn and granted to Sir George Carew. Nevertheless they moved to a house within the town and in 1616 were continuing their work while in his will that year Robert Blake fitz Walter left ten pounds for the repair of the abbey. Father Mark Skerrett was Guardian of the Franciscans at Galway in 1629 and able to hold a school there and after some years of severe persecution, was able to resume in 1635. Not all matters connected with the Franciscan were so pleasant. “A dreadful murder happened in this town, the 22 August where a certain thief, John, in the middle of the night killed the wife of his uncle (who was called William reagh, a fisherman) and his son and grandson a little boy of 12 years, with a hatchet, which he threw into our garden which was adjacent, in the year 1625.”

Many persons connected with the abbey ended their lives very far away from Galway yet were not forgotten at home. Known as the Angelic Friar, John Brown was nineteen when he died on 9 September 1623 at Saint Francis’s Convent at San Lucar in Spain. His death and details were recorded in the obituary book.

Interments continued that years, notably Sir Valentine Blake of Menlo and his notorious brother, Captain James ‘Spanish’ Blake. Elected Mayor in August 1642, Richard Martin fitz Oliver of Dún Guaire gave eight hundred pounds to built a chapel in Saint Nicholas’s plus another in Saint Francis’s. That the order were again in possession is demonstrated by such grants, with Father Valentine Brown then Guardian.

After the seizure of the town by the English Commonwealth in April 1652 they destroyed all the buildings of the abbey save the church, which was turned into a courthouse. In the 1820s this was rebuilt into the present-day courthouse of Galway.
Thus the Franciscans had to move to a new site and they did so further down Saint Francis’s Street from the courthouse. By 1781 they turned their small

thatched chapel into a stone building under fathers Francis Burke, Nicholas Lynch, Joseph Banks and Nicholas French. The present building was built in 1820 and the graveyard lies at the back, opening on Newtownsmyth Road. Almost no memorials survive from before the 17th century due to the general destruction by the English Commonwealth in the 1650s. One for Báitéar Ó Maonacháin is dated 1579 while that of alderman Dominic Browne of Gloves is dated 1596. The Nolan monument dates from around those decades while the Darcy vault dates from 1603. Another reads: Here lieth the body of Elizabethe Lynche the foundress of the Order of S. Clara who died the 14 of September 1626.
Sir Peter French died 27 February 1631 and part of his tomb survives, featuring two bishops on either side of his coat of arms and that of his wife, Mary Browne.

Walter Joyce of Corgary was ninety when he died 4 July 1853 and was buried in the Franciscan graveyard. His family were successful wine merchants during the 18th century, helping them regain wealth lost in the troubles of the 17th century. Walter was an Irish Volunteer, a leading supporter of Daniel O’Connell and a magistrate. His father Walter bought the Mervue estate around 1850. One of his descendants was Pierce Joyce who participated in the Arab Revolt during 1916-22 which reshaped the Middle East.
No burials were permitted after 1879 save a very few cases. The graveyard remains in the possession of the Franciscans.

title: Ceann an Bhalla, the Spanish Arch
summary: While Mayor Martin extended the town wall in the 1520s further west to the river, the final extension was done over the next decades, with Mayor Lynch overseeing the creation in the 1580s of what was then called Ceann a Bhalla, alias ‘Head of the Wall’.
heading: All Tribes: Ceann An Bhalla Alias Spanish Arch
paras: While Mayor Martin extended the town wall in the 1520s further west to the river, the final extension was done over the next decades, with Mayor Lynch overseeing the creation in the 1580s of what was then called Ceann a Bhalla, alias ‘Head of the Wall’. It contained arches which stored merchandise transferred to and from ships while also extending some protection from wind and waves to said ships docked where the river meets the sea.

Ceann a Bhalla was the scene of political drama and violence on the morning of 19 March 1642 when a group of young Galwaymen seized the Elizabeth and Francis from its master, Captain Robert Clarke. An attempt had been made the previous day by John Martin fitz Geoffrey, Captain James Lynch, Captain Tully of the Young Men’s Company and Walter Martin, but they failed to gain access to the ship.

Merchandise aboard the Elizabeth and Francis was bought in France by factor Dominick Kerwin for merchant Thomas Lynch. While it included a commercial cargo of salt, Kerwin had purchased for Lynch canon, gunpowder, guns and ammunition. Anchored in the Galway road, its military cargo was disputed between the merchants who wanted it for the town, and the English garrison on Forthill who wanted it for the fort.

Relations between the Irish (Gaeil and Gaill) with the Scots, Welsh and English colonists in Ireland had been deteriorating for years. Since the rebellion the previous October they had erupted into open warfare with hundreds killed across Ulster and Leinster. And a massacre of between thirty to sixty Protestants had since taken place on the Galway-Mayo border at Shrule, survivors making their way to Forthill. The garrison, which had from time to time being firing cannon shot at the town, were incensed. The Galwegians were not responsible for the massacre but urgently felt the need to have means of defence.

So early on the morning of 19 March another group rowed out to the Elizabeth and Francis: Walter Óge Martin, Dominick Kirwanfitz Robuck, Brian Rua Mathún Mór, the brothers Thomas and Stephen Lynch fitz Andrew, Murchad Ó Morda, Andrew Óge Lynch of Anbally, Richard French fitz Roland and Lawrence Óge Bodkin.

Once onboard they murdered the master’s mate plus two or three others either killed or injured. They then sailed the Elizabeth towards Ceann a Bhalla. Overlooking this was the garrison on Forthill, who began firing canon at the ship. All missed and they safely docked. Sir Valetine Blake came on the ship to take possession of the ten cannon, seven barrels of gunpowder plus what was described as a considerable amount of arms and ammunition. The canons
were unloaded and set upon the walls while the gates of Galway closed, proclaiming they were at war.

Claimed by several to be among them was Thomas Martin fitz Jasper, armed with a rapier and scian. But he claimed to be already aboard on his own business and claimed to have saved the life of the ship’s surgeon. This man, Robert Rawlins, testified that he was attacked and wounded by Dominick Kirwan but his life was indeed saved by Martin, who aimed a gun at Kirwan and spoke with him as Gaeilge, Kirwan then ceasing his assault.
Less lucky was the ship’s carpenter, brought into the town for medical attention but was too severely wounded and died.

According to the later testimony of clerk of the stores John Turner, the group did so at the direction of Patrick Darcy and Richard Óge Martin. They were part of the Council of Eight constituted by the mayor, aldermen and freemen. Turner held that this group was “convened by the instigation of Richard Óge Martin and John Blake fitz Robert with an intent to rebel against the government of the English Nation.”

The Council were Sir Robert Lynch, Francis Blake fitz Valentine, John Blake fitz Nicholas, Andrew Browne fitz Dominick, John Blake fitz Robert, alderman Patrick Martin plus Darcy and Martin, apparently chaired by and Mayor Walter Lynch.

Afterwards certain factions within the town allowed in a mob from Iar Connacht who began ransacking the houses of English Protestants in Galway, murdering John Fox and his wife, Mrs Collins and her husband plus a son of John Fisher. In the case of the former four their heads were cut off and used by the mob as a football. Only through the intervention of the town’s civic authorities and Catholic priests were the attacks stopped.

Richard Óge Martin was elected Mayor that August and the following June, when the garrison evacuated the fort, set forth on a Sunday morning with a pick axe setting people to demolish the fort. According to Patrick Darcy and Martin Lynch he also executed the Iar Connacht people who murdered the English Protestants in the town.
John Turner maintained that Darcy, Martin and the council did nothing to punish the perpetrators, “but rather abetted and maintained them in their barbarous cruelties.”

Ten years later Galway was the last town in the independent Irish state to surrender to the English Commonwealth. Brian Rua Mathún Mór, Stephen Lynch, Dominck Kirwan and Walter Martin were specifically excluded from the terms of the 1652 Articles of Surrender because they “had their hands immediately in the effusion of the blood of Captain Clark’s men”.
Much of the rest of the history of Ceann a Bhalla was more peaceful and from 1833 it became obsolete as a new dock were created.

With the publication of James Hardiman’s History of Galway in 1820, Ceann a Bhalla became the latest scene of the fictional murder of a Spanish friend of a fictional son of a Mayor of Galway. In another demonstration of the story’s lack of veracity, it was said to have taken place there in 1493. Impossible, as it was not built until the 1580s!
But the fiction became so popular that the name Ceann a Bhalla was slowly replaced during the 19th century by the name the Spanish Arch, after the nonexistent Spaniard supposed to be murdered there.

title: The Athy house
summary: The Athy family were descendants of Gérard d’Athée from Athée-sur-Cher just south-east of Tours in central France.
heading: Athy: Market Street Car Park
paras: The Athy family were descendants of Gérard d’Athée from Athée-sur-Cher just south-east of Tours in central France. A minor knight of no great background, in 1198 he was part of the court of King Richard I in France and was retained by his successor, King John. By August 1202 he was Seneschal of the Touraine for John, married to a woman named Lue alias Lupa, and had two sons who with him escaped to England when King John’s French domains were captured by King Louis. Along with Gérard came several relatives and their families.

Gérard became Sheriff of Nottingham and Derby, first in a string of appointments made for him and his families by King John which incurred the wrath of English barons and earls. This coupled with the king’s severe corruption and incredible incompetence led to Gérard and his family being barred from future landownership in the Great Charter, alias Magna Carta: “We will entirely remove from their bailiwicks, the relations of Gérard of Athée (so that in future they shall have no bailiwick in England); namely, Engelard of Cigogné, Peter, Guy and Andrew of Chanceaux, Guy of Cigogné, Geoffrey of Martigny with his brothers, Philip Marc with his brothers and his nephew Geoffrey, and the whole brood of the same.”

Having to recourse to further lands in England may have been what led to the family emigrating to the King’s realms in Ireland. Starting with William de Athy in the 1250s and John de Athy in the 1260s are references to about ten de Athys in Ireland, all employed in royal service. William and John were possibly sons of Gérard or more likely his grandsons. They and their relatives working as lawyers, sergeants, constables, castle stewards and custodians of lands for Kings Henry III, Edward I, Edward II and Edward III.
The most famous of the family was John de Athy, who in 1310 was Sheriff of Limerick, Constable of Limerick Castle from 1312 plus another term as Sheriff.
By 1317 he was knighted Sir John de Athy, while in 1320 William de Athy was described as his squire.

In 1315 Prince Edward Bruce of Scotland led a massive Scottish invasion of Ireland supported by various Irish and Anglo-Irish lords. An army led against Bruce by Earl William de Burgh was comprehensively defeated, leave Bruce in control of what is now counties Antrim and Down, save Carrickfergus Castle. And its constable was John de Athy. Carrickfergus town was burned around them, leaving them with the sea as their only escape route. But the Irish Sea was controlled by Bruce through his pirate, Thomas Dun. Relief was promised but never came while Bruce attacked towns all over south Ulster and northern Leinster. At Ardee he burned a church full of people while those who submitted to him had their food stolen; this was during the Great European Famine of 1315-18 when upwards of a third of Europe’s people died. From within Carrickfergus Castle de Athy led a daring night raid where the garrison succeeded in stealing supplies from the Scots, but remained trapped. During 1316 great storms, near continuous rain and low temperatures destroyed the crops, killing thousands from famine and causing epidemics. To survive “some are said to have taken the bodies of the dead from the graves, to have cooked the bodies … women also devoured their infants.” In July, matters were made even worse when King Robert Bruce of Scotland arrived with a large army to support his brother. De Athy and the garrison were reduced to eating leather and, it is supposed, some of their prisoners. Finally in September 1316 after a fourteen month siege, de Athy negotiated a surrender with the Bruces and were allowed to march south to Dublin.

It was during those months in Dubin he was knighted Sir John de Athy and appointed Admiral of the Irish Sea. Early in 1317 he and the Irish fleet set out to hunt and destroy the pirate fleet of Thomas Dun, whose Scots ships were blockading Irish ports and stealing their goods. On 2 July “Sir John de Athy met at sea Thomas Dun, a famous pirate, who he took prisoner; there were slain of those who were with him about forty, but he brought his dead and the heads of the rest to Dublin.” And that August, Prince Edward Bruce was killed in battle at Faughart, ending the invasion.

In 1325 de Athy was appointed Marshal of Ireland, officially making him Ireland’s greatest knight. He continued in royal service in Carrickfergus, Trim and eventually Roscommon Castle. But he was owed back wages and not always paid on time, obliging him to take out loans he could not always pay which resulted in court cases. In 1342 he was described as “old, deprived of his sight and impoverished” so was granted five pounds and again in 1343. In the 1330s and 1340s, William and Elias de Athy were described as of Athenry while in 1388 a later William de Athy was Treasurer of Connacht.
Because much of English rule across Ireland collapsed in those decades, his role must have been limited.

Thus the family transitioned from royal servants to town merchants in Galway town. John Athy was alive during 1404-44 and was Sovereign of Galway at least four times in his life. It was almost certainly he who built Athy’s Castle on Market Street north of Saint Nicholas’s Church. The 1662 Pictorial Map shows it to have been a massive town house, significantly larger plus taller than Lynch’s Castle and with a large adjacent garden.

But in 1440 “the peace of the town was … disturbed by some deadly disputes which arose between the rival families of Blake and Athy; and in the commotions occasion by them, several of the latter were slain. The precise nature of the dispute and how long it last remains unknown but what is known that the Athy family never again rose so high. Nevertheless they retained status and worked as merchants in and beyond the town. By the 1670s the Athys were still living in the town as well as in Renvile near Oranmore, in County Mayo plus Maryland in English America.

In the early 1800s Philip Lynch Athy of Renville was High Sheriff of Galway while in the 1850s Randall Athy owned Rinville House and another at Cottage in Ballynacourtry, the family owning over fourteen hundred acres in the county up to the 1870s. By 1906 Edmond Lynch Athy owned Rinville House plus over six hundred and sixty untenanted acres in Rinville West. In 1904 he was High Sheriff of Galway and was also the master of Galway Workhouse. His wife Annette Lynch Athy died 14 January 1923 at Renville House of influenza, aged sixty-seven, married and a landowners wife. Edmund Lynch Athy who died 1 March 1935 aged seventy-six. A plaque commemorating the family in Saint Nicholas’s Collegiate Church reads: This transfiguration window was bequeathed by Charles Walpole Crofts of Renville Oranmore Co. Galway who died April 21st 1946 to the Glory of God and in memory of his late wife Muriel Pauline Crofts nee Lynch Athy himself and the Athy family.

Other kinsmen were tenant farmers in the Oranmore-Maree area. One was Michael Athy who captained the Maree company of the Irish Volunteers during Easter 1916 and during the War of Independence. His brother Joseph was captured, tortured and murdered by the His Majesty’s Forces, nicknamed the Black and Tans. His death certificate of16 September 1920 states he died from “shock and haemorrhage caused by the bullet wound fired by a person or persons unknown.” It is said he was shot to put him out of his misery.

Michael survived the war and in 1947 was one of those who had a statue erected to Joe Howley at Oranmore. He married Mary Agnes Cavanagh of Kinvara in 16 January 1933. After her death in January 1947, he remarried at Oranmore Church to Ellen Cavanagh of Kinvara on 10 February 1948, his witnesses his brother-in-law William Bermingham. He was seventy-seven when he died 21 April 1970 and was the last of the Athys of Galway. Athy Castle survived until the end of the 18th century when it was demolished and eventually the town’s Monastic School was built on the site. It too was demolished in the 1980s and it has since become a car park.

title: Flood Street and Quay Lane
summary: For much of its history between 1124 and the late 1400s, what is now Quay Lane was the town docks.
heading: Athy: Flood Street And Quay Lane.
paras: For much of its history between 1124 and the late 1400s, what is now Quay Lane was the town docks. Caistél Bun Gaillimhe was built in 1124 on the corner of Quay Street and Quay Lane while ships would have docked where the houses of Quay Lane are as that was where the river bank was, at the point where the river Gaillimhe met the sea of Loch Lurgan. Hence the location was called Bun Gaillimhe – ‘the mouth of the Galway river’.

But at some point during the 14th and 15th centuries efforts were made to extend the town westwards and create a new docks while building new housing on Botharidirdá Strand. These houses were later demolished and made way for the Fish Market alias Spanish Parade and the road from Wolfe Tone Bridge into Flood Street.

Flood Street was well-named because it was regularly flooded from the river and has done so into living memory. But in the 14th and 15th centuries houses town merchants had properties there, not necessarily homes but given their location on or near the quays, stores for goods outgoing and incoming. The main Athy house seems to have been the one on the site of what is now Saint Augustine House on Saint Augustine Street-Flood Street but the family had a property on the south end of Quay Lane and on its Flood Street side can still be seen the Athy coat of arms, dating from the late 1400s or early 1500s. Among the goods the Athys sold abroad were skins from wolves, stags, hinds, hares, rabbitts and even cats! Clothes, hats, caps and clothes were also manufactured and in that category was the Gaelic brát; this was a great cloak which was a popular export item across Ireland and those in Galway specialised in ones coloured blue. But they came in many forms, types and colours, plus a variety of fashionable fringes.
Barrels of salmon, eels, herrings, honey, corn, butter, cheese, garlic and onions were among the food items exported. Almost none of these goods

could be produced just within Galway town or its liberties so merchants had to act in partnership with communities’ further inland. While the annals frequently mention dynastic violence, documentary evidence from merchants both Gaeil and Gaill show there were deep networks of cooperation working for mutual benefit.

Most poplar of the imports Galwegians imported was wine. As it could not 7779be produced in Ireland or Britain, merchants had to travel to France and Iberia to purchase it. Trade with Brittany, Poitou and Gascony probably dates back to the 13th century but voyages to Spain probably came a little later, likely when the Camino Santiago de Compostela celebrated 1450 as a Holy Year, leading to an upsurge in traffic to and from Ireland. By the 1460s Galway merchants were recorded trading in Lisbon. The connection lasted into the 18th century when emigrant Galwegians established brands like Chateau Kirwan Athy: Saint Augustine’s house, Saint Augustine Street.

Up to 1947 a late medieval building in Saint Augustine Street featured a doorway which bore the Athy arms and the date 1577, signifying that it was once their home. While the house was demolished that year, the doorway was saved and is now held by Galway Museum.

The doorway was made by John Athy and became the home of his son Walter, born around 1560 and died after 1612. He was married to Anne Martin and among their children was Francis, born about 1593 and died about 1644. He too married a Martin, a daughter of George Martin and their marriage stone, dated 163? is kept in storage by Galway Museum.

Their known children were Walter, born 1638; George, born 1642 and called after his maternal grandfather; John, born 1644. Walter’s descendants remained in Ireland and eventually came to own the Renville estate south of Oranmore. But George and John emigrated around 1662 to Maryland in English America, working as indentured servants – on 26 March 1663 Thomas Dent noted to the state authorities he was due land for transporting George Athy plus other indentures.

George worked as a servant for Thomas Dent until 1668 when his indenture ended in November 1668 when the Land Office of Maryland stated “George Attee of Saint Mary’s County [has] proved his right to fifty acres of land due for his time of service performed to Mr. Dent.” In 1670 he married Anne Moorehead, having with her children John and Elizabeth.

Throughout the 1670s Athy was recorded as a farmer trading in crops, hogs, cattle plus at least one court case. His chief crop was tobacco, which one case recorded a year’s crop was worth eight hundred pounds. George Athy’s descendant Darlene Hill shows he used the profits from tobacco to buy more land: Athy’s Hopewell in June 1675, consisting of one hundred acres; Hopewell

in 1680, eighty acres; Stoney Hill in 1688, eighty-eight acres. In 1692 he was living at Nanjamoy in Charles County and sold land on Broad Creek to his church and helped buil an Episcopal Church that year. This shows that despite his family’s religious background, in common with most Irish emigrants in colonial America he changed denomination. Much of the reason for this was because the colonies were overwhelmingly English, so the comparatively Irish conformed entirely religiously and culturally.

Another sign of his standing was that during the 1690s he was made a captain of a company of militia, military units which guarded against native American attacks and were used to kept the African slave population subdued. This responsibility was not one handed lightly, so it indicates Athy was fully accepted by the English authorities as a man who could be trusted to keep the colony white and free, his Irishness notwithstanding.

What records survive for the rest of his life show Athy bought and sold lands – sometimes several hundreds of acres - while being mentioned in some court cases and depositions. He died shortly before 21 December 1709, where his inventory was assessed as twenty-eight pounds, twenty-eight shillings and one pence, witnessed by Sarah Athy and John Athy.

His son John Athy was born about 1676 and by 1691 had his own registered cattle mark, denoting trade in the cattle business. In 1719 he was paying tax and leasing two plantations. In 1711 he married widow Margaret Lewis and they had children Thomas and George before his death early in 1730. Descendants of the family are still to be found in Maryland but have since spread across north America George Athy’s life story was relatively typical for thousands of Irish emigrants who emigrated to 17th and 18th century north America both as free emigrants and bond servants. Their story remains almost unknown today in Ireland because it took place so long ago and well before the great emigrations of the 1800s. Another factor is they so fully assimilated into the English Protestant colonial society at such an early date, and because unlike their 19th century fellow nationals rarely formed distinct Irish communities. But their stories can still be found in colonial records, from which historians can tell their tales.

title: Blake’s Castle
summary: On 18 January 1610 a jury found that Christopher Blake died 20 July 1609 “seized in fee of a castle, a stone house adjacent thereto, two thatched houses and three gardens, all situate in the town of G…
heading: Blake’S Castle: Quay Street.
paras: On 18 January 1610 a jury found that Christopher Blake died 20 July 1609 “seized in fee of a castle, a stone house adjacent thereto, two thatched houses and three gardens, all situate in the town of Galway and held of the Mayor, Bailiffs and Commonalty of Galway in free burgage tenure; and was also seized in fee by way of mortgage of the half-quarter of Legenleaghe and one cartron of Spiddell, held of the King in capite; that William Blake was his heir and then aged seventeen and not married.”
In 1905 Martin J. Blake identified their wider family as the Blakes of Kiltullagh and Frenchfort, Oranmore. All their property in the town had been forfeited in 1655 and they settled in Kiltullagh.

Seventeen-year-old William Blake fitz Christopher in 1610 was identified in 1637 as the owner of Blake’s Castle. His ancestor John Blake fitz William fitz Geoffrey was Mayor 1488-89 and died in 1508. He married Annabel Burke and among their sons were Geoffrey; Walter, Bishop of Clonmacnoise; Andrew; Peter. Annabel’s father appears to have been Uilleag Rua a Burc, lord of Clann Riocarde from 1430 to his death in 1485.

This list of accomplishments and his lifetime suggests Mayor John was the man responsible for the castle. Also known as Blake’s Southern Castle, this was built in the late 1400s or early 1500s on what was up to then the town quays; this is modern day Quay Lane or the area just west of it. But over time the area was gradually filled in and the quays moved to their current location at Spanish Arch, greatly narrowing the river from its original width.

Blake’s Castle was first mentioned was in 1592, depicted on the 1662 Pictorial Map and drawn in the late 1700s from where O’Brien’s Bridge begins today. Though shown as a simple if tall tower house in 1662, the later drawing shows it to have been quite a long, bulky building. In 2019 Paul Walsh noted “Archaeological investigations on the site in 1990 revealed it to be a very substantial building measuring a little over 7.8 metres along the street frontage and 14 metres in depth. Its owners evidently were very conscious of the need to protect themselves and their merchandise for it was heavily defended at roof level with bartizans or small projecting towers at each corner and a machicolation in the centre of the façade directly above the entrance.” This almost certainly denotes the tensions and violence between the townspeople and surrounding Burke and Ó Flaithbeartaigh lords during those

years. Mayor John Blake’s marriage to Annabel Burke may have placated her father, but what about her uncles, brothers, nephews and cousins? Its location also suggests that from the late 1400s into the 1640s it was put to good use storing goods brought into the town from the country for export while doing the same for goods imported through the nearby docks. The late 18th century drawing showed a two and a half-storey house stood between it and the river, possibly one described in 1657. Visible on the other side of it is a gable of another house on Martin’s Mill Lane, also described in 1657 and all owned by the Blakes.

Third son of Mayor John Blake was Andrew, who was father of William, who in turn was father of Christopher Blake who died in 1609. Christopher’s son William died around 1652 and was survived by a son, Christopher fitz William. He was one of the one hundred and four townsmen who refused to sign the Articles of Surrender in April 1652. In 1657 he was the previous owner of property seized by English solider Mathew Browne, described as a dwelling house slated, two and a half stories, valued at five pounds five shillings. This must have been one of the buildings attached to the outside of Blake’s Castle. His late father was described as owner of a slated dwelling house of three stories with a backside and a castle with a slated roof, three and a half stories high worth twenty-one pounds. By February 1657 it took was taken out of his ownership, now held by William Woodward.

Woodward eventually sold it to another solider, John Morgan of Kilcolgan, a native of Wales and like him one of the English Commonwealth garrison. By 1686 Morgan had leased it out to be used as the county jail and it continued to be used as such in ever decreasing circumstances and featuring an embarrassing number of escapes until a new jail was opened in 1811. From that time onwards Blake’s Castle became the site of a corn store, surrounded by a mill and distillery while a fish market was held on the open ground between it and the Spanish Arch. Like many surrounding buildings by the mid-1900s it was seriously derelict and due for demolition; luckily, the surviving façade was preserved, restored, and incorporated into the front of Jury’s Hotel upon its opening in early 1992. It remains one of the few buildings in the town whose ownership can be almost perfectly traced from the time it was constructed into the present day.

title: Sir Richard Blake’s mansion
summary: Richard Blake was born in 1595 to Robert Blake of Ardfry and Katherine Darcy of Gorteen, whose father Richard seems to have been a brother or cousin of James Riabhach Darcy.
heading: Blake: Sir Richard Blake’S Mansion, Bridge Street.
paras: Richard Blake was born in 1595 to Robert Blake of Ardfry and Katherine Darcy of Gorteen, whose father Richard seems to have been a brother or cousin of James Riabhach Darcy.

His father Robert fitz Walter in May 1612 purchased the estate of Wallscourt near Kilreekil in east Galway and Ardfry on the coast of inner Galway Bay, plus lands in County Mayo. His great-grandfather Andrew was a son of John Blake fitz William, the first Blake Mayor of Galway in 1488 and probable builder of Blake’s Castle at the bottom of Quay Street.

Blake went to London in 1612 to study law but upon his father’s death in 1615 returned to manage their properties. Lord Deputy Falkland knighted him in 1624 while in 1627 he was elected Mayor of Galway with sheriffs Edmond Kirwan and Nicholas Blake. He and Sir Henry Lynch were agents for the 4th Earl of Clanricarde. Besides being the leading Catholic noble in Connacht who sponsored the careers of several young lawyers, Clanricarde spent much time at the king’s court in England speaking for Connacht affairs. This because increasingly necessary when in the 1630s the English made plans for a Plantation of Connacht, which in turn led to younger men like Blake in the Clanricard group to become politically active.

Blake was elected to the Irish Parliament in 1640 as MP for County Galway and in June was among those who drew up articles of impeachment against the lord chancellor, the lord chief justice, the bishop of Derry plus the unscrupulous deputy governor of Ireland. All of them were New English Protestants who were actively seeking to undermine titles to properties held by the Gaelic Irish and Anglo Irish, who as Catholics were disfavoured by the king and his administration in Ireland.

The catastrophic winters and summer weather from 1636 onwards led to famine conditions across Ireland and fed into the great anger felt by the population at the appropriation of properties and incomes by the New English. This in turn caused the rebellion in October-November 1641 which spread from Ulster and Dublin across all Ireland.

Blake plus his associates Patrick Darcy and Roebuck Lynch were in Galway town when it went into open rebellion against the English Parliament in March 1642 under Mayor Walter Lynch and present when rebel Richard Martin fitz Oliver was elected Mayor in August 1642. Nevertheless was for a long time slow to commit to any side; but by 1646 he was serving on the Connacht provincial council of the Irish Catholic Confederation, the first independent Irish state.
In those years Ireland was riven with distinct armies whose leaders had very different agendas. The Confederation featured the bulk of the Catholic
population, both Gaeil and Gaill. Their capital was Kilkenny and controlled most of Ireland.

The royalists were led by the Duke of Ormonde mainly based around Dublin whose forces were Irish Catholics and Protestants loyal to King Charles I. In east Ulster were the Scottish Covenanters who fought with the Scots colonists in east Ulster. In west Ulster was the Laggan Army, virulently antiCatholic Scots Presbyterians. Under Lord Inchiquin in Cork was army made up of English and Irish Protestants. In 1644 the English Parliamentarian Army seized Cork, then Dublin in 1646, before being massively reinforced by the English Commonwealth army in August 1649 under Oliver Cromwell. In addition to all these, there were numerous bands of toraidhe (‘Tory’) raiding across the country. They did not always belong to any ethnic, political or religious faction but were purely thieves making use of the breakdown of law and order.

Unfortunately for the Confederation it was riven by factions; hardliners were utterly opposed to making any strategic peace or alliances with any of the other armies and wanted the total expulsion of all colonists from Britain, be they Scots, Welsh or English, with total return of their confiscated lands. The more moderate faction among the Confederates were more pragmatic because they understood how difficult this would be to achieve and were prepared to make truces and treaties in order to use their resources for what goals they could achieve in the present.

The hardliners were supported by papal nuncio Rinuccini who used his religious authority to damn men like Blake who were attempting to reach settlements with the Royalists. Blake was authorised by the Supreme Council of the Confederation to go to Spain seeking their help but remained in Ireland because the Spanish were bankrupt and in the middle of their own rebellions. When a pragmatic truce was made with the Protestant army of Lord Inchiquin, it caused a Confederation civil war and one of the targets condemned by the zealous Rinuccini was Sir Richard Blake, who was by then Speaker for the Irish Confederation. Rinuccini attempted to hold a synod in Galway but was prevented by Blake.

In September 1648 the Confederation held what was to be its last general assembly and as its chairman, Sir Richard Blake was among those who successfully negotiated a peace treaty with the Duke of Ormond, which brought an end to their internal civil war in January 1649.

Blake afterwards returned to Galway and was present in the town in August 1649 when a ship from Spain arrived, carrying people infected with the bubonic plague. The first house which succumbed to it was Blake’s Bridge Street mansion which was seen by some as the vengeance of God upon him
because of his opposition to Rinuccini. Over the next nine months it killed over three thousand seven hundred people.

Sir Richard Blake survived as did his wife Gylle Kirwan and children Robert, Andrew, Peter, Bridget, Christine, Catharine and Margaret. By the time it ended the English Commonwealth army was conquering all before it, with Galway left as the last town representing independent Ireland. In April 1652 after a nine-month siege the town was seized by a garrison of English Commonwealth soldiers and all of his property was taken by them; in lieu of it Blake accepted an estate in Loughrea. He hoped to be restored to his lands when Charles II became king in 1660 but this had not occurred by the time of his death in June 1663. His eldest son, Robert, finally regained the lands in 1681. His descendants include the Barons Wallscourt of Ardfry near Oranmore.

title: The Blakes at Woodquay
summary: Sometime in the 16th century a castle was built on the east bank of the Gaillimhe upstream from Galway town at Mionlach in Castlegar parish.
heading: Blake: Woodquay.
paras: Sometime in the 16th century a castle was built on the east bank of the Gaillimhe upstream from Galway town at Mionlach in Castlegar parish. Almost nothing is known of its early history save that it was owned by Patrick Coleman in 1574 and that it was among castles built on either side of the river during those generations – Tír Oiléan, Newcastle and Dangan. Given that Menlo Castle is little more than a mile upstream from the town, Coleman must have travelled to it from Woodquay in the town suburbs.

The Uí Cholmáin lived in the town since at least the 1490s. The will of Valentine Blake was made 12 July 1499 and he bequested “To the two daugthers of Tomás Ó Colmáin a cask of wine.” Aodh Ó Colmáin alias Odo Coleman was recorded living in a house in the town during 1503-06, possibly as a Wadenship tenant.

A later Thomas Coleman was notary for Galway Corporation in 1558, recorded as living in the town in April 1570 and owned of Menlo Castle in 1574 He was one of a number of men listed as occupying and owning castles in the area that year - Dominick Lynch held Tír Oileáin, Roland Skerrett held Short Castle alias Castlegar, Carrowbrowne was held by DonálÓge Ó hAllmhuráin, plus Newcastle by Marcus Lynch. On Michaelmas Day 29 September 1589 Edmond Colman was allowed by town statute “from thenceforth and for ever afterwards to have the calling of bailiff.”

Notary was a person enabled to act on behalf of others in legal matters and Coleman was used as such by the Corporation, denoting his importance. Where he trained is unknown, but his education was likely paid for by his family which in turned enabled him to purchase land and build a castle.

Sometime during 1591-92 “the castle of Menlo was demolished for hindering of boats to come into town.” Presumably this was while the Colmans owned it. Sometime between then and the 1620s they sold Menlo to Valentine Blake who was very active in the wine trade with Spain and Portugal during the late 16th century, so much so that he was described in 1592 as the richest man in Galway. While he inherited land and property from his father Walter Blake and mother Julia Browne son of James, he used his profits from the wine trade to buy lands throughout the county and Menlo was one such purchase. Elected a Member of the Irish Parliament in 1613, to mark his rise into the upper ranks of society in 1622 Valentine Blake bought a baronetcy from King James VI and I. The king only did so to gentlemen who had a minimum income of one thousand pounds a year. King James allowed at least two hundred men across the three kingdoms to purchase baronetcies during his reign because he was short of cash and did not want to ask three parliaments for financial aid. So naturally, wealthy men like Valentine Blake were allowed to purchase ranks of nobility in exchange for payments to the king.

But a feature of the widening break between Anglo-Irish and New English was their differing Christian denominations. Blake refused to swear the Oath of Supremacy to King James when elected Mayor of Galway in 1611 and went on Catholic pilgrimage to Loretto and Rome during 1616. On his return he paid for the building of the Chap of Saint Mary of Loretto. It was in this chapel he was buried after his death on 2 January 1635. If he died at Menlo then his body would have been conveyed into Galway down river to Woodquay, then across Horse Island to Saint Francis’s Island and the abbey.
His younger brother was the infamous James ‘Spanish’ Blake, a merchant and double agent.

Sir Valentine was succeeded by his son, Sir Thomas, who had served under his father as bailiff of Galway in 1611-12, became MP for Galway town in 163435 and was Mayor during 1637-38. Blake was among those who led the town into rebellion against the English parliament in 1642 only to be killed by an exploding cannon he was inspecting upon the town wall. He was succeeded by his son, Sir Valentine, who was active with the Irish Catholic Confederation and served on the Connacht Council in 1647, in what was up to then first independent Irish state. The Confederation began to collapse with the invasion of the English Commonwealth under Cromwell in August 1649; even so, Galway town held out until April 1652 when after a nine-month siege, Sir Valentine was one of the few Galwegians to sign the Articles of Surrender. He seems to have died later that year and was buried with his father in the Franciscan. That decade all Blake lands and properties were confiscated by the Commonwealth, though after the 1660 Restoration.

Sir Valentine Blake was the 12th baronet, born in 1780 and elected MP for Galway in 1813. He was a supporter of Catholic Emancipation plus fully opening the electoral franchise to Catholics of all classes. He lost his seat in 1820 and after failing to win it in 1830 and 1838, was elected as a MP who supported dismantling the 1801 Union between Ireland and Britain. He remained MP until his death in 1847.

Sunday Boy Blake was the nickname of Sir Valentine Blake, who was fortyone when he succeeded his father Sir John in 1875. By then his finances were at the point where he could not appear in the town in case he would be arrested by bailiffs for his many outstanding debts.

But such writs could not be served on Sundays, so on the seventh day of each week Sir Valentine would leave Menlo Castle by boat from its dock and travel a mile downriver to Woodquay to spend time in the town. But he always made sure to return to Woodquay before midnight to return to the legal safety of Menlo Castle.

Known to his tenants as Sor Váidín a Blác, he once spat on an elderly tenant who could not, or would not, pay rent. The tenant’s son was Tomáisín Laighléis and was so angered at his father’s treatment that he punched Sir Valentine to the ground. The RIC were called and Sir Valentine told the constables he would not purse the matter if Tomáisín came to Menlo and apologised on his knees. “Tomáisín refused, saying that he would rather go to prison until he was carried out in a wooden box.” Lawless was not jailed and Blake was not prosecuted, mainly because Blake was supposed to be too ashamed to go to court and admit his shameful deed.

On 26 July 1910 Menlo Castle caught fire, plainly visible from Woodquay. James Kirwan the coachman escaped by claiming down the ivy. From the ground he saw servants Delia Early and Anne Browne trapped on the roof. Browne plus two locals named Ward and Faherty placed bundles of hay on the ground and implored the women to jump. It was forty feet from the roof to the ground and twenty-five-year-old Delia Early from Parkaveara jumped badly, landing on her head and was killed instantly. Anne Browne landed on her feet and was severely injured but alive and survived.

Unable to escape was Miss Ellen Blake, an invalid. No trace of her body was ever found so when the family returned from Dublin, the ashes of the house was gathered and buried nearby under a cross dedicated to her. The fire marked the end of the Blake’s habitation at Menlo and 1923 the estate was broken up by the Land Commission.

title: Saint Augustine’s Church
summary: At the bottom of Buttermilk Lane in Middle Street was built in 1750 the first dedicated Catholic place of worship since 1691.
heading: Blake: Saint Augustine’S Church, Middle Street.
paras: At the bottom of Buttermilk Lane in Middle Street was built in 1750 the first dedicated Catholic place of worship since 1691.

Before he became Archbishop of Armagh, Anthony Blake was Warden of Galway from 1742 to 1756, years during which official persecution under the Penal Laws had formally lapsed but were personally renewed by Stratford Eyre, Governor of Galway.

“Blake’s most notable contribution to the Catholics of Galway was the erection of a new Parish Chapel in Middle Street”, noted by Eyre as being built 12 May 1750. Since Warden Bodkin had surrendered the key of Saint Nicholas’s Collegiate Church on 28 July 1691, the majority population had no dedicate place of worship. “This was the only parochial Chapel in the town till it was taken down in 1833 and another built upon the site by Dr. Browne, the first bishop of Galway.”

Anthony was the second member of his family to be Warden. His grx5 granduncle, Patrick Blake, was Warden 1542-53. Patrick’s nephew, Richard fitz John fitz Walter, had a grandson, alderman Andrew fitz Patrick fitz Richard, who was granted Ballyglass in Clanmorris barony, County Mayo, and the family settled at Dunmacrina in that county.
Anthony had siblings Walter, Valentine, Sybil, Magdalen Murphy, Mrs James Browne and Mrs. Thomas Lynch.

The first archbishop of Armagh from ‘County Galway’ since 1180, Blake was nominated by the King over the Water, King James VIII and III. This indicates that he did favour any concessions to the House of Hanover yet during those years repressive measures on Catholics were informally relaxed. This allowed Archbishop Blake to begin much-needed reforms in his diocese and Ireland as a whole, something even his immediate predecessor was unable to do due to persecution and Penal Laws. So administration, liturgy, statues, jurisdiction and the building of mass houses alias chapels in every parish was undertaken. These had by 1769 irritated then outraged some of his parish priests, who complained to Rome, saying that Blake spent only one month each year in the diocese. However, evidence from the poems and songs of Art Mac Cubhthaighagus Peadar Ó Doirnín indicates that certain priests were really angry at the effect Blake’s reforms were having on their lifestyles. Ó Doirnín once acted as spokesman for the parishioners of Creggan to Archbishop Blake, who reduced the revenue of Creggan’s priest back to the customary standard.
Then from 1772 other matters led to Blake’s suspension in 1778, a troubled reinstatement.

title: Bodkin’s Lane
summary: This ran from Lombard Street through what is now Saint Patrick’s School on Mainguard and Lombard Streets.
heading: Bodkin: Bodkin’S Lane.
paras: This ran from Lombard Street through what is now Saint Patrick’s School on Mainguard and Lombard Streets. It was called after a family who originated in Athenry who migrated into Galway during the late 1400s. John Bodkin was one of the two town Bailiffs during 1499-1500 and was elected Mayor in August 1518, serving from September 1518 to September 1519with bailiffs Dominick Deane and Martin Lynch fitz James.

He is associated with an infamous town statute made while he was Mayor. Neither Ó nor Mac shall strutt nor swagger through the streets of Galway. So says the popular saying and like most popular beliefs, entirely wrong. Among the statutes passed during his Mayoralty, one stated: “That no man of this town shall host or receive into their houses at Christmas, Easter nor no feast else, any of the Burkes, Mhic Uilliam, Uí Chellaig, nor no sept else, without license of the Mayor and Council, on pain to forfeit five pounds.” It was James Hardiman who in 1820 appended the notorious saying to the statute So contrary to popular belief Irish people were not excluded from Galway. Mayor Bodkin’s statute allowed them in by license.

What the statute really concerned was behaviour. The ClannRiocaird and Mhic Uilliam a Burca plus the Uí Chellaig and several other lineages were powerful and bellicose finte led by warlords who tried to impose their will upon the Galwegians through aggression. There were good reasons for them to build the town walls and maintain them. As recently as 1504 the town was occupied by the ClannRiocaird and only freed by their defeat that August at the battle of Knockdoe by the Earl of Kildare.
Notably, both the Burkes and Fitzgeralds were Gaill or Anglo-Irish, like most of the leading merchant families of the town.
The statute was not anti-Gaelic. Townspeople not survive without civil interactions with local Gaeil lineages such as the Uí hAllmhuáin, Uí

Flaithbertaigh, Uí hEidhinagus Uí Shaughnasaig, so they made efforts to keep good relations with them. And several Gaeil families lived in the town. Colmans, Darcys, Fallons, Kirwans, Nolans, Quins and Tierneys plus dozens of others are recorded in the same classes and castes as the Tribes. All concerned were Gaeilgeoirí, as demonstrated by town records and the fact that Mayor Bodkin’s pedigree was preserved as Gaeilge in LeabharnanGenealach. James Hardiman invented the tradition. Like other fictions it gained great popularity and continues to distort how people think about medieval Galway and its merchant families.
John Bodkin died in 1523, survived by at least six children. One of whom was Christopher, who became Archbishop of Tuam.

Bodkin: Saint Augustine, Abbeygate and Middles Streets plus Eyre Square: While the fictitious execution of a Lynch by his father is commemorated by the so-called ‘Lynch window’ on Lombard Street, actual connections to genuine murders of the Bodkin family lies at the end of that street. On a fireplace in the upper floor of what was until recent years Cooke’s Restaurant in Upper Abbeygate Street are arms of the French and Bodkin families, dated 1648. Living on Abbeygate Street in November 1724 was Widow Bodkin and Nich. Bodkin.

The latter, merchant Nicholas Bodkin of Galway, witnessed a lease and release deed made 22 March 1725 and one of the parties was John Bodkin esquire of Carrabeg. Carrowbeg House is in Belclare near Tuam and Bodkin was a counsellor-at-law, married to Mary Clarke and were parents of Dominick and John. Their townhouse was noted in 1820 by James Hardiman: Bodkin of Carrowbeg mansion in Backstreet, opposite Whitehall and that of another branch of the same name opposite the old Augustinian convent. Backstreet is now Saint Augustine Street so their mansion must have been one of the two large houses at the top of the street facing Whitehall, which is now the back entrance to the Eyre Square Shopping Centre.
The mansion of “another branch … opposite the old Augustinian convent” was in Middle Street. This must be the large building west of Buttermilk Lane or on the east side, now Anthony Ryans.

Councillor Bodkin’s brothers were Oliver and Dominick Dáll. Oliver and his family lived in Carrowbeg while Councillor John mostly lived in Dublin and Galway for his law work, only residing at Carrowbeg for a few weeks a year. In 1737 while on a visit, Councillor John’s son Dominick was found to have died in his sleep.

Councillor Bodkin’s brother Dominick Dáll was so-called because he was blind in one eye. He was also facially scarred by smallpox and had an unsavoury reputation which caused him to be ostracised by his brothers. Concurrently, his nephew John fitz Oliver became estranged from his father and fell in with his heavy-drinking uncle. The two came up with a plan to kill Oliver, his second wife Margery Lycnh and their son Oliver Óge in order for John fitz Oliver to inherit the property from which he had been disinherited. Thus on the evening of 18 September 1741 the two Bodkins and a herd called John Hogan went to Carrowbeg House. They first killed the family dogs lest they bark and wake the household. They murdered the servants sleeping in the outhouse and one sleeping in the hallway. In the guest room they found an unexpected visitor, Marcus Lynch, whom they also murdered. They then murdered Oliver, Margery, and Oliver Óge. Ten to eleven people were murdered that night.

Francis Bermingham (Lord Athenry) was summoned to the house the following day and led the hunt for the murderers, all of whom were soon captured. As custom was to execute murderers near the scene of the crime, they were brought to Belclare crossroads and hung from a tree; Dominick Dáll and John fitz Oliver were gibbetted after death while Hogan’s head was placed on a spike on top of Tuam market house.

Just before they were hanged each made a statement and John fitz Oliver stated that his first cousin John fitz John had murdered his older brother in his sleep by suffocating him at Carrowbeg in 1737. Shocked, John fled the scene on his horse but was apprehended and tried. At the gallows in Galway’s Eyre Sqaure on 20 March 1742 he refused to confirm either his guilt or innocence “and would make no other answer, but forgave Mankind; upon which he was thrown off and in 3 minutes cut down alive, his Privy Parts cut out, and his Bowels taken from him and his Head severed from his body.”

The old Bodkin home in Abbeygate Street still contains the 1648 Bodkin arms while the body of John son of Councillor John Bodkin was possibly among the bodies excavated near the site of the gallows in Eyre Square in the early 2000s. Thomas Bodkin inherited the Carrowbeg estate and was member of Galway’s common council in January 1764. His son and heir was Hyacinth Bodkin. By the early 1820s the estate had passed to the Bodkins of Castletown and Lynches of Shannonbridge.

title: The Bodkins at Saint Nicholas’s
summary: John Bodkin was Catholic Warden of Galway during the War of the Two Kings, retaking Saint Nicholas’s Collegiate church from the Church of Ireland in 1688.
heading: Bodkin: Saint Nicholas’S Collegiate Church.
paras: John Bodkin was Catholic Warden of Galway during the War of the Two Kings, retaking Saint Nicholas’s Collegiate church from the Church of Ireland in 1688. His name appears in the parish register of baptisms during 1690. War in Connacht ended at Aughrim on 12 July 1691 and on 26 July, the troops of Queen Mary II and King William III of Orange entered Galway town led by General Godert de Ginkill. Naturally this meant that Saint Nicolas’s would revert to the Church of Ireland.
Warden Bodkin handed over the keys in great despair, exclaiming: “My God! That my right hand may not decay until the key of this church be restored to its proper owners.”

While Warden John Bodkin is said to have died in 1710, the parish register for the year 1723-26 record baptisms carried out by Father John Bodkin. And at the back of the Despite the denominational change, Protestants allowed certain Catholics to be buried in Saint Nicholas’s after 1691 into the mid-1800s and among them was Warden John Bodkin, interred in a vault near the main altar. This was despite the Penal Laws, and despite the fact that Protestants were under no obligation to oblige Catholics.

During March 1838 repairs within the church were made under the supervision of Mr. Clare and uncovering the vault they found a near-perfectly preserved body, which was determined to be Warden John Bodkin. Like the rest of his body, his right arm was intact.

This seemingly miracle greatly excited the general population, thousands of whom believed that it signified the return of the church to Catholics and for three days came into Saint Nicholas’s to view his body, most particularly descendants of the Tribes. Due to their number Henry Clare was obliged to stop work, clear the church and lock it up with sexton Henry Caddy. Clare went home and got a good night’s sleep only to be woken in the darkness early the next morning by carpenter John McMahon and was told that during the night someone had entered the church and desecrated Warden Bodkin’s body by taking off his undecayed right arm.

Clare, McMahon and other workmen questioned sexton Henry Caddy as he was the only one who had the key enter and exit the church. Caddy denied doing any such thing. He continued to deny this as Henry Clare and the workmen dragged him down the street towards O’Brien’s Bridge, intending to throw him over it unless he told them what occurred. Possibly not a strong swimmer, Caddy admitted he gave the key to Timothy Murry, who on interview by Mr. Clare said he had it but would only give it to Reverend Roch, his parish priest.

While all this was ongoing, so too were rumours which caused large crowds to gather outside the church. Matters were tense and could have turned ugly but Reverend Roch directed them to disperse and return in the afternoon, which they did in hundreds if not thousands. At four pm Reverend Roch arrived with Warden Bodkin’s arm, minus the fingers which someone (presumably McMahon) had cut off.

The excitement was ended by Henry Clare who with a carpenter made a coffin and put the late Warden’s body, plus his right arm. He stated “Mamy persons there stated it was the fourth time that a coffin had been worn out by the remains. I then closed the coffin and vault in such a way that there can be no access to it except by ripping up the floor.”
And there he lies to this day while Church of Ireland ceremonies continue, untroubled by whatever condition his hand is currently in.

title: Prospect Hill and Eyre Square
summary: By the late 1800sthere were few Bodkins in Galway town. In Nun’s Island was labourer John Bodkin and his wives May Fallon and Louisa Burke while out in Oranmore was butcher Andrew Bodkin and his wife Mary Freney.
heading: Bodkin: Prospect Hill-Eyre Square.
paras: By the late 1800sthere were few Bodkins in Galway town. In Nun’s Island was labourer John Bodkin and his wives May Fallon and Louisa Burke while out in Oranmore was butcher Andrew Bodkin and his wife Mary Freney. Living in house 1 Prospect Hill on the night of 31 March 1901 was fiftyseven-year-old provision dealer Patrick Louis Bodkin and his forty-six-year-old wife, Winifred. Both were born in Galway town, spoke Irish and English, and were Catholic. Living with them was their eighteen-year-old son Leo Bodkin, a scholar, plus domestic servant Katie Joyce. On the 1911 census form Winifred stated she and Patrick were married thirty-five years and had four children, only one alive. This was twenty-nine-year-old Leo who was a law student living at 35 Saint Peter’s Road in Phibsborough, Dublin.

They were married in Dublin’s Marlboro Street cathedral on 29 March 1876. Patrick gave his address as Quay Street in Galway and his father as corn dealer Patrick Bodkin. Winifred was recorded as Minnie Pattie, daughter of mason Michael Pattie of Eyre Street in Galway. Father Bernard Farrell married them, their witnesses Timothy Dempsey and Helena Colclough, an in-law or cousin of Winifred. Why they were married in Dublin rather than Galway is uncertain.

Her father, Michael, died 18 April 1879 aged sixty-three; her likely grandfather, James, was ninety when he died in Galway during 1869. Later generations of the Paths are buried in Bohermore Cemetery.
Civil registers show that at Prospect Hill on 19 April 1882 Patrick Leo Bodkin was born to Winefred Path and shopkeeper Patrick Bodkin. On 9 April 1884

was born Mary Ellen Bodkin. Another was Michael (nicknamed Sonny), who died at their home aged nineteen on 7 February 1900. An unmarried clerk working for the local gas company, he died from some form of heart disease and would be unremarked save for a relationship he had in the final months of his life with another local, Nora Barnacle.

Nora’s mother was one of the Healy’s of 24 Upper Abbeygate Street West. Above the doorway is a cross date 1816 with the name John Healy. What little can now be said of Michael and Nora is due to the efforts of an tAthair Pádraig Ó Laoi, who investigated the matter when some of their contemporaries were still alive. Nora was fifteen and Michael was eighteen when they met, so met about 1898-99. Ó Laoí stated Nora was impressed by Michael’s “gentility and manliness” and visited the family sweetshop to “throw eyes” at Michael, chatting and flirting. According to Nora’s friend Mary O’Holleran Morris, Nora fell deeply in love with Michael. He was black-haired. Nora was auburn-haired. He gave her a present of a bracelet. She gave him her love. But whatever might have come to pass ended when Michael took ill and was confined to bed in the months before his death. Nora had already lost one boyfriend to premature death, Michael Feeney, and while tragic, it was a series of events both unfortunate and common.

None of this would matter any more than most teenage romances but for Nora meeting and being attracted to a man who resembled Michael Bodkin. On Dublin’s Nassau Street on 10 June 1904 she met James Joyce, and for the rest of her life and afterlife was defined by him.

Joyce fused Michael Feeney and Michael Bodkin into the lost love of the protagonist of his finest short story, The Dead. This fiction overpowered the boys on whom it is based, long since less than ghosts.

Winifred Path died 18 February 1915 aged sixty-five. Her husband Patrick Bodkin died 11 June 1928 aged eighty-five. Both were buried in Rahoon New Cemetery in an impressive above-ground vault. Its initial inscription reads: “Erected by Patrick L. and Winifred Bodkin in loving memory of their dearly beloved son Michael Maria who died on the 11th February 1900 aged 20 years. Lord Jesus deliver him. Comfortess of the afflicted intercede for him.” The Bodkin home and shop was sold and became John O’Loughlin’s drapery business, which he closed in July 1994 and is now part of Richardson’s Pub on the corner of Prospect Hill and Eyre Square. It is just yards from the Liam Mellows statue which stands on the site of the town gallows and where John fitz John Bodkin was executed on 20 March 1742. In January 2024 a plaque concerning Bodkin and The Dead was unveiled by President Higgins beside the family vault in Rahoon. Present was Michael Bodkin’s grandniece, Mrs. Mary O’Connor and her family.

title: The Browne Doorway
summary: Dominick Browne fitz William had been the first generation of his family to settle in the town.
heading: Browne: Browne Doorway, Eyre Square.
paras: Dominick Browne fitz William had been the first generation of his family to settle in the town. Up to then residing in and around Athenry for centuries, he plus his brothers Andrew, Nicholas, Robert and Richard became freemen in Galway between 1539 and 1542, their migration likely caused by the warfare then occurring around Athenry between the Berminghams and the Burkes, a fight the Berminghams would lose.
