Dominick worked well enough as a merchant to buy property within Galway as well as outside of it – a townland north of the town he bought was renamed Ceathrú an Bhrúnaigh, modern Carrowbrowne.

He had a house at Barna, suggesting much of his trade was carried on in Iar Connacht. Greatly helping to facilitate this was a canny marriage he made with Onóra Ní Fhlaithbhertaigh, a daughter of the ruler of Iar Connacht, Conamara agusnaOiléanÁrainn, Sior MurchadnadTuadh Ó Flaithbertaigh.

Dominick died in 1596. He and Onóra had eleven known children and among the eldest was Oliver, a town bailiff in 1583-84. In August 1609 Oliver was elected Mayor but denied from serving in September because he refused to take the Oath of Supremacy to King James as head of the church. Thomas Browne, who was possibly his son, was elected in Oliver’s place only for him too to refuse to swear and be fined one hundred pounds.
Among Oliver’s children were two sons, Andrew of Gloves and Martin. It was his second son Martin who was responsible for erecting the Browne Doorway during 1627.

The street was then called Skinners Street or Glovers Street, names which denoted it was called after men who skinned small animals and made gloves. Browne must have dealt in considerably more lucrative matters because the house he built, or at least remodelled, stretched down half his side of the street, had a four-bay front with a central doorway with a ground floor and two stories. It was backed by a smaller one storey house and possessed a courtyard.
It remains unclear if Browne inherited or purchased the house. Its great size and ostentation in his latter years suggest he at least heavily remodelled it
in an open display of his great wealth. Given his lack of profile in corporation records he must have been almost exclusively a merchant and his mansion shows that he was extremely good at it.

The doorway erected in 1627 by Martin Browne and Maria Lynch was broadly similar to the doorway Martin Darcy and Christine Martin made in 1624. But where the Darcys had their arms on either side of the door and a balcony above it, the Brownes went one better by having a six-bay oriel window (three on top, three on bottom) with two more on each side, projecting from the façade of the Mansion. This allowed the viewer to look out on the street as well as north and south without sticking their head out the window. And like a similar window over the doorway of Sir Peter French’s Mansion on Market Street, windows in the Browne Doorway were of glass. In another display of his family’s Catholicism, Browne had a biblical quote on the keystone of the doorway: ‘Unless our Lord build the house, they have laboured in vain that build it’. And like a number of buildings in the town during those years the doorway displaces the Christogram IHS, the first three letters of the name Jesus in Greek. This religious symbol was already by then becoming a political symbol for Irish Catholics.

Martin Browne died around 1637 and survived by his eldest son Oliver. He was among the many who refused to sign the Articles of Surrender of the town in April 1652. All his properties both in the town and county were confiscated by the English Commonwealth during the 1650s but in 1677 he was regranted lands in the county in Dunmore and Athenry baronies. He settled on his former estate at Coolarne, several miles north of Athenry, and died in 1696. He and his wife Julian Lynch, who died in 1718, were buried in a tomb he erected for them in the ruined Dominican Priory of Athenry. descendants lived in Coloarne and nearby Kilskeagh into the 1800s. Their mansion does not seem to have been among the properties returned to the Brownes yet in November 1724 Brownes were still living on Abbeygate Street - merchant Bartholomew Brown, James Brown and another James Brown. Nevertheless over the next hundred years it became severe dilapidated because photographs taken in the 1860s show the Browne Mansion was an utter ruin with only the outer walls and some interior ones standing.

By the early 1900s only the outer walls it was in a severely derelict state so eventually in 1905 the Urban District Council, with funding from the Galway Archaeological and Historical Society, moved the doorway and oriel window to Eyre Square. There it formed the entrance to the park, which at the time was enclosed by railings. With these and the presence of several trees along the
park boundary, the area looked quite elegant and the doorway fitted in perfectly.

In the 1960s the park was redesigned and the railings removed to around Saint Nicholas’s Church. This, plus the removal of several trees, left the Browne Doorway as a free-standing entity, alone and odd-looking. On top of that it was by then beginning to suffer from weathering which had by the end of the century significantly degraded it as a structure and its insignia. Eventually after decades of complaints it was in 2012 enclosed in protective plexiglass and provided with an explanatory plaque, unveiled by Mayor Terry O’Flaherty on 15 September that year. Even so its condition has not improved, leading to calls since then to remove it to an indoor location and prevent further deterioration.

title: Upper Abbeygate Street and Bodkin’s Lane
summary: In July 1663 at the Court of Claims in Dublin appeared “Francis Browne, late of Galway, gentleman” to claim nine properties he had held and six other he claimed through mortgages, all of which had bee…
heading: Browne: Upper Abbeygate East And Bodkin’S Lane.
paras: In July 1663 at the Court of Claims in Dublin appeared “Francis Browne, late of Galway, gentleman” to claim nine properties he had held and six other he claimed through mortgages, all of which had been seized during the 1650s by the English Commonwealth in Ireland.

Browne identified himself as the eldest son and heir of “Andrew Browne fitz Dominick of Galway, deceased”, who had “being seized of all the rest of the premises long before the war, did in consideration of a marriage portion and for other good considerations dated in annis 1616 and 1619 and 1636 convey all and singular the same premises to his own use for life, and afterwards to the use of the claimant and the heirs male of his body, with several remainders to his younger brothers”.

The first property in Galway town which he identified was a house near that of his grandfather Sir Dominick Browne’s mansion; another was “a long house in Bodkin’s Lane in Galway, containing many dwellings, and one other stone house opposite thereunto”. He also declared an interest in Ballybritt Castle with about twenty acres of land there, now famous as the site of the Galway Races.

The mortgages Browne had were enabled by wealth inherited from his father Andrew, which he had inherited from his father Dominick and which Dominick had inherited from his father, William Browne fitz Stephen of Athenry. Because while the Brownes had lived in Athenry since about the 1280s and possessed some property there, Francis’s grandfather and his
brothers were forced by warfare between the Berminghams and the Burkes to migrate to Galway and start all over again.

Andrew must have inherited some of his father’s business acumen because Francis’s case at Dublin identified certain properties which seem to have been inherited from Andrew. But Francis likewise must have been a good merchant too as made plain by the properties he claimed through mortgage, scattered across County Galway in the baronies of Athenry, Dunkellin, Kiltartan and Tiaquin plus one each in counties Mayo and Clare.

What’s important to remember is that until the late 1500s and early 1600s, almost none of the Galway merchants owned any large landed estates nor were they notable landlords. What they owned was overwhelmingly confined to the twenty-five or so acres within the walls of Galway, generally their family houses plus gardens. Their wealth came through business and trade, not war or theft like lords, earls and kings. And the confines of Galway meant their fortunes accrued rather than being spent. So when the English conquest which began in 1534 finally ended in 1603, they were land poor but cash rich. Landlords out in the county, on the other hand, were land rich but cash poor. So in the first half of the 17th century there was truly enormous numbers of land transactions made, purchases and mortgages, leases and loans. Unfortunately there were other agendas at play, namely the land greed of New English colonists plus the avaricious corruption of the Stuart kings of the three kingdoms, James VI and I and his son Charles I. James disliked having to go to the English parliament for funds, so got around this by refusing to call parliament and indulge in other ways of raising money. He sold knighthoods, baronetcies, lordships, earldoms, and every mark of nobility he could think of or invent to those willing to pay for it. He awarded income monopolies to favourites who would pay him their due. And he planned plantations across Ireland which would pay dividends to loyal subjects from Scotland, England and Wales which would evict hitherto loyal subjects in Ireland. The New English in Ireland were generally younger sons of landed gentry with no inheritances or severely impoverished middle-class men with nothing to lose and everything to gain by brutal means. They were exemplified by the Earl of Cork, Richard Boyle, who arrived in Ireland from his home in Canterbury in June 1588 and by his death in 1643 had through marriage, warfare, land speculation and fraud had been ennobled and gained hundreds of thousands of acres across Munster. Oliver Cromwell later remarked that if there had been a man like Boyle in every Irish province, there would never have been an Irish rebellion in 1641. But this was to grossly misunderstand that it was the avarice of men like Boyle which caused that rebellion. The theft, corruption and what

Irish Catholics saw as blasphemy on the part of the New English were what drove them to rebellion and the creation of the first independent Irish state. Francis Browne was much lower down the social scale from any lord, baronet or even a knight. Even so his court claim showed that three generations worth of hard work, inheritances and business acumen plus a strong dash of gombínism could result in a very enviable property portfolio. And in a reflection of that, plus his lack of involvement in the troublesome politics of the era, the court found that the crown had no claims on his properties. This did not mean nobody else did, and in an Ireland where New English authority was contested but actual, such claims were rarely considered settled. Suffice to say there is no record of Francis Browne regaining all his properties and with the defeat of the Jacobites in 1691, the English ascendancy in Ireland was fully secured.

title: Lower Abbeygate Street
summary: A monumental doorway relocated from Abbeygate Street to the Convent of Mercy in the 1860s memorialises a Gaelic family who moved to Galway and became one of the Tribes merchant families.
heading: Darcy: Lower Abbeygate Street East.
paras: A monumental doorway relocated from Abbeygate Street to the Convent of Mercy in the 1860s memorialises a Gaelic family who moved to Galway and became one of the Tribes merchant families.

During the mid-to-late 1400s the Ó Dorchaidhe family of Cera barony in modern south County Mayo migrated into Galway town, headed by BáitéarRiabhach Ó Dorchaidhe. The Uí Dhorchaidhe were among a number ofGaeil families from that area who settled in the town during those decades such as the Nolans and Tierneys. The town’s increasing prosperity drew them, as did the town’s increasing independence from the Gaeil and Gaill warlords to the west and east of it.

Living in the town since at least the 1300s were the Develin family, who as their surname denoted originated in Dublin. James Develin was Sovereign of Galway for the term 1461-62. At some point in the next five generations a Develin woman married an Ó Dorchaidhe man and when the Develins died out in the male line, the Darcys inherited their property on Lower Abbeygate Street. The antiquarian Ruairí Ó Flaithbertaigh was a descendant of both families and in 1684 wrote that “The Develins’s arms, still extant [in 1684] carved in stone in James Reagh Darcy’s house in Abbeygate Street, is the same with the Dillons’ arms.” These arms feature a cross which divides the arms into four quarters, with a smaller cross within each quarter.

So the Uí Dhorchaidhe inherited the Develin arms and took them as their own because in 1624 they were used by Martin Dorsi with his initials on a doorway he erected on the front of his house on Lower Abbeygate Street East.

On the opposite side of the doorway were the initials and arms of his wife, Christine Martin. The doorway led into a courtyard where a large three storey tower was locate and surrounded on four sides by other buildings, all presumably owned by the Darcys. Behind that again was another mansion, apparently owned by the Brownes. The entire property is clearly visible on the 1662 pictorial map of Galway, with the doorway just visible on the street with its pillars supporting what appear to be a balcony.

Martin Dorsi was a son of James Reagh Dorsey, Martin and his brothers Nicholas, Anthony, James Óge and Andrew were all described as merchants, while the youngest brother, Patrick, was a lawyer and became a noted politician. Their father James Reagh was a great-great-great grandson of BáitéarRiabhach and it was to James Reagh that the family owed its elevation in status, transitioning from Ó Dorchaidhe into Dorsey or Dorsi into Darcy. James became a noted partisan for the English and who profited hugely from helping to advance their governance in Connacht, serving as Vice-President of Connacht during the 1590s while he and the English pacified the province through often extreme violence. He served as Mayor of Galway during 160203, dying in office and buried in the Franciscan graveyard; becoming Mayor made his family one of the Tribes while his rise in status enabled all his sons to achieve greater things than they could otherwise have done.

But their actual roots were well-known in 17th century Galway. During the 1640s the genealogist Dubhaltach Mac Fhirbhisigh of County Sligo lived in the town and obtained a genealogy from the Galwegians themselves (presumably the Darcys) which traced them back to BáitéarRiabhach and further connected them to the Fear Ceara of the Uí Fhiachrach dynasty of northern Connacht. Yet while the family were politically loyal to the crown, they and the rest of the townsfolk began to diverge sharply from the English over the matter of religion. Anti-Catholicism was by then a core part of English identity and so as Protestants, they were always suspicious of even loyal Irish Catholics. During the 1600s this denominational difference slowly drew together the different ethnic groups of the Irish nation in opposition to the English, their colonialist agendas and Protestant denominations.

Among those agendas was the Plantation of Connacht for New English settlers which required the displacement of native landowners. The people of Galway town were foremost in opposing the scheme so when in 1635 Lord Deputy Sir Thomas Wentworth asked a jury headed by Martin Darcy to find the King’s Title for the county, they refused. Furious, Wentworth had the jury imprisoned and abused, which resulted in the death of Darcy in Dublin during June 1636.

Martin Darcy’s descendants purchased an estate in Kilkerrin parish near Tuam called New Forest, living there into the 1950s when the estate was purchased by the Land Commission and the house demolished. The property on Abbeygate Street seems to have been confiscated by officers of the English Commonwealth army who entered Galway in April 1652. By the early 1800s the building seems to have been much dilapidated, leading to Father Peter Daly removing the doorway to his house on Saint Francis’s Street where it remains today.

title: The D’Arcys at Woodquay
summary: While the anti-Treaty IRA destroyed the first four Irish censuses at the Four Courts in June 1922, some fragments survive from the first complete census, taken 28 May 1821.
heading: Darcy: Woodquay.
paras: While the anti-Treaty IRA destroyed the first four Irish censuses at the Four Courts in June 1922, some fragments survive from the first complete census, taken 28 May 1821. On that date at the Woodquay in Galway was recorded seventy-year-old boatman Andrew Darcy, his fifty-five-year-old wife Bridget and their twenty-two-year-old son, Patrick.

Galway had two distinct fishing communities. The most well-known in popular memory was in The Claddagh and their saltwater fishermen worked out in the bay, their ships taking them out to Conamara and the islands, across to County Clare and inner bay destinations like Oranmore, Clarenbridge, Stradbally and Kinvara.

But the freshwater fishermen at the Wood Quay like Andrew Darcy had a narrower remit, their working days on the four miles of the river from to Menlo, or from there out into Lough Corrib, where matters might take them to Moycullen, Oughterard, Corr na Móna, Cong, the lakeside villages west of Headford, from there down to Annaghdown and Menlo before again docking at the Wood Quay.

Salmon and eel fisheries were on the river and town records contain many references to their delivery to the town and the fishermen who caught them. Illustration made in the 16th and 17th centuries show boatmen like Darcy working on fishery weirs, or sailing up and down the river.

Besides these their main tasks, the Wood Quay boatmen took on passengers who found travel by boat generally easier and swifter than roads. Some would be emigrants brought from their home to catch a train to Britain or a ship to America. Others would be migrants travelling from Annaghdown to Moycullen, or Oughterard to Headford; a case can be made that several families who settled in late medieval Galway from south County Mayo may
have made their journeys on the lake and river: Nolans, Tierneys and even the Darcys.

Besides people some of the larger boats could carry animals such as hens, goats and sheep, while the more adventurous would trail cattle, though only for short trips. These would be transported to the Wood Quay and brought into the Claddagh, where the main town fair was held at Fair Hill until the mid1800s. It was on once such voyage that a boat from Annaghdown sank off Menlo in 1828, drowning twenty people.

Nothing else is currently known of Andrew Darcy or his family. By the end of the century his livelihood was becoming obsolete and by the mid-20th century the community of freshwater fishermen at Wood Quay ceased to exist. However, their descendants continue today as members of the nearby Galway Boat Club.

title: Number 3 Eyre Square
summary: In the Galway City Tribune of Friday 15 November 1985 was announced the death of Hyacinth Darcy of McDonagh Avenue in Merve.
heading: Darcy: Number 3 Eyre Square.
paras: In the Galway City Tribune of Friday 15 November 1985 was announced the death of Hyacinth Darcy of McDonagh Avenue in Merve. He was survived by his wife Mary, their sons Michael, Tommy and John in Waterford, daughters Mary, Kathleen and Bridie in the USA and his sister Nancy in England. The Tribune stated that “Hycie, as he was commonly known, was born in 1906 and would have been eighty in a few months’ time. He was reared in Eyre Square where his family had a business. He worked for forty-six years as a bus conductor for CIÉ until he retired in 1971. In that time he became one of the city’s best known conductors and had spent a number of years on the Mervue run. He was also a well known character throughout the city. Mr. Darcy was a founder member of Mervue United Soccer Club in 1960 and had served as Chairman and Treasurer in the clubs early years. He was also a founder of the Mervue Athletic club and served as Treasurer in the early sixties. One of the first residents of Mervue, he organised buses to take people to Mass in in town in the days before the area had either a church or a regular bus service.” In 1901, Hycie’s father Thomas was a forty-year-old publican and confectioner living in house 3 Eyre Square with his thirty-seven-year-old wife, Margaret of County Mayo. Their children were John Joe, aged ten, and Thomas Francis, aged six. Three shop assistants and a domestic servant lived with them. Their premises was quite close to the Bodkin family at 2 Prospect Hill. The couple had married in Saint Nicholas’s Cathedral on Abbeygate Street 1 February 1901. Margaret Keville was a twenty-four-year-old shopkeeper

from Eyre Square and daughter of deceased farmer, James Keville. Thomas was a twenty-four-year-old shopkeeper from Dominick Street and son of living farmer, John Darcy. They were married by Father P. Dooley and witnesses were John Joe O’Connor and Lena Connolly.
But Margaret died from apparent heart failure on 15 June 1902. She was thirty-eight.

Hyacinth was born 14 February 1906 at Eyre Square to Henrietta Conway and confectioner Thomas Darcy. The couple were married at An Spidéal 23 February 1903 by Father McDonnacha, their witnesses J. Thornton and Maggie Kelly. Henrietta was a daughter of shopkeeper Timothy Conway of Spiddal West, Thomas recorded that his father John was still alive. He may be eightyone-year-old married farmer John Darcy of Newtown, Moycullen; he died 29 October 1915 and his informant was his son, Andrew.

Besides Hyacinth, the couple had children Patrick, born 7 March 1905; Anne Josephine, born 9 November 1907. But forty-six-year-old Thomas was found dead in a local canal on 26 April 1908, having drowned. So when the family were recorded by the census in April 1911, Henrietta had remarried to fortytwo-year-old Martin O’Donohoe from County Clare, a publican and grocer. Henrietta was thirty, their family recorded as Mary Agnes Darcy, seven; Patrick Darcy, six; Annie Darcy, three. Living with them was barmaid Annie Kearns. Where Hyacinth was is unknown; the only two men named Hyacinth Darcy were a forty-five-year-old druggist on Berkeley Road in Dublin and eight-one year old gentleman Hyacinth Darcy of Newforest in Kilkerrin, near Tuam. Their forename was very uncommon. The first known Hyacinth Darcy was born during the 1700s in the Kiltullagh family and was a first cousin to Count John Darcy of Paris. Hyacinth married in 1785 and his eldest son, John, founded Clifden around 1815. His son, Reverend Hyacinth Darcy, was born in 1806 and was notable for evangelising hundreds of Catholics into the Protestant denomination; unlike most evangelisers, Reverend Hyacinth Darcy was very popular in the area due to his extraordinary efforts to save people in and around Clifden during an Gorta Mór. Perhaps some memory of that led to Thomas or Henrietta giving the name to their son.

Hycie reappeared on the 1926 census. Martin and Henrietta O’Donohue, aged fifty-seven and forty-six, headed a household at Ropewalk in the Claddagh. Their family were Hyacinth Darcy, stepson, twenty; Martin O’Donohue, son, fourteen; John O’Donohue, son, thirteen; Michael O’Donohue, son, aged eleven; Joseph O’Donohue, son, age ten. Hycie’s siblings John Joe, Thomas, Patrick and Annie were not apparent.
In Saint Joseph’s Church on 6 June 1932 Hyacinth Darcy married Mary Collins of Salthill, a daughter of farmer Michael Collins. By then Hycie was living

on Saint Helen’s Street and working as a bus conductor. The celebrant was Father Peter Davis, witnesses Thomas Collins and Mary Reilly. They had eight children: Michael, Tommy, Mary, Kathleen, Martin, Patrick, John and Bridie; Patrick and Martin died as children. He and his family are buried in Bohermore New Cemetery, a short walk from his original home at 3 Eyre Square.

title: The Deanes of High Street
summary: In August 1667 Captain Lawrence Deane of Galway petitioned King Charles II “for preference of a Dutch caper, which is to be sold, that the king will issue out a commission or order for valuing her; th…
heading: Deane: High Street.
paras: In August 1667 Captain Lawrence Deane of Galway petitioned King Charles II “for preference of a Dutch caper, which is to be sold, that the king will issue out a commission or order for valuing her; the said ship was lately taken by the king’s hip the Forester, commanded by Captain Country, on the coast of Ireland and brought into Galway.”
During the 17th century a fast, lightly-armed ship used by Dutch privateers were called Dutch capers, the later denoting such ships were used for what many perceived as high seas crimes.

On 30 May 1672 the lord lieutenant and council wrote to the earl of Arlington; they have examined the matters about some violences offered to the people of Galway and give an account of these and their petition; relates to the freedoms of the ancient natives, freemen and inhabitants of Galway and gives details about a disturbance during an election there. … One Lawrence Deane (who in the so position, was alleged to have been very much abused by the soldiers) being present at this Board upon ??? ?? having declared before us, During August 1672 statements in the form of affidavits, but unsworn, by Captain William Hamilton and Lawrence Deane of Galway, a merchant; verifying the statements in the petition about the events of 1 August, and adding that that afternoon a great fire was made in the High Street opposite the sheriff’s [John Geery] and John Clerk’s houses, believed to be a sign of joy for the expulsion of the said old natives.

On 12 March 1688 he was included in the Galway Charter of King James VII and II as one of the sixty burgesses for life. Ranked above him were Stephen Deane and Thomas Deane among the twenty-six aldermen for life. No other Deanes were listed. In Lord Bophin’s infantry during the 1688-91 war was Lieutenant Laurence while Dominick Deane of Cong was attained for treason; they must have been of the next generation.

Captain Lawrence Deane was at one stage noted as of Castlemoyle, the house of an estate in Killererin parish near Tuam which was part of the 1500 acres of lands merchant Thomas Deane of Galway was granted in Clare, Dunmore and

Kilmaine baronies in June 1677. Stephen Dean was granted by patent of May 1677 lands in baronies of Loughrea, Moycullen, Athenry and Carra. What survives there the ruins of an 18th century two storey house with five bay windows on the ground floor, home into the 1780s of a Mrs. Deane. By the 1850s it was owned by Edward Blake and afterwards by Sebastian Nolan into the 1880s.

title: The Deanes of Middle Street
summary: Prior to February 1657, Oliver Deane had two houses in Galway town, both worth fourteen pounds and seized by English soldiers John Peters and John Bingham.
heading: Deane: Middle Street.
paras: Prior to February 1657, Oliver Deane had two houses in Galway town, both worth fourteen pounds and seized by English soldiers John Peters and John Bingham. It was somewhere in the High Street-Middle Street area so there may have been others unaccounted.

One set of Deane properties were outlined at Dublin in the Court of Claims during 1662. Patrick Blake and his wife Christian were acting on behalf of her son John Deane fitz Richard who claimed one stone house in Galway town “and the several parcels of land of Gortigany, Killogenmallow, Killogecoshawe and all the houses and tenements built thereupon; a parcel of land and a plot for a house, sometime in the occupation of one Teige McJury; the parcels of land of drumblakes and Gortincarra, all situate within the francihes of Galway.” Unusually for most Galwegians, John also claimed “one house, garden or park containing one acre of land in Rathcoole, County Dublin, and three houses and twenty-three acres of land in Tassagart County Dublin; the remainder of a term of years yet to come and unexpired in two houses in Cooke Street, and two houses in Bridge Street.”

Two years after become King of the Three Kingdoms, Charles II issued The Act of Settlement to settle the conflicting claims from the seizure of lands across Ireland by the republican English Commonwealth during the 1650s. He had to balance the claims of his supporters who had lost lands fighting on his behalf against the soldiers who now owned them but helped bring him back to power in 1660. And of course the many innocent people who played little to no part in the conflicts but suffered anyway.

The Deanes were neither among the most wealthy nor most well-known of the merchant families yet unlike many in such families had managed to gain land in the capital. The Blakes explained that the Dublin properties were gained by Richard Deane’s only brother, Nicholas, who evidently migrated to

Dublin and did quite well for himself as a merchant. Nicholas died about 1648 without issue so his estates devolved upon Richard, who was in full ownership of them when he died in 1660, meaning John Deane “as son and heir and administrator of the said Richard”, was the legal owner.

The court concluded the properties both in Galway and in Dublin were not subject to royal seizure nor Church of Ireland control, so formally John Deane’s title to them was clear. However, such cases rarely ended happily ever after. Having put so much effort into entrenching themselves, the New English were determined to protect their ascendancy and as events proved, they did. What became of John Deane is unknown. It is just possible that he was the John Dean of Dublin who on 17 July 1727 took out a Protestant certificate. Most Catholics did so to ensure they were in full legal compliance with the authorities and prevent any further losses. One way or another, the house always wins.

title: The Fonts of Abbeygate Street
summary: In the 1660s when the concept of ‘the Tribes of Galway’ began, its basis was being part of the town’s notable merchant families.
heading: Font: Abbeygate Street.
paras: In the 1660s when the concept of ‘the Tribes of Galway’ began, its basis was being part of the town’s notable merchant families. This is why on the 1662 Pictorial Map families like Bermingham, Butler, Colman, Fallon, Nolan, Tierney, Tully, Quin and White were included. As some of these surnames denote, several of the town’s merchant families were Gaeil not Gaill, demonstrating the supposedly anti-Irish attitude of the Tribes was not entirely true. And there were at least two if not four Gaeil Tribes families. Over the next century criteria for inclusion among the Tribes shifted. Only in 1820 did James Hardiman declare there were fourteen families and who they were. the crucial criteria for inclusion was that they had at least one Sovereign or Mayor in the family. This allowed inclusion of comparatively obscure families like Deane, Joyce, Morris and Font.

Walter Font was Provost of Galway in 1443 while John Font was Portreeve of Galway in 1472. Martin Font was Mayor during 1520-22, Adam Font was Mayor in 1524-25 while the last Font Mayor, Givane, served during 1569-71. The family claimed to be natives of Leicestershire in England and this seems plausible because unlike certain families, the Fonts made no great claims about their ancestry. Their tradition was they settled in Galway “at the beginning of the fifteenth century”, possibly under Provost Walter Font or his parents. Families of the same surname are recorded in 13th and 14th century Wicklow and Limerick, but seem distinct families.

Thomas Font was a son of Provost Walter and was first recorded in Lisbon during 1465 with John and Dominick Lynch (the latter of Lynch’s Castle fame). In Thomas’s lifetime some of the Galway Fonts seem to have settled in Lisbon
and Cadiz, while other Fonts from Galway were recorded in both cities during the 17th and 18th centuries.

They were never a prolific family and unlike so many did not transition from merchants to landowners during the 1600s. Forfeited Galway town properties in February 1657 included the dwelling house of Geoffrey Font somewhere in the High Street area. It was described as three stories high, with a yard in which was another house also three stories high with a slate roof, plus another house two stories high. It was confiscated by the English Commonwealth army and became the property of soldier John Morgan of Kilcolgan.

The only other Font property was that of Dominick Font, which consisted of a three-storey slated house backed with a thatched house of two stories plus a slated two storey house apparently in Middle Street. These show that unlike many of the Tribes, they were never many Fonts. John was in 1696 described as a merchant and was probably father of Geoffrey Font, living on Abbeygate Street in November 1724. That he was living there rather than High Street area shows that the family properties confiscated in the 1650s were never restored. Several otherspersons with Tribes surnames were documented on that street that year, all of whom were most certainly tenants rather than home owners.

Writing in 1820, historian James Hardiman stated: “The name is now nearly extinct. Geoffry Ffont, who died near Galway in 1814, aged 105 years, is supposed to have been the last survivor of the Galway branch of this family.” Been born around 1709 means he was likely a son of Geoffrey of Abbeygate Street.

title: Sir Peter French’s mansion
summary: Peter French fitz Valentine was known as Peter Óge to distinguish him from his grandfather Peter, who was Mayor in 1565.
heading: French: Sir Peter French’S Mansion, Market Street.
paras: Peter French fitz Valentine was known as Peter Óge to distinguish him from his grandfather Peter, who was Mayor in 1565. His great-great-great grandfather Walter French was the first of the family to settle in the town in the early 1400s. French was one of the bailiffs during 1589-90 under Mayor Richard Browne.
He was elected Mayor in August 1616 and would have served in office from 29 September that year to 29 September 1617 but refused the office because of
the Oath of Supremacy. As a result Pierce Lynch took his place and French was fined one hundred pounds.

During those years there was serious difficulty in governing the town because relatively few were willing to take the Oath of Supremacy and serve as Mayor. Besides Peter French, Oliver Browne and Thomas Browne both refused in 1609, as did Valentine Blake in 1611 and Peter Lynch in 1615. In March 1619 French made a little-known yet highly interesting intervention concerning Irish economic sovereignty. According to Raymond Gillespie, … for the greater part of the period between 1603 and 1641 Ireland appeared to have had a surplus in the balance of trade … yet … remained a poor country … French’s conclusion [was] that the central problem … was a severe deficit in the balance of capital flows and hence a shortage of coin … his solution … recommended the establishment of a mint in Ireland to hold foreign coin and bullion … since no mint existed in Ireland there was no incentive for merchants trading abroad to bring back foreign currency or bullion which could be reprocessed into Irish coin at home. They tended to bring back goods … The central problem was that the Kingdom of Ireland, while politically distinct from both Scotland and England, was through the recent conquest ruled from London. The Kingdom had a Parliament in Dublin, but its legislation was always superseded by that of the imperial parliament at Westminster in London. Furthermore, all its legislation and policies were uppermost for the benefit of the New English colonists.

Peter French’s proposal was “an effective devaluation of the Irish currency which would boost exports and curb imports, the net effect of which would be an increase of coin and bullion brought into the country, which could then be processed through the newly established mint.” In his own words, French saw this as brining in “old plate, ingots of gold and silver, Spanish reals, pistoletts in great plenty.” He further explained: “The thing which hinders all sorts of craftsmen … is only the want of money”; economic sovereignty and security would set the public peace of the kingdom … become tradesmen or other good members in the commonwealth and … enable … their children to learning and other employments at home and so many will not wander about the world at the devotion of foreign princes as now they do out of all parts of that kingdom.
By saying this French was alluding to social capital, that the country’s primary wealth was its nation and by investing in them could provide a state worthy enough to afford and nurture them.

The mint was never established and partly in consequence the nation suffered greatly when economic crises’ hit. Matters were only worsened by the terrible famines of the mid-to-late 1630s, on top of which came the political disintegration of the three kingdoms from 1638. In the case of Ireland, the matters French outlined were underlying causes to the 1641 Rebellion and the atrocities which resulted.

Interestingly, two of his sons-in-law were Patrick Darcy and Richard Martin, both who played leading roles in the creation and government of what was the first independent Irish state in 1642, the Irish Catholic Confederation. Some of his thoughts on sovereignty may have influenced them.

French was knighted on 10 August 1623 by Viscount Falkland, the then Lord Deputy of Ireland. His funeral entry in the Ulster’s Office at Dublin reads: “Sir Peter French of Galway, knight, deceased the 27th day of February 1631; he had to wife Mary, daughter of Geoffrey Browne of the aforesaid city, alderman, by whom he had issue Mary, married to Patrick Darcy councillor at law; Margaret alias Maggie, married to Richard Martin esquire; Ellis, married to Sir Robert son and heir to Sir Henry Lynch, baronet; and Jennet French, unmarried. His will appointed executors his wife Dame Mary plus Sir Henry Lynch and Dominick Browne and that he be buried in the Franciscan. His wife Mary made her will on 15 November 1659 and died soon after.

A rather magnificent tomb was made for him, only parts of which now survive as it and many others like it were vandalised by Commonwealth soldiers during the 1650s. In his case it was demolished by John Morgan of Kilcolgan who sold parts of it for chimneys. His mansion house had a doorway which led into a courtyard where there was a four-storey tower house surrounded on four sides by buildings. It passed into the possession of the 4th and 5th Earls of Clanricard. By 1698 it was the Poor Clare Convent, used up to 1712 when they were dispersed and the property was a temporary barracks by 1717. It became an Augustinian nunnery by 1837 and up to 1876. It was unoccupied during 1893-1913 and in 1928 its doorway was removed. After this the entire property was demolished and replaced in 1944 by the Connacht Tribune offices, itself more tastefully modified in the early 2020s. French: Cooke’s Restaurant on Abbeygate Street.
This restaurant features a fireplace dated 1648 celebrating a marriage between a Mr. French and a Miss Bodkin.

Born in 1489, Seán an tSalainn French was Mayor of Galway 1538-39 and a great-grandson of Walter, the first French in Galway. His father, Edmond fitz Robert, was third son of four while his grandfather Robert fitz Walter was youngest of four sons. So his branch were not the senior line nor could they be expected to be the wealthiest.

Yet Seán an tSalainn became the most well-known among the early generations of the lineage because of the great mercantile wealth he made. His nickname denoted ‘John of the Salt’ due to the quantities he successfully imported to Galway over the course of many voyages, probably from the salt flats along coast of western France.

Besides using his wealth for his own benefit, Seán used it to pay for religious works such as a new wing to Saint Nicholas’s church within the walls and a chapel at the abbey of Saint Francis outside the walls. He also made what was called John French’s Chamber on a set of arches over the river just north of the West Bridge. Though its purpose is uncertain.

Seán French’s family included four sons who became Mayors of Galway: Dominick in 1568, Peter in 1576, Robuck in 1582 and Marcus in 1604. He was Mayor again in 1609 Marcus French fitz John was Mayor, with bailiffs Martin Font and Christopher Blake. According to An Account of the Town of Galway, … in or about the year [1609] … Marcus French being mayor, that one Andrew French being destitute of all livelihood went with both is sons called Edmond and Geffry for Spain, where on account of their good education, his eldest son Edmond was made receiver of the King of Spain’s plate and his son Geffry was made governor of a considerable coast in the West Indies belonging to the King of Spain …. Edmond was knighted one of Saint Iago’s knights and general of his fleet coming from the West Indies with his plate, and the said Edmond’s son made the King’s page and afterwards made Captain of Horse in the war against the French King, and there taken prisoner and ransomed by the King with £3000, whose name was Anthony, whose son afterwards died, leaving only one sister, now honourably married in Spain.

Their tale shows that contrary to popular belief, hard times effected the merchants of Galway too and drove them to emigrate. In the cases of this branch of the Frenches their background and education enabled better upward mobility than most of their émigré nation. The traumatic events of the later 17th century would send many more Frenches abroad, not all of whom would do so well.
Joyce: Finnegan’s Restaurant, Market Street.

The Joy family originated somewhere in Wales, possibly the Gwyr peninsula in the south and were first recorded in Ireland in the 1220s. They may have participated in the invasion of the Kingdom of Connacht in the next few years because by the 1270s-80s were recorded in south Connacht William, Philip, Hugh of Seafin and Thomas of Caherskeehaun while in the next generation was recorded Simon Óg of Craughwell and Henry of Caherhenryhoe, places in the Athenry and Loughrea area.

During the 14th century the family appears to have been based primarily in and around Athenry town while a branch under Tomás Rua mac Dabhóic settled in northern Iar Connacht, their territory named after them – DuchasaSeóighe, known in English as Joyce County.

During the latter 1400s several Gaeil and Gaill families from east Galway and south Mayo migrated to Galway and were accepted by the merchant families as fellow freemen and burgesses. Darcys, Kirwans, Nolans, Tierneys and from the Athenry area came the Joyces.

William Joyce settled Galway during the late 1400s. He was likely closely related to Archbishop of Tuam William Joyce fitz Thomas, who was also a native of Athenry. In November 1507 he was a town bailiff when he, bailiff Anthony Lynch and Mayor Arthur Lynch fell off the West Bridge and drowned. He was survived by his wife Agnes Morris and their children James, Henry and Robert.

Henry Joyce became a wealthy merchant and during 1542-43 was Mayor and one of their descendants, Richard Joyce, married Richard Skerrett around 1589, a date which appears on the coat of arms in their house in Market Street. They display an eagle on the background, fronted with a two-bar fess featuring a crescent moon and scallop shells; these were later homogenised into a bland ermine but as symbols tell a story.

The crescent moon, which lies on its back, is often a heraldic symbol of a second son. Scallop shells were awarded to people who had made a successful pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela in northern Spain. The fess was also found in the Morris arms while the eagle was from the Browne coat of arms. It seems the original Joyce arms was composed by William Joyce and his wife Agnes Morris from elements of their coat of arms. Henry Joyce was a second son, either he or his father a Santiago pilgrim. While her maiden surname is unknown, Henry’s wife Catherine was the widow of Thomas Browne of Athenry and that explains the origin of the eagle.

These facts were re-told as a fairy tale: William Joyce, who was married to Agnes Morris, being on his travels from Italy to Greece, he was taken prisoner by the Saracens, and brought to Africa, from when after a variety of adventures, and undergoing captivity of seven years, he escaped to Spain; while there, his exalted virtues were rewarded by heaven … an eagle flying over his head pointed out to him a place where he discovered vast treasures; with which returning to Galway he contributed large sums towards building the walls, church and other public edifices of the town, he died leaving three sons James, Henry and Robert, and was buried in the Franciscan friary.

Much of this was made up in the 18th century and is based on the life of Richard Joyce, who while emigrating to the Caribbean was captured by Barbary Cosairs and enslaved for seven years in Algiers. But behind this were older stories. One was where a Joyce ancestor, William made pilgrimage to Spain, perhaps made great profits from carrying pilgrims from Ireland to Spain and back. Another was Henry who made a profitable marriage to a Browne (alias the eagle).
It just so happens that four Brownes from Athenry were made freemen of Galway in the years around when Henry was Mayor.
So three different Joyces were blended into one and their story confabulated into a charming tale which overlooked years of hard work, trade voyages and strategic marriages.

How long the house remained owned by the family is unknown as almost all the Tribes had their properties confiscated by the English Commonwealth during the 1650s. Yet Reverend Henry Joyce made the Pictorial Map of Galway around 1662 in Antwerp while John Joyce was a town freeman in 1686, and at least five were recorded living on Abbeygate Street and Shop Street in 1724. One of them was merchant Gregory Joyce, who emigrated to Madrid where he died in 1745; his pedigree states he was a descendant of Henry Joyce.

title: The Pictorial Map
summary: Reverend Henry Joyce was a vicar of the Collegiate Church of Saint Nicholas from about 1637 to 1652.
heading: Joyce: Pictorial Map, Lynch’S Castle.
paras: Reverend Henry Joyce was a vicar of the Collegiate Church of Saint Nicholas from about 1637 to 1652. His brother Gregory was Warden of Galway during
those years while their brother, William, was a military officer in the army of the Irish Confederation.

After the town surrendered to the English Commonwealth army under Sir Charles Coote in April 1652, Joyce and his brothers went into exile and settled in Spanish Flanders. Among those who remained were John Joyce, who was one of only eight who signed the Articles of Surrender; Richard Joyce, Walter Joyce and George Joyce refused to sign while absent townsmen that day were Martin and Patrick Joyce fitz Marcus, Walter Joyce fitz John and James Joyce fitz Marcus. Among the many who by 1657 had forfeited lands and properties within and without the town were the families of Patrick and Walter Joyce, the men having since died.

In 1658 Henry became vicar general of Irish troops serving Charles II in exile. In 1665 Philipe IV of Spain appointed him dean of the chapter of Saint Ursmer’s church at Binche southwest of Brussells, which he later resigned for a chaplaincy. At Brussels in 1666 he and Gregory secured certification of their noble descent from eight noble Galway families. He was elected one of the eight vicars of Saint Nicholas’s church in 1688, 1689 and 1690 but was abroad as Father John Skerrett fitz Dominick stood in his place.

In 1684 William Molyneux stated the map was printed in Antwerp “about 20 or 30 years ago.” In 1709, Samuel Molyneux stated “twas done at Brussels by a friar who was born and bred in this town, and, they tell you, had been at Brussels 8 years when he made it.” Joyce was exiled in 1652, which suggests the year 1660 the year Charles II was restored to the Three Kingdoms, while William’s estimate of twenty years previous to 1684 gives us 1664, certainly more correct that thirty years previously when Joyce was only two years in Brussels.

Moreover, in 1661-62 the disposed families were encouraged by letters Charles II who praised their loyalty and bravery, leading them to seek total restoration of their homes and properties within and without the town. Creating the map may have been part of their programme.

Reverend Henry Joyce was the person most responsible for the creation of the Pictorial Map of Galway. Generally dated to 1651, evidence actually points to its creation in the early 1660s after the restoration of the monarchy to the three kingdoms in 1660. Thus it is dedicated to King Charles II by his “most devoted client”, a “citizen and pastor” of Galway who identified himself as R.D.H.I. – Reverend Doctor Henry Joyce. And it includes the arms of Tangier, acquired by the crown from Portugal in June 1661.

Notably, it mentions none of the men and families who from 1652 had taken over the town: Eyres, Shaws, Handcocks, Morgans, Ormsbys, Revetts, Russells, Cartwrights, Stubbers, Sadliers or Dodds. As historian Paul Walshe has

pointed out, the statement that it was ‘engraved at the expense of the Corporation’ cannot mean any of these new families. Rather, the Pictorial Map was a statement by the old families of the town – the Tribes plus the Berminghams, Butlers, Colmans, Fallons, Nolans, Quinns, Ryans and Tullys. And their statement was that despite war and conquest by the New English they were still here and not going away.

One curious feature on the map are seven box-shaped objects which obstruct the middle of some streets but were explained in the index as temporary altars for the feast of Corpus Christi, held eight weeks after Easter. Historian Paul Walsh has commented that “their inclusion on the map undoubtedly reflects Father Joyce’s yearning for that time in the 1640s and early 1650s when the Catholic inhabitants publicly celebrated their faith without restriction or hindrance.”

Maps of this type were common on the mainland and at least two can be seen in contemporary paintings by the Dutch artist, Vermeer. Not only does it show the town, it details dozens of buildings and their occupants, secular and clerical, while displaying over fifty coats of arms of the merchant families and allied dynasties.

Joyce was unlikely to be the only person responsible for the project. Its scope in delineating contemporary and recent Galway required massive attention to detail which could not be done from Antwerp. Its financing was certainly beyond that of a humble priest so much must have come from the recently disposed merchant families who hoped to be fully restored to their homes, properties and fortunes. These, plus a team led by Henry Joyce, must be indicated by the phrase S[enatus] P[opulus] Q[que] G[alviae] – the Senate and People of Galway Town, denoting the old Corporation and its families. One term which may begin with the map is ‘the Tribes of Galway’, one not recorded any time before its production. Its seems to be in a Latin phrase on the map which says of Galway: “Bis septemillustres, has coli tilla tribues” – “she boasts twice seven illustrious families.” The Latin tribues does not quite equal families but it seems enough to popularise the phrase. Wardenship documents from the 1790s show that by then, the Tribes denoted the fourteen families who had Sovereigns and Mayors of Galway.

Reverend Henry Joyce died at Binche in Hainaut province of the Spanish Nederlands in 1697 aged eighty. While dozens of copies of his map were kept in the town during the 17th and 18th centuries only two survive. One copy is on public display inside Lynch’s Castle at the Four Corners.

title: Joyce House
summary: Walter Joyce of Mervue was born 1763 and died 1853. Around 1795 he built Joyce House and store on Saint Augustine Street while his brother John built the adjoining house.
heading: Joyce: Joyce House, Saint Augustine’S Street.
paras: Walter Joyce of Mervue was born 1763 and died 1853. Around 1795 he built Joyce House and store on Saint Augustine Street while his brother John built the adjoining house. Walter’s house was used during 1836-67 as the Galway office of the National Bank.

Several Seoighe are interred in the graveyard around and interior of the ruins of Saint James’s church in Mervue. One memorial reads Have Mercy O Lord on the Soul of Thady Joyce died 16 of July 1884 aged 85 years. Erected by his son Thady Joyce for him and Posterity. But in the same place are buried some more elevated kinsman, not least Pierce Joyce of Mervue House (1809-83). He was a son of Walter Joyce (1763-1853), a successful merchant and banker. A descendant was Pierce Joyce who fought with the Arabs in the Hejaz along the Red Sea, helping them establish independence from the Sublime Ottoman State, an empire based in what is now the Republic of Turkiye. In October 1916 Joyce was sent from Egypt by the British, commanding over four hundred troops and who along with Colonel Lawrence aided Prince Faisal capture Jerusalem in Palestine and push the Turks out of the Middle East back to their homeland. On 4 June 1918 he was intermediary and interpreter at the meeting between Prince Faisal and the Zionist leader Chaim Weizmann from Belarus. The Turks sued for peace in October 1918 while Faisal strove to become King of Syria. Pierce Joyce predicted in 1919 that there would be severe and long-lasting problems in the region if the British and French empires – who despite the native Arabs were taking over the region from the Turks – did not allow Palestine, Lebanon and Syria independence. Like similar advice from his colleague Colonel Lawrence, he was not heeded. By 1920 Joyce was back in Egypt and retired in 1932.About 1954 he sold Mervue House, the estate around it becoming housing estates and industrial estates for the rapidly-expanding city. Pierce Charles Joyce died at his Berkshire home 1 February 1965 and was buried in nearby Crowthorne. While it was higher authorities who made decisions which reverberate today, the Middle East owes some of its issues to him.

ÓglaighnahÉireann have been on UNIFIL peacekeeping missions in Lebanon from 1978, suffering forty-seven dead. In April 1981, Caomhán Seoighe ó Inis Óirrwas disappeared during violence at Dayr Ntar; “the Palestine Liberation Organisation denied responsibility … blamed … Israeli-back militia.”Seoighe alias Joyce remains one of two ÓglaighnahÉireann missing in action.

title: The Kirwans of Shop Street
summary: On 5 January 1887 on Shop Street died Peter Martin Kirwan. His death certificate states he was a married sixty-four-year-old and soap manufacturer.
heading: Kirwan: Shop Street.
paras: On 5 January 1887 on Shop Street died Peter Martin Kirwan. His death certificate states he was a married sixty-four-year-old and soap manufacturer. He died from chronic nephritis and bronchitis. Informant was his widow, Bessie M. Kirwan, present at death.
He may or may not have been related to John Kirwan who ran a pawn broker’s shop on nearby Abbeygate street in the 1860s and 1870s, dying aged seventy-seven in December 1876.

During those decades other Kirwan families were then living on Williamstreet West, Lombard Street, Middle Street, Helen Street, Francis Street, Bowling Green, Quay Street, Dominick Street, Bohermore and Eyre Square.

Forty-year-old Peter Martin Kirwan of The Castle in Galway town and Bessie Burke of William Street were married in the Presentation Convent Chapel at Galway 8 January 1870. He was the son of deceased merchant Peter Kirwan, she was a daughter of deceased merchant William Burke. They were married by Father Peter Dooley, curate and administrator, their witnesses James Colman and Mary Bodkin.

Among Peter and Bessie’s children was Elenor, born 23 October 1872 on Shop Street. Her sister Catherine died aged seventeen on 27 March 1888 on Shop Street, her cause of death was given as debility. Peter Martin Barnaby Kirwan was born 4 June 1876 on Shop Street. He died 28 February 1904 at “Castle, Shop Street” with a stated age of twenty-seven from phthisis for some years. He was unmarried and of no stated occupation. Their third known child was Elenor, known as Nellie and who later married a Mr. Burke Bessie was recorded in the Shop Street property by the 1901 and 1911 census, aged seventy-one and seventy-seven respectively. In those years she lived alone with just a servant, sixty-eight-year-old Margaret Keane in 1901 and with eighty-three-year-old Catherine Hayden in 1911. She died 18 January 1916 aged eighty, her informant one Gretta Fitzgerald, “in attendance present at death Shop Street.”
In 1918, Bessie and Peter’s daughter Mrs. Nellie M. Burke leased Lynch’s Castle to the Munster and Leinster Bank. The bank subsequently purchased the building outright in 1920.

title: Kirwan’s Lane
summary: The Kirwans were among several Gaelic families who lived in Galway town and were one of upwards of four Tribes families of Gaelic origin.
heading: Kirwan: Busker Browne’S, Cross Street And Kirwan’S Lane.
paras: The Kirwans were among several Gaelic families who lived in Galway town and were one of upwards of four Tribes families of Gaelic origin. Orginally from Dunbally near Dunmore, they ancestry lay among the Conmaicne Dúin Móir conquered by the Uí Chonchobhair during the 11th century. In 1420 one Diarmaid Ó Ciardubháin was recorded while in 1432 Báitéar Ó Ciardubháin was termed a king’s justice. Both references denote that even by then the family had integrated into the English communities of Connacht.

They did so through living within the de Bermingham lordship, which encompassed Milltown and Dunmore in north Galway. Tomás Ó Ciardubháin was in 1465 Provost of Athenry, town of Lord Bermingham. But even before then they had contacts with the Galwegians; by 1440 Éiblín Ní Chiardubháin was already married to merchant John Font of Galway and by the end of the century they had married Lynches, de Berminghams and Bodkins. While not nobles, this demonstrates that even when living in de Bermingham’s lordship they were already of some middle-class states.

Uilliam Ó Ciardubháin led that branch of the lineage who migrated into Galway around 1488. Their tradition was the family remained at Dunbally from the above period to the year 1488 when Uilliam Ó Ciardubháin, the owner and proprietor of this castle, was obliged to flee to Galway in consequence of a quarrel that took place between him and Thomas Bermingham, 9th Lord of Athenry.

From then on they were documented in town records as merchants, bailiffs and mayors. They even had Dunbally returned to them when Lord Athenry made amends upon the marriage of his son Tomás Óge to Ó Ciardubháin’s daughter, Úna.

In Galway they lived in a town run by families of Irish and English backgrounds: Athys, Blakes, Bodkins, Brownes, Butlers, Carrs, Colmans, Cunninghams, Currans, Deanes, Dermodys, Fallons, Flynns, Folans, Fonts, Frenches, Glynns, Keanes, Kennys, Joyces, Martins, Morrises, Mullens, Lynches, Nolans, Quinns, Quirks, Ryans, Skerretts, Tarpeys, and Tierneys. Unlike Athenry and Loughrea, however, Galway had no resident lord overbearing it so was closer in political structure to a republic than a lordship.

Also unlike the lords of Athenry and Loughrea, its rulers were working merchants not warrior landlords. All these factors fed into the town’s spirit of political independence and commercial sovereignty from the kleptomaniac lords all around them.

By the first half of the 1600s the Kirwans had proliferated and owned impressive properties in the town. Like most of the Galwegians up to this point they were cash rich but land poor, whereas Gaeil and Gaill landlords out in the county were land rich but cash poor.So they sold lands to the merchants, allowing urban families like the Kirwans to for the first time buy substantial estates out in the county.Kirwans then or later purchased estates at the Blindwell, Castlehackett, Cregg, Greenfield and Hillsbrook. By coincidence or not, several of these were in the same broad region where their Conmacineancestors originated.

What is now called Busker Browne’s was once the home of John Kirwan, who was likely born there in 1650. It faces Cross Street while the south side of it runs along Kirwan’s Lane to the west. The size and scale of the buildingmeans it was probably built after the great fire of June 1473 while demonstrating the great wealth of the Kirwans in being able to purchase property in Galway’s senceathrú or old quarter. It is similar in age and design to nearby Tigh Neachtáin, home of the Martin family.

John Kirwan was almost certainly the last of his family born and raised in the building as six Kirwans had all their properties in the area confiscated by the English Commonwealth town garrison in February 1657. Besides these there was at least one other Kirwan home, facing the south aisle and tower of Saint Nicholas’s Church His father Stephen fitz Richardwas documented between 1637 and 1652. His grandfather Richard fitz Thomas was the unhappy Mayor who, after a nine month siege, oversaw the town surrender to the English Commonwealth in April 1652.

Yet John Kirwan appears to have retained his family home or perhaps manged to buy it back. By the 1680s was a wealthy merchant in his own right. With much of his family property and inheritances confiscated, he turned to trading in wool within Ireland while importing tobacco and sugar from the Caribbean plus wines from France and Iberia. Other town families such as the Blakes, Darcys, Deans, Quins and Skerretts did likewise and similarly profited from Caribbean trade. This enabled him to build a new property portfolio which came to include the Castlehackett estate near Tuam.

On 1 August 1686 he was elected Mayor, the first since 1654, serving from 29 September to the same date in 1687. His election was due to the ascension to the crown of the three kingdoms of King James VII and II, the first Catholic monarch since Queen Mary and King Phillip in the 1550s.
While Mayor, he helped obtain a new town charter from the king which appointed himself, Sir Walter Blake, Robert Blake and Dominick Brown justices
of the Peace. Warden Bodkin reclaimed Saint Nicholas’s Church and baptisms performed there are recorded in the parish register.

During his Mayoralty “multitudes of the former natives and their families flocked to the town and were restored to their properties and freedom. The Catholic clergy also returned and reclaimed their respective places of worship, to the inexpressible mortification and grief of the Protestant inhabitants, who were quietly obliged to submit to this … without even daring to remonstrates against the encroachments which were daily making upon their rights.” But with the Irish defeat at Aughrim on 12 July 1691 all their gains were set back and thousands left the country with na Geanna Faine, alias the Wild Gesse.

While he was Mayor in 1686 the property became the Dominican Nunnery, established by Julian Nolan and Mary Lynch. Possibly Kirwan donated it to them. By 1698 persecution forced the nuns to abandon the house and by 1716 it was an army barracks. Yet in 1717 the nuns returned to Kirwan’s Lane and rented two adjoining houses, which they amalgamated into a convent, now known as the Slate House.

Kirwan’s Castlehacket estate lay southwest of Tuam between Belclare in the east and Caherlistrane in the west. Upon the English invasion of the Kingdom of Connacht in the 1230s, the townland of Sciathanach alias Skehanaghwas seized from its owners,either the Mhic Aodha alias McHughes or a related family. The new owners were the Hackett familywho built the castle after which it is now named.

By the 1650s it had been owned for centuries by a branch of the Burkes from whom it was seized by the English Commonwealth, obliging the Burkes to move to nearby Ower. In the 1690s it was owned by transplantee Sir Patrick Barnewall who sold it to John Kirwan. He and his family first lived at Castlehackett itself while building a more modern home, Castlehacket House, which was finished in 1703. Two centuries later his descendants had an estate of over eight thousand acres spanning seven parishes in the barony. So if it was a house owned, built and lived in by the Kirwans, why is it now called Busker Brownes? The building plus others on the lane were in deep dereliction for decades before it was conserved and rebuilt around 1994 into the present bar and restaurant. The name came from local folklore, which told of a young boy surnamed Browne who used to busk in the area on a drum. He died young but his ghost was said to haunt the area long after, busking on his drum. And so it was in his memory the present premises was named.

title: The Kirwans of High Street
summary: On 8 December 1731, gentleman Francis Kirwan of Galway and merchant Valentine fitz Oliver Martin of Galway were two parties of a deed concerning a house and shop in High Street.
heading: Kirwan: Murphy’S Shop And Pub, High Street.
paras: On 8 December 1731, gentleman Francis Kirwan of Galway and merchant Valentine fitz Oliver Martin of Galway were two parties of a deed concerning a house and shop in High Street. Witnesses were gentleman John Browne of County Galway, David Kirwan of Galway town and shopkeeper William Murphy of Galway, aged about twenty-six. The house and shop seems to what is now Murphy’s Pub on High Street, then owned by Francis Kirwan and leased to Valentine Martin.
David Kirwan and his wife Jeanne Lynch had a son in 1734, Mark, who was seventy-one when he died in Cantenac, Médoc in France on 3 November 1805.

Mark had emigrated to Bordeaux about 1760 with his cousins, siblings Mark and Julienne Kirwan. All three were naturalised French subjects by 1763. On 17 May 1768 David married Elisabeth Collingwood, a daughter of Sir John Collingwood of Eslington and cousin to Admiral Collingwood of Trafalgar. The Collingwoods were a Catholic family and Jacobites from northern England, Sir John emigrating to France and naturalised in 1745.

Elisabeth inherited from her father the La Salle house and estate which she and her husband David turned into the famous wine property, Cháteau Kirwan. The couple had fifteen children, born between 1769 and 1790. Some stayed in the Bordelais, others migrated to elsewhere in France while other emigrated across the Atlantic to the French West Indies.
Kirwan and other Irish merchants were responsible for popularising Bordeaux wine. Cháteau Kirwan was sold by the Kirwans in 1827 but the wine brand continues today.

title: Crann Mór mansion, part one
summary: The house of the senior branch of the family has many stories attached to it, spanning centuries and countries.
heading: Lynch: Crann Mór Mansion, Bridge Street I.
paras: The house of the senior branch of the family has many stories attached to it, spanning centuries and countries.

In 1815, Galway resident John Lynch (son of Alexander son of Richard) described his family as the senior branch of the entire Lynch lineage of Galway, hence their nickname, Crann Mór (‘great tree’). They were also known as Lynch of Newcastle after their home and estate there to the north of Galway on the west bank of the river. In the 1574 castle list, Newcastle was owned by Martin

Lynch. In the opinion of Martin J. Blake, Martin was a son of Christopher son of Stephen son of Dominick Dubh Lynch, who was a son of Éamonn a Tun, who was a son of Thomas Lynch son of James son of Thomas son of William Mór son of Thomas, Provost of Galway and alive in 1274.

John Lynch stated their house in Galway was built in the 1400s by his ancestor Éamonn a Tun Lynch and stood in a square on Bridge Street. Lynch shared his seniority with Jean Baptise Lynch, Mayor of Bordeaux 1809-15. Jean-Baptise was a son of Thomas Lynch and Lady Petronella Drouillard. Thomas in turn a son of John Lynch, a Jacobite who was born in Galway during 1669 to Margaret Lynch and Thomas Lynch.

During the war of 1688-91 several Lynches of Galway fought for King James, almost all of whom were charged with treason afterwards by King William. Sir Henry Lynch had a commission to raise a regiment but does not seem to have done so. However in Lord Bophin’s infantry regiment were Captains Rober, Joseph, Arthur, Nicholas and Matthew Lynch, Lieutenants Stephen and Thomas Lynch, plus Ensigns Stephe and William Lynch. John Lynch son of Thomas may have held a lesser rank or was gazetted later in the war. He fought at Aughrim and after the Jacobite defeat there, eventually left Ireland with na Geanna Fáine, alias the Wild Geese. Among a later generation was Colonel Lynch of Lally’s Brigade who was wounded at Lauffield in 1747.

In French exile John Lynch settled in Bordeaux. There on 26 November 1709 he married Guillemette Marie Constant. Their two sons were Thomas Michel and Jean Jaques. Thomas married well and completely integrated while Jean maintained relations with his cousins in Galway. They both received patent of nobility in 1756.

By then their ancestral home no longer existed. In 1749 thirty-year-old Alexander Lynch witnessed its demolition. It was replaced by the Shambles Barracks which too was later demolished and is where Saint Patrick’s National school now stands.

title: Crann Mór mansion, part two
summary: From the late 17th century, Irish exiles on the European mainland were nicknamed naGéannaFáine ‘the Wild Geese’.
heading: Lynch: Crann Mór Mansion, Bridge Street Ii.
paras: From the late 17th century, Irish exiles on the European mainland were nicknamed naGéannaFáine ‘the Wild Geese’. Thousands of them served in the Irish Brigade in the Army of France, including Patrick Lynch who was born in Galway during 1662. As a young man he joined Luttrell’s Company in Galmoy’s Regiment and fought throughout the 1688-91 war in Ireland, then joined the

exiles in France. He was shot through the body by a musket shot in Germany during the 1697 campaign and so applied to stay at the army veterans hotel Les Invalides, which was in Paris where his wife and family lived. While he was admitted on 10 February 1702 he was deemed fit enough for certain reserve duties and died on detachment at Ardres on 1 July 1704 As it happens one of the last of naGéannaFáine was a namesake kinsman, Patrick Lynch of Galway and Bordeaux.

Patrick was born in Galway 25 January 1786 to Mary and Martin Lynch and as a young man emigrated to Bordeaux so was presumably related to the Lynchs of Bordeaux. Around 1809 he joined the Irish Regiment in the French Army, serving first in 2nd Battalion in Spain. However, because of the disaster engulfing Emperor Napoleon’s Grande Armeé in Russia, 2nd Battalion under Colonel William Lawless assembled at Bergen-op-Zoom in The Netherlands, met 1st Battalion under Lieutenant-Colonel John Tennant at Osnabrook in January 1813 and marched to Magdeburgh on the Elbe, arriving 28 February and joined 3rd Division.

3éme RégimentEtrangerIrelandais contained many United Irishmen who fled to the mainland after 1798 alongside other Irish emigrants in France and French-occupied territories who enlisted. Others were descendants of Irish families in France. But most in the ranks were ethnic French with the regiment led and administered by Irish officers.

Patrick Lynch was by now a Lieutenant and his regiment saw regular action that spring and summer: Uelazen and Seehausen in March, Celle in April and at Haynau/Chojnów in June. With the Truce of Pielazowice, lasting from 4 June to August, 3éme RégimentEtrangerIrelandais bivouacked near Goldberg/Zlotoryja.

But the Truce allowed the Russians and Prussians time to regroup their forces who attacked on 19 August near Ober Mois alias Mojez Górny, a village between the Srebrna and Bóbr rivers. The Irish formed squares against a Russian calvary attack, only for the calvary to roll back to let Prussian artillery open fire. By the time survivors reached a nearby wood, over three hundred of their comrades were dead but there was only more slaughter in the days ahead. Actions of the regiment led to promotions and eleven candidates for the Legion of Honour, but no respite. Then torrential rain fell for three full days and nights during 26-28 August. The Bóbr burst its banks, washing away every bridge and trapped Puthod’s entire 17th Division - including 1st and 2nd Battalions. Coming straight for these weary four thousand were thirty thousand energetic Russians and Prussians. On 29 August between Plagwiz and Lowenberg, the 17th Division fought from 8 am to 4 pm, hoping the floods would lessen and allow them to escape.

It didn’t. When their ammunition ran out around four o’clock “there was nothing for it but the river and every man for himself … a mere handful of men of the division reached safety” of the far bank, half a mile away. Those who were not swept away and drowned by the speeding floods were carefully shot dead by Russian and Prussian sharpshooters. Lynch fell in neither category – arguably, into a worse one. By then a wounded Lieutenant, he was captured on the Bóbr’s east bank. Becoming a Russian prisoner of war meant an unenviable walk back into Russia and for most this was a death-sentence.

In March, the sixteen hundred men of the Régiment marched out from Bois-leDuc in the Netherlands. At Wesel on 1 October, about one hundred survivors attended roll call. “The rest lay dead on the battlefields of Silesia or at the bottom of the Bóbr River or were being goaded through Russia as prisoners of war.” Patrick Lynch of Galway was among the very last of naGéannaFiáine ‘the Wild Geese’. It was the long wars of terrible Napoleon which terminated the tradition. Few survivors participated during March 1831 when le 3éme Régiment étranger (irlandais) became part of a new unit created by King Louis Philippe, called Légion étrangére alias the French Foreign Legion.
Incredibly, by 30 October 1816 and confirmed 17 February 1817, Patrick Lynch was living in La Réole in La Gironde. How he made it back from Russia and what became of him after remains unknown.

title: The Great Gate
summary: As their surname denoted, the de Linche family came from a place somewhere in southern England named Linche.
heading: Lynch: The Great Gate, Galway Camera Shop, Williamsgate Street.
paras: As their surname denoted, the de Linche family came from a place somewhere in southern England named Linche. As they were not an important family, the exact place remains undetermined but they were probably among the thousands of lower-to-middle class Norman families who seized lands in England after the 1066 invasion. It was common for such families, who had never previously owned any land, to surname themselves after their property and from this came surnames de Linch, de Burgh, de Bermingham, de Staunton plus many others in Ireland.

The de Linches probably participated in the invasion of the Kingdom of Connacht in the 1230s, ousting the Uí Chonchobhair Kings of Connacht. William de Lenche sat on a jury in Athenry in 1278 and descendants claimed their ancestors held land at Ballygarran, Ballybane and Mote-Lynch alias Castle Ellen around the town. If not an outright owner, they were was at least
significant tenants of the de Bermingham lords of Athenry. For generations after, certain Lynches were associated with that town.

But it was further west in Galway that they made their greatest mark. After Richard de Burgh forced the Uí hAllmhuráin and Uí Flaithbertaigh out of the town he made it one of his principal residence. But the nature of the de Burgh’s lordship meant they were never in any one place for very long so could begin the year in the Connacht or Ulster estates and end it on the king’s service in France while in between be anywhere from Limerick to London. This meant successive de Burgh’s needed on site managers to look after their properties and in 13th-14th century Galway, such responsibilities fell to families such as Lynch and Blake. The same William de Lenche who sat on the Athenry jury was in 1277 collector of the customs of Galway. In either 1273 or 1308 de Burgh granted him the tenement of Moynedan in ClannFhearghaile which denoted the territory where Galway was located.
It was by one of the next generation that the Great Gate of Galway was made.

Nicholas Mór de Lynch was the town marshall and built it during 1312, a massive fortification which resembled Saint Laurence’s Gate in Drogheda and narrowed access to the town for both friend and foe. The Great Gate was however only part of the town defences, incorporating the town walls plus a moat which ran around it from the river to the sea so making it more defensible. It was similar toGáta an Lár in Athenry which allowed people into that town from the Galway road, and was built during those years. Nicknamed ‘the Black Marshall’, Nicholas Mór de Lynch appears to have been a grandson of Thomas de Lynch who in 1274 was town provost, another military office and Nicholas’s father appears to have been the William noted between the 1270s and 1308. Nicholas’s family appears to have included a sister called Sylina who was by 1315 married to Thomas Hobarchyon, while a possible brother was called Thomas. Marshall was applied to descendants of Nicholas so the family used the surnames Lynch and Marshal interchangeably until their branch died out in the early 1400s.

Nicholas’s Great Gate was featured on the second coat of arms of Galway, which bore the Lynch chevron and the three town gates on the east, north and west of the town walls. It survived into the 17th century so was depicted on the 1662 Pictorial Map. It shows it as a long and tall building with an arch allowing access in and out of the town. Above that were two stories while a third allowed access to a walkway at the top of the tower, giving a view of anything approaching from the east on Bohermore and Boherbeg to the east, the river and lake to the north, over the town plus Iar Connacht to the west, and on Loch Lurgan alias Galway Bay to the south.

Additions made including the incorporation of the Galway coat of arms, plus a large clock over the inner arch in 1638, topped by a bell on the gable. Flying above that was a flag initialised SPQG – ‘Senate and People of Galway’, derived from the SPQR motto of Rome. Historian Paul Walsh has remarked that while the bell was generally rang to let people know when the gate was opening or closing, it had further functions. In 1642 it was used to warn the townspeople besieging Saint Augustine’s fort on the hill that a sally against them was being made by the fort’s garrison.

Walsh also noted that by then additional defensive works had been done around the Great Gate and by 1685 it had all but disappeared. The Upper Citadel had been built to block access to the gate by making traffic pass through it but was so bothersome that in 1686 a passage called Saint James’s Gate was made through the defences around the Great Gate and this twist at the top of Williamsgate Street still exists, around Galway Camera Shop where the Great Gate once stood.

title: Lynch’s Castle
summary: While some form of habitation was on the site for several centuries, sometime in the late 15th century it was owned by a family who began building much of the present structure.
heading: Lynch: Lynch’S Castle, The Four Corners.
paras: While some form of habitation was on the site for several centuries, sometime in the late 15th century it was owned by a family who began building much of the present structure.

Stringent historians correctly state nothing is known about its early history and that even who built it is not certain. Yet there are a host of circumstantial if compelling contemporary clues.
