The Lynch arms are prominent on the façade, along with those of the Fitzgeralds of Kildare and Henry VII who reigned from 1485 to 1509. The latter two were certainly placed there to celebrated the victory of the Earl of Kildare over Uilleag nagCeann a Burc of ClannRiocaird at Knockdoe in August 1504. The Galwegians in general and its leading families in particular were grateful to be free of Burke domination.

As to who precisely among the families of the Lynch lineage, only a few present possibilities as its central location and building expense mean it can only have been built by the wealthiest among them. These included descendants of James Mór Lynch, who was alive around 1400; descendants of James Lynch fitz Thomas, who died in 1419; the ancestors of the Lynch baronets. While each are variously plausible those with a really strong claim are descendants of James Mór via his son Éamonn a Tun, alive 1434-43. Éamonn alias Edmond was famed as a wealthy wine importer (tun=barrells) who was Sovereign of Galway in 1434 and 1444. He was also wealthy enough
to build the Great West Bridge in 1442 across the river into Iar Connacht entirely at his own expense.
In 1485 his son John and John’s his first cousin William were respectively last Provost and last Sovereign of Galway.

John fitz Éamonn was father to Dominick Dubh (d. 1508), Pierce (d. 1507), John (d. 1496), Nicholas (alive 1496), Robuck (alive 1490) and Margaret (alive 1508). Dominick Dubh was responsible for getting Galway its Mayoralty, making his brother Piers first Mayor in 1485 and himself in 1486, 1497, a post held by their brothers John in 1489 and 1502 and Robuck in 1490, 1501 and 1514.

Into the next generation all four sons of the sons of John fitz Dominick Dubh’s became bailiffs or mayors, while John’s older brother Stephen was Mayor in 1505, 1508, 1517 and 1522. On top of that, James Hardiman credited the same Stephen fitz Dominick Dubh for successfully petitioning the Pope to obtain the Wardenship of Galway. While perhaps exaggerated, it is a fact that Stephen’s wife Margaret Lynch financed the building of Saint Augustine’s Monastry on the Hill, just south of the town.
No other family so close in relationship held so many of the top offices in the town during those generations and that makes a compelling case for their line building Lynch’s Castle.

Among them the single most plausible candidate in Dominick Dubh Lynch fitz John. He is first recorded during 1465 in Lisbon, Portugal with his father John and John’s brother-in-law Thomas Font, who was father of Mayor Martin Font which cinches yet another link to the town’s prime office. His first wife was Anastasia Martin, who died before 1481 and was mother of his sons children Stephen, John, Kathleen, Anastace and Agnes. His second wife was Juliana Deane, likely a sister of Edmund Deane (fl. 1451) but before legitimising their relationship had with her sons Peter and Gabriel. Besides gaining the town its Mayoralty and playing some role in establishing the Wardenship, Dominick Dubh was a patron of Saint Nicholas’s College House, located where Galway’s Saturday Market meets.

Dominick Dubh wrote or dictated his will on 12 July 1508, ordering Stephen to complete the works he began in Saint Nicholas’s and build an altar to Saint James the Apostle – whose tomb at Sandiago in Spain he may have visited. He left bequests and directions to his sister Margaret, each of his children and several grandchildren.

Sadly, he does not clearly identify his home, saying only that he bequeathed to Stephen “my chief house where I now dwell”. He also mentions a stone house he bought from David Bodkin, another stone house he purchased from William Lynch fitz Sander “and another stone house in front of the other where
Fuke now dwells” plus a number of buildings he calls tenements - seemingly less grand than the stone houses.

If the early history of Lynch’s Castle is not clear, neither is its later history as nothing remarkable seems known of it for long after. There are no apparent accounts of it during the entire of the 17th and 18th centuries. In 2003 Tom Kenny pointed out that around 1808 the section to the west on its Shop Street section was added to the original structure, with the interior remodelled and outer masonry altered to their current positions. Who did this and why is unknown, as is anything about it for the next fifty years.

Writing in 1935, John Hynes related that in 1859 Lynch’s Castle was owned by a George Stainforth and others. By 1880 it was property of a Mary Hall and others but during that year “conveyed by the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice to Peter Kirwan, who resided as a tenant in the house in Abbeygate Street abutting the Castle.”

Tom Kenny stated that up to 1880 it was owned by the Right Honourable Henry Ormsby, a native of Powerscourt in County Wicklow who was Irish Solicitor-General and Attorney-General. In that year was purchased from Ormsby by Peter Kirwin, a chandler and soap maker. In 1918 Mrs. Nellie M. Burke, a daughter of Kirwan, leased Lynch’s Castle to the Munster and Leinster Bank, who purchased it in 1920. Since then it has become the property of the Allied Irish Bank who have overseen various works and alterations such as the round-headed windows and doorways while sculptor Lawrence Capbell of Dublin carved the doorway, which features arms of the four provinces. An early modern fireplace uncovered in the rear building has since been incorporated into the ground floor which also features a copy of the 1662 Pictorial Map of Galway, created under direction of Reverend Henry Joyce. Since then it has mainly seen only peaceful commerce though there have been exceptions, sometimes tragic. On Thursday 15 August 1974 two republicans robbed and murdered Jerome O’Connor on the Abbeygate Street side of the Castle. O’Connor was a wages clerk for Sisks Construction and was attacked and shot. Provisional IRA’s Galway Command denied responsibility, as did their Belfast Brigade. Seven people were later charged and six served sentences; one, Peter Burke, skipped bail and was not rearrested until 1991. Sometime during those years a copy of the 1662 Pictorial Map was placed on the ground floor, where it hangs today for the edification of the public. Printed in Antwerp by Reverend Henry Joyce, it was published at a time when the disposed merchant families believed they were to be fully restored to their properties and fortunes; the Map may have been with this in mind as its detailed notes on the town and its families completely omits any of the New English who has seized the town from them.

In 1996 Lynch’s Castle saw the launch by Senator Michael Yeats of the latest volume of the journal of the Galway Archaeological and Historical Society. Around 1903 its Honorary Secretary Matilda Redington wrote to the Kirwan family concerning what the Society saw as its poor preservation, so the Society has since its foundation taken an interest in the castle, as well as publishing articles concerning it and the Lynch family.

title: The Lynch Window
summary: For at least two centuries, a story has been told that one Mayor Lynch found his own son guilty of murder and hanged him from the window of his town house.
heading: Lynch: Lynch Window, Market Street.
paras: For at least two centuries, a story has been told that one Mayor Lynch found his own son guilty of murder and hanged him from the window of his town house. There is even a monument with a window where the event is supposed to have taken place. The story is well-believed and told by town guides today and has the pillars of a dramatic story – except for facts.
James Lynch fitz Stephen was Mayor of Galway for the terms 149394, 1510-11 and 1516-17. He is last mentioned in town records during 1519, so likely died then or in 1520.
Where he was buried is unknown.

Other members of his immediate family were his father Stephen, alive in 1445. James’s son Stephen was bailiff during 1499-1500, Mayor 1509-10, 1523-24 and 1526-27. Later pedigrees gathered by Hardiman state Marcus Bodkin married Sheela, daughter of James Lynch while genealogical material in the Ulster office compiled during 1597-1632 state that a Stephen Lynch – apparently James Lynch’s father – married Joanna Penrise and had a daughter named Margarita Lynch. Almost certainly a brother of James fitz Stephen was Andrew, Mayor in 1498-99 and ancestor of the Lynchs of Lavally. He was documented in 1477 as Andrew Lynch fitz Stephen and died while imprisoned in Dublin in 1523.

These are the known and likely facts concerning Mayor Lynch. The story with which is most known first occurs in a copy of the Collegiate Manuscript, copied from the Latin original in 1674 and which translated reads as follows: Mr. James Lynch fitz Stephen undertook, at his own cost, the building of the choir of the church of the Blessed Virgin in the western part of the town of Galway. It was he, again at his own cost, who caused the collegiate church of Saint Nicholas to be adorned with glass windows, well and richly coloured, in the year of our Lord, 1493.

It was also this James who, without any other form of law, hanged his son, guilty of murder and of broken trust given to the same stranger, from the window of his own house, leaving to posterity a memorable example of sincere fidelity.

Note that it did not identify the stranger by name or nationality, nor where Lynch’s house was located. As the original Collegiate Manuscript no longer exists it cannot now be said if this was part of the text or added to it. The extracts were to confirm Dominic Lynch in the Dominican Order and so carried testaments and testimony concerning the civic history of the family. Yet the story was absent from the testimony Father Daniel Nelly, a native of the town, while another, Archbishop of Tuam James Lynch, stated guardedly that in 1674 the story was “publicly believed throughout all the province.” By 1752 the unidentified stranger had become a Spanish captain murdered on a ship by Lynch’s son. In 1789 Lynch had become Blake, son of a Mayor in the reign of Queen Elizabeth. This version of the story added that the wife of Mayor Blake gathered two hundred of her family to oppose the execution but failed. It was next dramatised in a novel by Reverend Edward Maginn, whose take was used by James Hardiman in his 1820 History of Galway. Hardiman’s highly romantic version popularised the story greater than any before and it is this version which told today. With various improvements!

In the 1960s and 1970s, Galway historian James Mitchell published two articles which examined the Lynch story in exhaustive depth. He noted that what is curious about the story are the sources which does not mention it. It is absent from contemporary town records like Corporation A. While notable events in Galway from the great fire of 1472 to the 1597 siege were reported in Gaelic annála, none mention a Mayor executing a son. The historian Reverend John Lynch was born in the town in 1599 and wrote at least four histories up to his death in 1677, including on his home town, yet never once mentioned the Lynch story. Neither did his student Ruairí Ó Flaithbertaigh, born in 1629 and whose mother Elizabeth Darcy was from the town yet never
mentions it. Neither did Dubhaltach Mac Fhirbhisigh who composed his monumental LeabharnanGenealach in the town during the 1640s and yet also made no mention of such an event.

Surviving extracts from the Franciscan Abby obituary book likewise do not have it. Neither does a manuscript history written by Geoffrey Lynch fitz Dominic in the 17th century and used by Hardiman as a source for his HistoryofGalway. Nor does Corporation Book A.

Most damningly, an older James Hardiman expressed severe doubt that there was any truth to the story. In 1846 he wrote about the 1674 statement: “This testimony, at the time, was highly respectable, as to the popular belief; and though at the present day it may be considered ancient testimony, yet it cannot be taken as conclusive on a transaction which occurred nearly two centuries before it was given.” He alluded to its complete absence from contemporary and later records and concluded that “The omission certainly renders the truth of the story somewhat suspicious.”

A notable absence is from AnnálaRíoghachta Éireann, compiled during 1632-36 by a team led by Mícheál Ó Cléirigh and was intended as a comprehensive record of Irish history up to AD 1616. The team travelled all Ireland compiling material from every source they could find, with Ó Cléirigh doing so in Galway. Not only that, the actual autograph volume for the years 1335-1608 ended up in Galway during the century and was in the possession of Ruairí Ó Flaithbertaigh. Yet under the year 1493 there is no mention of Mayor Lynch hanging his son, or under any year.

Around 1662 Reverend Henry Lynch of Galway made the celebrated Pictorial Map of Galway in Antwerp. It is a detailed study of the town which tells the viewer and reader everything notable about the town. And yet again, what to us is the most famous story of the town is not mentioned. So sometime between the 1640s and 1674 a story grew in the telling about a Mayor Lynch of Galway who was so justly severe that he hanged his own murderous son. How and why it came about, who first told it, remains a mystery. Yet it is a fact that a lie will travel the world twice before the truth leaves the house!

Perhaps its lies in what happened in between, namely the destruction of the old corporation by the English Commonwealth who also stole their houses and properties while evicting them from the town. Just as the term ‘Tribes of Galway’ is supposed to have originated as an abusive term by the Commonwealth soldiers in those years, perhaps the story was a reaction to the same events. Left with almost nothing, they were nevertheless conscious that they came from people “famous to the world for their trading faithfully, discharging their credit, good education, charity and hospitality both at home
and abroad.” In fact for many their word was about all they had left – but it is something crucial in business and trading relationships.

In 1661 Geoffrey Lynch fitz Dominic wrote that “in old times they would rather hang themselves than break or discontent strangers”, such was the credit the merchants of Galway held with their word. So perhaps someone came up with the story as an extreme example of the fidelity the merchants when their word was their bond. Perhaps.

In 1848 Father Peter Daly assembled different bits of town architecture dating from the 1500s to the early 1720s and erected it on the supposed site of Mayor Lynch’s house, featuring a window from which his son was supposed to have been hanged in the 15th century yet the window dates from the 16th or even 17th century. And on a site where no house ever stood.

The conclusion of James Mitchell and every other historian who has examined the story is that it is pure fiction and has no basis in fact whatsoever. Yet almost daily during the tourist season tour guides recount the story with great enthusiasm to thousands of fascinated people. Not because they are wilfully lying but because it is a great story which they and their audiences become spellbound. And stories are what people remember and are most invested, not facts or history. That it has been dismissed by historians and shown by historians why it should be dismissed matters not at all. Once people become personally invested in good stories they will happy bend or break facts to keep believing in them, to keep hoping that they are true. In our own time many such alternative facts have been malicious and had hurtful outcomes. The story of Mayor James Lynch fitz Stephen is one classified as mostly harmless.

title: The King’s Head
summary: Colonel Peter Stubbers Regiment of Foot was raised in Kent during May 1649.
heading: Lynch: The King’S Head, High Street.
paras: Colonel Peter Stubbers Regiment of Foot was raised in Kent during May 1649. He had already served in Ireland and was adjutant general of the Parliamentary Army during the Second English Civil war. In January 1649 he was among the Guard of Halberdiers present at the execution of King Charles; whether he was also the masked executioner is unknown.

His regiment marched for Chester but were by June in the west country. There they were nicknamed Goring’s Bastards due to great number of thefts they carried out and general disorderly conduct; their nickname suggests some

had served with Lord Goring during the First English Civil War. They were in Dublin by winter and participated in the Siege of Limerick during July to October 1651. By May 1652 they were part of the Galway garrison with Stubbers appointed Governor of Galway. By 1655 Stubber’s Regiment was disbanded but for a company keeping garrison in Galway.

Thomas Lynch fitz Ambrose was elected Mayor in August 1654 and took office on 29 September. But that very day “the English inhabitants did … petition the … Lord Deputy and Council [in Dublin] that the government of this town by the charter might not be any longer in the hands of the Irish and Papists, but that it might be put into the hands of the English and Protestants.” And so it was that on 25 October Mayor Lynch was replaced by Colonel Peter Stubbers, while recorder John Blake plus sheriffs Richard Lynch and Anthony French fitz Peter were replaced by Robert Clarke, Paul Dodd and Marcus Lynch fitz Thomas. All garrison soldiers of the English Commonwealth were then made freemen, while the old corporation was disenfranchised.

On 30 October 1655 house owners were given until 10 November 1656 to ‘dispose’ of their property to the Commonwealth. Sir Charles Coote stated by 7 November that of the original inhabitants all that were left were the old, sick and disabled, though he had plans to remove them too soon enough. This resulted in the near-depopulation of the town, with most of its buildings dilapidated by their new owners. It was a grim irony that the urban republic of Galway was ruined by puritan English republicans.

Colonel Thomas Sadlier and Colonel Peter Stubbers were among the most highly-ranked men who seized forfeited properties in and around Galway town during the 1650s. Sadlier seized lands in Renmore, Gortstephen and Murough valued at fourteen pounds plus Jordan’s Island, previously owed by Alderman Martin Lynch, John Blake and John Bermingham. Edward Stubbers, seemingly a relation of Peter, seized fifty acres of land in Ballybane once the property of Sir Walter Blake.

Within the town during February 1657 a schedule was made of forfeited properties with the previous owners and their new ones. Colonel Peter Stubbers was now the new owner of a one-story house and a backside, and a dwelling house thatched, one storey, previously owned by Stephen Lynch fitz Nicholas and valued at five pounds. Ensign Edward Stubbers now owned one beside it of one story and a half, valued at five pounds ten shillings which was once owned by Thomas Kirwan.

Adjacent to it was a slated three storey house with a yard plus two more houses, also slated and three stories, in addition to one of two and a half stories, all once owned by Thomas Lynch fitz Ambrose but now owned by Peter Stubbers. This was the property now known as the King’s head on High Street
plus houses behind it. Other property he seized included the houses of Dominick Bodkin fitz John.

Thomas Lynch fitz Ambrose’s great-great-great grandfather seems to have been James Lynch fitz Martin, a bailiff under the first Mayor Pierce Lynch during 1485-86 and who became Mayor in 1499. His son was Martin Lynch fitz James, Mayor for the term 1537-38 and his son Ambrose bailiff during 1545-46 under Mayor Thomas Kirwan and bailiff again under Kirwan during 1547-48 before becoming Mayor himself during 1558-59. Ambrose’s son James had a belfry erected in Saint Nicholas’s in 1590 during his Mayoralty while his son, Ambrose, in 1620 made a complaint against the corporation because they had not paid his father nor him for the cost of the belfry works.

During the late 1640s the inhabitants of Galway were deeply factionalised; Thoms Lynch fitz Ambrose was however mentioned positively as one of the more responsible citizens. In 1651 Lynch was one of twelve townsmen who petitioned the Duke of Lorraine to come to the aid of their town. He was alive in May 1656 but how long after he lived, where and how, remains unknown. Colonel Stubbers entered into the tobacco business with either Thomas or Stephen Deane. The profits from the trade were good enough for the Deanes to eventually purchase estates at Castlemoyle in Clare barony and Toghermore in Dunmore barony plus in Kilmaine barony, which came to over fifteen hundred acres. Presumably the returns were just as good for Colonel Stubbers, adding to his Galway properties.

All changed in 1660 when Charles II, son of the executed king, was restored to the throne of the three kingdoms. While an amnesty was passed for many of his opponents this was not so for executioners of his father and he had them pursued for the rest of his reign, they fleeing as far apart as Switzerland and north America.

In Ireland too they were targeted. Tom Kenny has related that in March 1661 the king wrote of “one Stubbers, a halberdier, that assisted at that execrable murder of our Royal Father [was] exempted … from pardon”. So Stubbers and others like him suddenly vanished.
Some years later one of the French family of Tyrone House near Kilcolgan was in London when he came across Stubbers, but he disappeared before giving an explanation of his new circumstances.
Dated 1677, the Prerogative Court of Canterbury records a will made that year by one Peter Stubber of London.

By the 1680s the property was in the possession Robert Bancks, a pewterer whose family resided in the property into at least the 1740s and from which it was called Banks’s Castle. Tom Kenny has stated that between the 1820s and 1850s it was home to Laurence Geoghegan, a gunmaker, while by 1881 it was

home to grocer and spirit dealer Sarah Molloy, becoming a public house afterwards under management of John Jospeh Kirwan, later under Thomas Finn and Peter Quinn. But it appears to have been leased out for much of this time by the Stubbers family in County Louth.

More information on the family is lacking; Robert Stubbers was High Sheriff of County Dublin between 1699 and 1711 while his apparent widow and son held lands in counties Dublin, Laois and Offaly. By 1901 only four Stubbers lived in Ireland. One was forty-year-old Ellen Stubber at Rathmines in Dublin, an unemployed general domestic servant living with her sister, Anne Heade. In Durrow County Laois fifty-six-year-old Robert Hamilton Stubber headed a household consisting of his wife Georginia and thirteen-year-old daughter Margery plus eight staff. By 1911 Robert and Margery were among thirty-four people boarding at an address in Queen’s Square, Fermoy; he gave his occupation as magistrate. Civil records state that seventy-two-year-old gentleman Robert Hamilton Sutbber died 12 August 1916 at Moyne in Abbeyleix district and he appears to have been the last of the family in Ireland. As for the descendants of Thomas Lynch fitz Ambrose.A later Ambrose Lynch was in March 1686 one of the twenty-six town alderman while Nicholas Lynch fitz Ambrose was a freeman; deeds of April 1699 and November 1718 state he was a merchant of the town. Made 3 June 1734 a lease mentioned the previous occupier was Nicholas Lynch fitz Ambrose of Newpark, County Galway, a gentleman who was by then deceased.

title: The Lynch-Penrise house
summary: For Anno Domini 1473, Annála Connacht stated: Galway town was set on fire by lightning on the second of June, Friday by the day of the week, and it would be hard to estimate the temporal wealth destroyed.
heading: Lynch: Lynch-Penrise House, Heart Of Galway Shop, High Street.
paras: For Anno Domini 1473, Annála Connacht stated: Galway town was set on fire by lightning on the second of June, Friday by the day of the week, and it would be hard to estimate the temporal wealth destroyed.
Evidence of this was uncovered in the late 1990s when excavations on a house on High Street uncovered oaks, black with age, which dendrochronology estimated were cut in or around 1472.

At the junction of High Street, Shop Street and Mainguard Street is a fourstorey building fronted by the Heart of Galway shop and Nally’s Barber. Also in the 1990s, archaeology at the back of it uncovered 15th century remains, so it too was likely built after the great fire of Friday 2 June 1472. The front of the building features a plaque bearing the coats of arms of the Lynch and Penrise families. The Penrises were among the other powerful families in 13th and 14th century Galway town and as their name suggests, were ethnically Welsh in origin. But eventually they died out in the male line. Due to marriages with one branch of the Lynch family, it was they who inherited both the Penrise properties and the use of the Penrise arms. In 1820, James Hardiman stated: Their sepulchre, until lately, remaining in the church of the friars minors of Galway, pointed out their former consequence. Particular mention is made of Thomas ap Rhys and his wife Eleanor before the year 1280. Stephen Penrise was provost of the town in 1313, he was afterwards bailiff and collector of the new customs and died in 1383. Thomas Penrise, who lived until about the end of the fourteenth century, was the last male heir of his family; he was succeeded by his Joan Penrise, who intermarried with Stephen Lynch fitz Thomas of Bridge Street. Stephen Lynch was a member of the senior branch of the family, the Crann Mór Lynches who lived on Bridge Street. By his marriage to Joan Penrise, Stephen came into possession of the Lynch-Penrise house. The three story building is at the end of Shop Street and adjacent to the King’s Head on High Street. Called High Street Castle, it was described in 1731 as formerly the property of Walter Lynch fitz George. It is three stories high and at the junction of Shop Street, High Street and Mainguard Street. In 1815 it was described as “the Mansion House of the Drimcong Lynches is opposite the Market Cross, or as it is now called, the Main Guard.” While the Market Cross is long removed,
the reference shows Stephen’s descendants had by then gained an estate out in the county at Drimcong.

title: The Lynches of Abbeygate Street
summary: On the street front a very small, modern Lynch coat of arms is above the door of this building, with the initials PB either side of the IHS symbol.
heading: Lynch: Gourmet Tart Shop, Abbeygate Street.
paras: On the street front a very small, modern Lynch coat of arms is above the door of this building, with the initials PB either side of the IHS symbol. It probably dates from sometime in the early 19th century and may have been made in 1816 to commemorate the start of building on 1 July of the Catholic Pro-Cathedral directly across the street, erected on the site of Sir Robert Lynch’s mansion and featuring Lynch insignia.

Who exactly they were remains unknown. The nature of life means there were many Lynches who did not feature much in documentary records as much as their better off kindred. But some few clues survive.
In November 1724, a roll was taken for houses in Galway to determine tax based on the number of chimneys or hearths in a house. On Abbeygate Street lived Mary Lynch, Anthony Lynch and Ulick Lynch.

The 1762 Address to Robert French did not give addresses but those who signed it included Francis Lynch, Matthew Lynch, Martin Lynch, Robert Lynch, Alexander Lynch, James Lynch fitz Henry, Mark Lynch, Andrew Lynch fitz Henry, Patrick Lynch fitz John. Some may represent a later generation of those recorded in 1724.

Among the three hundred newly enfranchised Catholics made freemen of Galway on 30 April 1794 were Mathew, Peter and Andrew Linch. None of them were given addresses either. Nor was merchant Peter Lynch of Galway town, who appeared with Mark Lynch on a marriage settlement dated 7 July 1821. Made 16 July 1847 the will of Thomas Browne Lynch of Duggary in County Galway had letters of administration granted to John Browne Lynch esquire of Flood Street.

The will of Patrick Mark Lynch was made 5 May 1864 but his Renmore Park address demonstrates he lived outside the town (beneficiary was John Wilson Lynch of same). Several other wills by Lynches are recorded during the rest of that century but their addresses were overwhelmingly out in the county. More and more they had left Galway town behnd By 1901 only forty-one Lynches lived within Galway town limits and an astonishing twenty-three of them were born elsewhere in Ireland or in England. The Lynch family living in 16 Saint Patrick’s Avenue just off Eyre Square were headed by Robert and Mary, aged fifty and forty-five. He was an engine clearner’s foreman and she was a housekeeper, born in King’s County and Athlone respectively. The birthplaces of their eight children outlined where their father had been deployed by the railway; the three eldest children
were born in their mother’s hometown of Athlone, County Westmeath, the younger five all born in Westport, County Mayo.

In the Claddagh lived forty-six-year-old widow Louisa Lynch of England, a lady of private means who was fully literate. Living with her was her sister-inlaw Ellen Lynch and Ellen’s brother Michael Lynch, natives of County Cavan. All were Catholic.

House 9 Dominick Street Lower was home to County Galway-born baker Andrew Lynch, aged eighty-four, fully literate and bilingual. A widower, he lived with his forty year old daughter Anne, who was single, spoke only English and was also fully literate. Lodging with them was fifty year old widow Catherine Neary while nineteen year old Sarah Egan was the Lynch’s general domestic servant.

Almost no Lynches then lived within the medieval city centre and among the few who did was born in County Wicklow; this was forty-six year old fisherman Henry Lynch, who lodged with the Hernon family on Quay Lane. Likewise on William Street a shop was kept by fifty-year old Michael A. Lynch and his wife Katie, both natives of Mayo.
Descendant of the original Lynches of Galway were alive but evidently no longer living in the town of the Tribes.

title: The Lynches at Woodquay
summary: Into 1900s there was much boat traffic on the river and from the lake, transporting people and goods from Corr na Móna, Cong, Headford, Oughterard, Moycullen, Annaghdown and their adjacent areas to Galway, as well as from Galway back to such places.
heading: Lynch: Woodquay.
paras: Into 1900s there was much boat traffic on the river and from the lake, transporting people and goods from Corr na Móna, Cong, Headford, Oughterard, Moycullen, Annaghdown and their adjacent areas to Galway, as well as from Galway back to such places. Freshwater traffic was after all generally safer and swifter than road traffic and its probably by such routes that south Mayo families like Darcy, Nolan, Tiereny plus many others came to settle in late medieval and early modern Galway.

Woodquay is so-called because boats docked there at a quay made of wood. Its original name, Barr an Chalaidh, denoted that area opposite Corrib Terrance had a quay for boats made of wood, with the river Gaillimhe once reaching right to the foot of what is now McSwiggan’s Pub. That area bounded by Woodquay, Riverside and Dyke Road was in fact Horse Island, accessible to the rest of the town by boat and small bridges.

So too was the area bounded by the river, the Court House and Town Hall plus Saint Francis’s Abby. These were not part of the east bank of the river but Saint Francis’s Island. And around this area lived a small community of fisherfolk distinct from the sea fisherfolk in the Claddagh.

On 31 October 1609 alderman Uilleag Lynch fitz Edmond was foreman of a jury of twenty-four men to enquire into certain rights of Saint Nicholas’s Church. Among their findings was that artificers like the freshwater (and saltwater) fishermen first paid five shillings to the church warden to be so qualified as fishermen.

While Lynch was a town merchant, among the jurors were Dáithí Ó Fuadacháin, master of the boatmen at the Woodquay; Conchobhar Dubh Luderagh, master of the fishers of the see; Lochlainn, freshwater fisherman. Ó Fuadacháin’s surname is now rendered Swift, the surnames of the others unclear or unknown.

For centuries after Foreman Lynch and his fellow jurors had died, boat traffic continued in and out from Woodquay. One of the few explicitly recorded as such was seventy-year-old boatman Andrew Darcy; he was recorded by census enumerators on 28 May 1821 living at Woodquay with his fifty-five-year-old wife Bridget and their twenty-two-year-old son, Patrick. The famous 1828 Menlo boating disaster, in which twenty people from the Annaghdown area drowned, was going to dock in Woodquay and make for the town fair at Fair Hill in the Claddagh. A rather magnificent colour painting by William Joseph Bond, made about 1870, shows boats at the Riverside docks while others can be seen in the background at Woodquay itself. But these areas were gradually filled in until in the years after 1900 it became the modern suburb of Woodquay as we know it.

title: Martin’s Tower and the Spanish Arch
summary: With an increase in commercial prosperity during the 15th and early 16th centuries there were civic works made across the town.
heading: Lynch And Martin: Martin’S Tower And Spanish Arch
paras: With an increase in commercial prosperity during the 15th and early 16th centuries there were civic works made across the town. Streets were paved, at least one hospital was built while to better protect the town a fosse or moat was excavated around the town and a branch of the river diverted into it “that completely insulated the town.”. Several tower-houses castles were built by the Athys, Blakes and Lynches.

In the west the quay was extended then built up and to better protect it “the town wall was extended one hundred and twenty feet westward of Michael’s tower” and terminated at what was called Martin’s Tower, commemorating the fact this was done by Mayor Wylliam Martin in 1519-20. However it seems that a further section was not built until about 1581 by Mayor Dominick Lynch, called Ceann a Bhalla ‘head of the wall’ which is precisely what it was.

The quay extension allowed ships to dock at high tide while the arches within it were used for storage spaces. But because this took place during the 15341603 English conquest of Ireland, a security aspect was added. James Hardiman stated in the 1580s or early 1590s “several considerable works were raised for the defence and security of the town. The point of Ceann a Bhalla, at the quay, was converted into a fortification and furnished with great guns; and a part of the adjoining walls was built at the expense of the corporation.” The other side of the walls, where now lies Merchant’s Road, the Long Walk and all the modern docks was then just a tidal mud flat stretching from the river at Ceann a Bhalla east back to Penrise’s or Shoemaker’s Tower, within what is now the Eyre Square centre. Only in the 18th century was a hole made thorough one of the arches and the tidal area filled in to make what was then called Eyre’s Long Walk and at the end of it, Eyre’s Dock. Several decades later was built the present Commercial Dock along Dock Road while filling in much of the land west of Fort Hill.
And due to the romance of a fictional murder told by Hardiman, the name Ceann a Bhalla was gradually changed into the Spanish Arch.

But during the 15th to 19th centuries all sea traffic arriving at and departing from Galway docked at the Quay along Ceann a Bhalla, unloaded their goods into the arches and through the town walls into the strand and were stored in houses and buildings like Blake’s Castle along Martin’s Mill Lane, Quay Street, Quay Lane and Flood Street. All the wines that were consumed in the town, county and beyond were landed here while it was also where departed thousands of travellers destined for Britain, France, Spain and Portugal, the Canary Islands, the Caribbean and North America. More mundanely it was for generations the place where Conamara turf was landed to heat homes in the town.

title: Martin’s Mill Lane
summary: From around the 1280s into the 1360s the Sepishend family operated the mills of Galway, located on the east bank of the river at the back of Blake’s Castle and the bottom of Kirwan’s Lane.
heading: Martin: Martin’S Mill Lane.
paras: From around the 1280s into the 1360s the Sepishend family operated the mills of Galway, located on the east bank of the river at the back of Blake’s Castle and the bottom of Kirwan’s Lane. The mill was at bottom of a courtyard and had a lane which led to the very bottom of Quay Street and Quay Lane, which had been the town docks.

But on 2 June 1365 Joan Sepishend daughter of William gave and confirmed to Thomas Martyn all “the profits and emoluments arising out of the said mills … to hold as quietly as her father, John, her grandfather and William her greatgrandfather”.

Evidently Joan Sepishend married Thomas Martyn and was likely mother of his son William, likely called after her father. By 1375 she appears to have died as Thomas was married to Margaret Ballach de Linch, possibly a daughter of John Ballach de Linch, Provost of Galway 1357-58. By 1386 Thomas was dead but survived by Margaret and their son Thomas, but were in dispute with certain unnamed persons to the point of damage and injuries. It is possible that Margaret was in dispute with her husband’s eldest son, William Martyn, but Richard Burke and Henry Blake were named as her antagonists in January 1387. Henry Blake fitz Walter fitz Richard (died 1421) was a powerful member of the Blake family, while Riocard Óge a Burc was ceann fine of the ClannRiocaird up to his death later in 1387.

Their background remains mysterious. While at least two coats of arms from the late 1400s are versions of the FitzMartin family of England and Wales, they may have been an unrelated family who ‘borrowed’ them. Yet it is possible that they were a Gaeil family surnamed Ó Martain from elsewhere in Connacht. Other such families settled in the town, most notably the Darcys and Kirwans but also the Colmans, Fallons, Nolans and Quinns. Who knows. Over the next two hundred years the Martin family were the chief millers of Galway town, the mills commonly called Muileann Martain. Their presumptive residence on nearby Flood Street bears a very early example of the cross, sun and cresent moon Martin arms, while the lane in which the mills were located was called Martin’s Mill Lane, or Martin’s Lane.

In 1558 another Thomas Martyn and his wife Eveline Lynch began building an entirely new mill across the river on the site of what is now the Bridge Mills. They obtained a rare government grant for doing so as long as they also rebuilt the West Gate of the West Bridge. These works were completed in 1562 and proudly proclaimed by a plaque they put upon it, now located on Shop Street. This mill remained within the Martyn family into the 1650s when it was seized by the English Commonwealth.

Martin’s Mill is shown on the 1662 Pictorial Map of Galway as a building projecting beyond the town wall above a mill-race on the river. At some point during that century or the next one it seems to have fallen ought of use, though when exactly is unknown. Instead the lane and its courtyard were habitations, though with some extra uses. By 1717, merchants avoided duties by smuggling goods into the town from the river through a hole in the town wall into Martin’s Mill Lane. From there goods were carried out into Quay Street and Kirwan’s Lane, then beyond.

Over the next two hundred years much of the area around the mill was further developed for industrial use while the houses in the lane fell into severe dilapidation. Unlike buildings on the north side of Kirwan’s Lane,

nothing was saved from either Martin’s Mill or the lane, destroyed during the 19th and 20th centuries. By the time the town began to be rejuvenated in the 1980s and 1990s, there was nothing left to preserve or restore, so the lane became nondescript.
It was last officially recorded in the 1901 census; by 1911 it was treated as part of Kirwan’s Lane and has been ever since.

title: The West Bridge and the mills
street: Shop Street and the West Bridge
summary: One of the great myths of medieval Galway is that one Mayor Lynch executed his son for murder.
heading: Martin. Shop Street West Bridge And Mills Plaque 1562.
paras: One of the great myths of medieval Galway is that one Mayor Lynch executed his son for murder. Another concerns a plaque which once adorned the west bridge and faced into Iar Connacht. According to repeated local legend, it read: From the ferocious O’Flahertys, Lord deliver us. And like many local legends, it is less that truthful.

Since they were partly expelled from their homeland in MaighSeóla west across the lough by the Uí Chonchobhair during the 11th and 12th centuries, the Ó Flaithbhertaigh lineage have been associated with what is now Conamara. They appear to have been constables of Caistél Bun Gaillimhe under the Kings of Connacht – on land originally owned by the Uí hAllmhuráin – and fought the forces of William de Burgh there in the 1230s. But they were expelled from there and based themselves there and further west in Conmmaicne Mara.
Unlike the Uí hAllmhuráin, the Uí Flaithbheartaigh were often gruff neighbours of the Galwegians. Unlike the former they were still great lords and capable of gathering great armies.

On 13 September 1558 Thomas Óge Martin was granted the place of a watermill at the father end of the bridge from Galway, backwards from it on the side nearest the sea, provided that within two years he built a gate at the west end of the bridge and a tower of stone and lime to guard the gate. As a mark of esteem for his work for the town, the council elected him Mayor for the term 1563-64. An Account of the Town of Galway states: Public and spiritual works and memorable acts. The within Thomas Martin fitz William built the remotest west gate at the end of the bridge where his arms lieth, for consideration of which work the corporation gave him the plot or ground whereon the small castle and mill lieth, called lately, Turners Mill.

In the year of the above named Thomas Martin’s mayoralty, the earl of Clanrickard, called Rickard Burke alias Rickard Sasanagh intended to put all Iar Connacht under contribution, or chief rent, took the whole prey of the country, and afterwards coming to Trá Bán westward of Galway, they were set upon by a small party, their prey taken from them, and forced to turn their backs, the most part either drowned in the sea or river of Galway and some others got over the river, they knew not how, such was their apprehension of death.

So the Uí Flaithbertaigh were certainly capable of ferocious actions! And the West Bridge was finished in the months before the battle of Trá Bán. However, the plaque did not contain the infamous phrase or anything concerning the Ó Flaithbertaigh lineage. This is known because the plaque still exits and is perfectly readable. When the original mills were demolished around 1800, the plaque was saved and incorporated into the façade of what is now the Claddagh Ring shop. The plaque contains the arms of the Martins and the Lynches, bearing a Latin text which in translation reads: Thomas Martin and Eveline Lynch caused this work and mill to be made, A.D. 1562.
So like many another tale told about old Galway, it is not true. But facts don’t matter to people who love a good story, so like the story of the Lynch window this too will continue to be told.

title: Tigh Neachtáin
summary: The building now called Tigh Neachtáin is quite large and besides that pub and restaurant also includes the Kasbah Wine Bar and Coffeewerk Press.
heading: Martin: Tigh Neachtáin, Cross Street And Quay Street.
paras: The building now called Tigh Neachtáin is quite large and besides that pub and restaurant also includes the Kasbah Wine Bar and Coffeewerk Press. The property is most associated with the Martin family and is at the top of Quay Street in the sencathrú or old quarter. At the bottom of the street lay Martin’s Mill Lane, where the Martins were first recorded in 1365. Three hundred years later in 1657 twelve properties in the area which had been owned by Martins were seized by the English Commonwealth and distributed to soldiers of its army. That so many were so close to the original family business in the Lane suggests descendants slowly spread out from there and that most of the twelve may have being long-time homes of various branches.

Tigh Neachtáin as it is now dates from the late 15th century and may have been among those destroyed during the devastating fire of Friday 2 June 1473. Whatever previously existed was made anew into a very impressive two and a half story structure, the second floor featuring an oriel window on the corner and with some small windows shaped in Iberian styles. What was once an alley on the north side of the building divided it from the building housing Piazza and Pasta plus Nelly clothes.

Tigh Neachtáin was the town house of Richard Martin of Ballinahinch in Conamara either side of 1801 yet associations may go back further in time. His great-grandfather Robert Martin of Ross had his home in the town seized and given to Edward Eyre, an officer in the English Commonwealth army who garrisoned Galway in April 1652. But in June-July 1661 Martin and most other disposed families had hopes that their properties would be returned by letters issued by King Charles II praising their loyalty to him and their bravery during the town’s nine-month siege.

So Martin said to Eyre that he would soon take possession but Eyre replied that because the King’s letters were not sealed by the Lords Justice they were not worth threepence. Martin angrily accused Eyre of demeaning the king’s authority and of treason. This was serious enough that their dispute ended up in the Irish House of Commons where, to Martin’s severe disappointment, Edward Eyre was unanimously acquitted with his loyalty and integrity praised. Worse still, in 1663 Edward Eyre became Mayor of Galway.

The brothers John and Edward Eyre arrived in County Galway with the English Commonwealth army in the 1650s and established what John Cronin described as “one of the most powerful Protestant ascendancy families in the region, if not the country.” Natives of Brickworth in Wiltshire in England, their father Gyles Eyre died in 1655 aged eighty-two having fathered ten son and five daughters. John and Edward were third and sixth sons which mean their inheritances would be minor so they had great incentive to gain Irish lands and did so by any means necessary.

Matters between the families did not much improve in later generations. Edward Eyre’s grandnephew Stratford Eyre was governor of Galway in 1747 by which time Robert Martin’s grandson, Robert, had conformed to the Church of Ireland to save his estates despite being a Jacobite. As he was now a Protestant, Martin was allowed to carry arms and via his servant Darby Brennan sent a pistol and gun into the town for repairs. Governor Eyre had ordered that all Catholic who carried arms in the town or its liberties be
arrested, so Brennan was arrested at the West Bridge on 9 November 1747 and jailed. The case was tried in April 1748 and this time it was a Martin who won with his pistol and gun returned to him.

Still unsatisfied, Martin followed Eyre to London, hit him on the head and told him to draw his sword. Both men were skilled swordsmen but at the end of the ferocious duel it was Governor Eyre who required medical attention. After the 1740s Eyre influence declined and in the following decades a great deal of their property in and around the town was sold. And relations between them and the Martins must have been greatly improved because in 1788 Edward Eyre leased to Richard Martin a house in Abbeygate Street. By the 1770s the property was the town house of the eldest son of Robert the Jacobite, Richard Martin, a larger-than-life character who survived duels and shipwrecks, was present in north America when the War of Independence began and in Paris when the French Revolution took place. He was famous for pursuing what was then considered a highly eccentric issue, the prevention of cruelty to animals.

But he was also a long-time supporter of full civil rights for Catholics. Despite celebrations at his town house on his election in 1826, he was unseated and obliged to flee to France to escape creditors. So he was absent from Ireland when Catholic emancipation became law in 1829.

Tom Kenny wrote that after the Martins, it was “occupied by the O’Connor family and was known as The Bear House. In 1894 … it came into the possession of John Naughton from Park, Spiddal, and his family have been running it ever since. He married Kate Murphy from Carnmore and they had three children, Paddy, Mary and Sarah. John died in 1904 and subsequently, Kate changed the name over the door to the Irish language version. … The Irish language name over the door did not please the Black and Tans who … threatened them and fired shots through the windows on a number of occasions. … One night, the Tans dragged Kate’s son Patrick, a medical student who occasionally helped wounded republicans, out on the street. It is not known what they were going to do with him but his mother followed them out and kicked up such a racket screaming and screeching that a lot of the neighbours came out on the street. This meant too many witnessesso they let him go.
It came under management of Kate’s daughter Sarah and her husband James Maguire whose son Jimmy runs it today.
On 22 July 2022 the two hundredth anniversary of The Ill-Treatment of Cattle Act alias Martin’s Law was celebrated outside Tigh Neachtáin. This was
to recognise it as the first animal welfare legislation in the world and ancestor of all which have since followed.

title: The Martin castle
summary: A mortgage made 15 May 1608 concerned three properties in what is now Williamsgate Street.
heading: Martin: The Castle, Williamsgate Street.
paras: A mortgage made 15 May 1608 concerned three properties in what is now Williamsgate Street. Alderman Marcus Lynch fitz Stephen mortgaged to Charles Nolan “a shop under the stone house of John Skerrett situated by the great gate of Galway between the house of Geffrey Linchfitz Dominick on the one side, and the castle belonging to Stephen Martin fitz Francis on the other side, now in the occupation of Robert Skerrett son of John Skerrett.” Geffrey Linch’s house seems now occupied by Holland and Barrett’s. This is closest to the Galway Camera Shop which is where the Great Gate was situated. After Holland and Barrett’s is where Alderman Lynch’s stone house, now occupied by Kruspy Kreme and Hartmann and Son. After that came Stephen Martin’s ‘castle’ where is now Mountain Warehouse on the corner of Williamsgate Street and Barrack Lane. This lane led to the area which into the 1800s was called the Castle.

Stephen was a son of Elizabeth Lynch and Francis Martin, who died in 1603. His aunt Mary was married to Peter French while his uncle William Óge Martyn was a notorious figure. Stephen’s grandparents Thomas Óge Martin fitz William and Eveline Lynch had during 1558-62 financed the building of the Great West Bridge and Mills. His branch were unusual among the Martins as they were among the few native Protestants in the town. Most of the Church of Ireland community were recently arrived New English or those who took the Oath of Supremacy purely to serve as Mayor. Among the few others was the family of James Riabhach Darcy, a strong supporter of the English interest and Mayor upon his death in June 1603, plus sons who were Mayor. He married Elizabeth Martin, a daughter Stephen’s older first cousin Richard fitz Wiliam Óge. Among her nephews was Anthony Martin, Church of Ireland bishop of Meath and father of Lancelott Martin, who in an ironic twist was counted among the ‘New English’ who seized property in Galway during the 1650s.
But in common with most of the population the bulk of Stephen’s family remained Catholic. Despite his grandfather William Óge, father Richard and

brother Robert being Church of Ireland, Oliver Martin was a convinced Catholic who when elected Mayor 1 August 1631, refused to take the Oath of Supremacy and so was deposed on 27 September. His son Richard only became Mayor in August 1642 because he was a rebel and the entire town in rebellion against the English parliament.

Stephen himself was a town sheriff in 1628. Statutes passed that year included one where ten pounds out of the rents and revenues be distributed among the poor widows “for the glory of God and the good of the common weal.”

title: The Morrises and the Franciscan Abbey
summary: The Morris family were resident in Galway by the 1470s when John Mares lived there and was married to Christina Lynch.
heading: Morris: Franciscan Abbey, Newtownsmyth.
paras: The Morris family were resident in Galway by the 1470s when John Mares lived there and was married to Christina Lynch. Richard Mares became one of the first bailiffs in 1486-87, shortly after the Mayoralty was granted in 1485 while a second John Maris was a bailiff in 1501-02 and 1515-16. William Morris was the family’s first Mayor in 1527-28, with three statutes were passed during his term. They mainly encouraged townsmen of all ranks to practise archery more often instead of playing hurling and handball.
The next Mayor was Andrew, who served from 29 September 1588 to 29 September 1589 during which time the Spanish sent an armada to attack England only to be blown off course to Scotland and Ireland.

At least several dozen Spanish sailors were rounded up from Conamara and brought into the town, though the figures are popularly put at two or three hundred. On orders of Lord Justice of Ireland Sir William FitzWilliam of Northampton they were all beheaded at Saint Augustine’s Fort on the Hill, overlooking the town. Little is recorded of the family over the next several generations. In 1684 George Morris fitz James of the west suburbs married Catherine Fitzpatrick and through her in 1709 obtained lands at An Spidéal.

One of their great-grandsons was Martin Morris was born to Deborah Lynch and James Morris fitz Andrew during November 1784. In a sign of the changing times he able to become a Justice of the Peace (magistrate) and in 1841 became the first Catholic High Sheriff of Galway since 1691. Upon his death in 1862 he was buried in the Franciscan graveyard, Newtownsmyth. It is likely this was where several of his medieval ancestors were buried. Martin was father of Michael, 1st Baron Killanin. He was a lawyer and judge, serving as Lord Chief Justince of the King’s Bench for Ireland. He died in

1901 and was buried in the New Cemetery, Bohermore. His sons were Martin Morris, MP, and Lieutenant Colonel George Morris of the Irish Guards, killed in battle at Mons in September 1914. Geoge’s son Michael, Lord Killanin, also served in the Irish Guards during World War Two but was more well known as the President of the International Olympic Committee. Lord Killanin’s children included film producer Red Morris and horse trainer Mouse Morris.

title: The Skerrett brewhouse
summary: In an indented lease made 22 April 1749, Francis Kirwan fitz John of the Blindwell and vinter Sebastian Skerrit of Galway made a lease of a house and cellar possessed by Skerrit “lying and being partl…
heading: Skerrett: The Brewhouse, Church Lane.
paras: In an indented lease made 22 April 1749, Francis Kirwan fitz John of the Blindwell and vinter Sebastian Skerrit of Galway made a lease of a house and cellar possessed by Skerrit “lying and being partly in church lane, partly in the yard of Galway, the use of the Brew house.” It was witnessed by merchant Richard Lynch and gentleman Bartholomew Hanly, both of Galway. The Brewhouse was recorded again on 31 July 1762 when gentleman Thomas Kirwan of the Blindwell demised by lease to vintner Sebastian Skerrett of Galway a house and farm formerly held by Ignatius Biggs and now tenanted by Skerrett in Church Lane, together with use of Brewhouse. It was witnessed by Joseph Seymour, John Hamilton and Bartholomew Hanly.
Sebastian Skerrit’s Brewhouse is not known to be otherwise documented but its location means it was on the east side of the lane and so either the building now occupied by Eason’s or Boots.
That the property included an area designated ‘the yard of Galway’ suggest it was quite large.
Given the nature of their production they would have to be.

Brewhouses concerned the production of ale and beer, staple drinks for centuries due to the doubtful nature of drinking water. This may partly account for what to modern people are the high number of assaults and casual violence occurring in early modern times; having to drink it instead of water could regularly lead to more highly intoxicated states than were needed for carrying out a good day’s work!

That Skerrett was described as a vintner does not mean he made wine – impossible in the Irish climate – but demonstrates he sold it. And as it happens the two products were for generally for distinct classes; beer was drank by the

lower and middle classes, wine by the middle and upper classes. Not that the former spurned beer or that the later ignored wine, rather that beer was cheaply produced and sold, while wine was expensively made and sold. Only in recent generations has the distinction broken down.

But perhaps Sebastian Skerrett and his peers were more ambitious than we give them credit. The French traveller Latocnay visited Galway in 1791 and said A wine merchant told me the cause … of the decay of trade in Galway. ‘Before they knew how to make wine in France it was made here in Galway’ ‘What? Sure there were never vines in this country!’ No, but the wine in France was barely the juice of the grape and it was brought to Galway to render it drinkable; unfortunately the merchants of Bourdeaux know how to prepare it as well as we did, and this has ruined our trade.’ In his will of 13 September 1749, Thomas Skerrett of Loughrea identified his nephews as John Skerrett fitz Henry, George Skerrett fitz Sebastian, John Francis Skerrett fitz Bartholomew and George Skerrett fitz Bartholomew. He specified that his brother Sebastian was dead. This seems to mean that the Sebastian in 1749 and Sebastian in 1762 were two different men, but of unknown relationship. To date, nothing further is known of him.

title: The Skerretts of Bowling Green
summary: John Skerrett was born in Galway about 1620; his baptismal name is unknown as he took the name John in religion.
heading: Skerrett: House Opposite Hertrich’S, Bowling Green
paras: John Skerrett was born in Galway about 1620; his baptismal name is unknown as he took the name John in religion. His maternal granduncle was Nicholas Skerrett, born 1546 who became Archbishop of Tuam in 1580 but died in exile in Lisbon during February 1583.

As a young man he joined the Augustinian Order, leaving Galway to study in Andalusia in Spain. After being ordained a priest he lived in Cadiz where he became known as a preacher. In time he moved to Orotava on Tenerife in the Canary Islands. He returned to Ireland around 1663 during the Restoration of King Charles II and by 1666 was prior of the Augustinian house in Galway. This house was at the top of Bowling Green across form Heterich’s Butchers while another was on the site of what is now the Mechanic’s Institute; by 1731 the Augustinians were based on the site of Saint Augustine’s Church in Middle Street. Skerrett also taught Latin in the town’s boys school.

Despite being well-regarded by his fellow clerics and well regarded by the town laity, around 1674 he chose to become a missionary in English America, specifically Virginia and the West Indies. There were already Galway connections to the region, with several of the towns merchant families trading there since the 1620s while over the decades hundreds had emigrated or being exiled to the region. John Skerrett spent his time not only ministering to such people but also actively attempting to convert English Protestants and native Americans. A contemporary stated that he “suffered much persecution during the time he spent in the mission on those islands, with great danger to his own life.”

During the Popish Plot hysteria of 1679-80, he was obliged to flee to Puerto Rico, arriving by August 1680, ultimately returning to the Canary Islands. Incredibly, Skerrett became a missionary in England. This was an extraordinary choice given that Archbishop Plunkett had been executed at Tyburn and the county was in the midst of anti-Catholic pogroms. Despite this he survived and was able to travel to Rome in 1685 for his Order’s General Chapter and received permission in April 1686 to return to his work in England. This was in the aftermath of King James VII and II becoming the first Catholic king of the three kingdoms since the 16th century, with Catholics enjoying a relaxing of penal laws and persecution while hoping for a more open revival across Ireland and Britain. Among those sent to England were fellow Connacht men Martin French, Dominic Martin, William Gibbon and John Burke, four of seven men who would be working there under John Skerrett. In November 1686 he was appointed commissary-general of the Order. John Skerrett died on mission in England during 1687 or 1688; soon after all Augustinians were forced to flee England. The Catholic revival in England failed when a coup d’etat unseated King James and Prince William of Orange was invited to rule the three kingdoms, starting a war which ended with Jacobite defeat in 1691. Bermingham: House in the Mews, Williamsgate Street.
Known as Bóthar Dubh in the 1600s, a Bermingham coat of arms above the entrance denotes that a house on Williamsgate Street or Bóthar Dubh was home to a Bermingham family.

John Bermingham and Dominick Skerrett were Sheriffs of Galway elected in August 1642 under Mayor Richard Martin fitz Oliver of Dún Guaire. Bermingham was mentioned in a letter by the 5th Earl of Clanricarde dated 17 March 1642, addressed to the Lord Justices in Dublin. Clanricarde asked the Lords Justices to “send to John Bermingham of Galway, merchant, who hath the charge of the magazine of a great quantity of tobacco that lieth in Galway, to sell the same at the price of other tobacco of the same quality, and that whether it belongs to his majesty or the contractors”.

But such commercial matters were disrupted when Galway town went into rebellion two days later. This merchant seems to have being the third of four sons of Lord Richard Bermingham who died in 1635. John, alias Seón, had an estate north of Tuam at Turloughvaghan and was married to Elizabeth Darcy. Among his children was Anne, married John French fitz Valentine and who was a brother of Sir Peter French.

Likely partners of John Bermingham included Matthew Quin and John Maddan of Galway town, who in June 1649 described themselves as planters on Saint Kitt’s island in the Caribbean and whose cargo of tobacco, sugar and indigo was stolen near Galway that month by a Breton merchant. They valued the cargo at five or six thousand pounds sterling, giving some idea how much income the likes of themselves and Bermingham could gain from just a single successful voyage.

All of the profits from such cargos derived from labour exploitation, firstly from English and Irish indentures from the 1620s to 1660s and from then on through enslavement of Africans which continued into the 1830s.

This family are not recorded in the town later that century yet it is possibly from them that came persons recorded in 17th and 18th century Caribbean. Mathew Bermigham of Antigua was recorded living there in August 1711 while a memorial within Saint Catherine’s Cathedral in Spanish Town, Jamacia, was for Gerald Bermingham. It stated he was “of the Noble and Ancient Family of Athenry of the Kingdom of Ireland” who died 11 December 1742 aged fortyeight, the memorial erected by his wife Anne Bermingham. An illegitimate branch of the senior line had by the 1790s gained ownership of a sugar estate called in Demerara in south America, calling it Dalgan after their home in Galway.

title: Hall of the Red Earl
summary: Richard de Burgh was born in County Limerick around 1193 to William de Burgh of Norfolk and a daughter Donál Mór Ó Brian, King of Tuamhain.
heading: Burke: Hall Of The Red Earl, Druid Lane.
paras: Richard de Burgh was born in County Limerick around 1193 to William de Burgh of Norfolk and a daughter Donál Mór Ó Brian, King of Tuamhain. He was raised both there and in England at the court of King John, who in September 1215 granted him all the lands his father held in Connacht, completely incompatible with a grant John gave the same day to King of Connacht Cathal Crobdearg Ó Conchobhair. This was the basis of his invasions of the Kingdom of Connacht after the death of Cathal in 1224. With his cousin Donncha Cairbreach Ó Briain of Tuamhain and ally Cormac Mac Carthaigh of Deasmumhain, in 1230 he led them into Connacht “and they reached Galway,

and Ó Flaithbheartaigh gave them battle at ÁthnaGaillmhe.” Two years later he returned, seized Dún Gallimhe and from 1234 onwards the English of Ireland spread all over Connacht, destroying Ó Conchobhair overrule and establishing English colonists from Leinster and Munster throughout it.
De Burgh farmed out lordships to followers like the de Berminghams, de Exeters, Barretts, Joyces, Lawlesses, Blakes, Lynchs, Powers, Blakes, Butlers, Roches, Walshes, Prendergasts and Stauntons.

However he reserved three areas in south Connacht for his personal use, all in what is now County Galway. The first was at Meelick on the Shannon, taken from the Ó Madáin linage. The second was at Loughrea, taken from the Ó Cellaigh kings of Uí Mhaine and was his personal home in south Connacht. The third was Galway, where he had expelled the Uí Flaithberthaigh and demolished the castle of their Ó Conchobhair rulers. As one of the greatest English barons in Ireland, de Burgh had other estates scattered across Munster and Leinster requiring his attention plus duties to the King of England. It was one such expedition to Poitou in France that he died in 1243.

His ultimate successor was his second son, Walter, who greatly consolidated de Burgh power throughout Connacht and by becoming Earl of Ulster in 1263 expanded his interest into that province. However a defeat at the hands of the King of Connacht in 1270 may have injured him, as he died shortly after at his castle in Galway.

His son, Richard, was known as the Red Earl and succeeded on reaching his majority in 1280. it is to him is credited the building of the hall beside Galway Castle where he held audiences and entertained as needs be. It served as a courthouse, customs house, town hall and in his frequent absences daily management of the settlement was left to his lieutenants, who in the early decades were the de Lynches and le Blakes.

BUT DURING HIS LIFETIME WHAT IS CALLED THE GAELIC RESURGENCE BEGAN, WHERE THE DISPOSED GAEIL KINGS AND LORDS BEGAN WINNING BACK VAST TERRITORIES LOST TO THEIR Fathers and grandfathers. this began in the 1270s and by the 1390s had RESULTED IN THE RETREAT OF THE ENGLISH OF IRELAND TO ENCLAVES IN THE EAST AND South of the country. the great european famine of 1315-18 coincided with the DEVASTATION OF THE SCOTTISH INVASION AND GREATLY WEAKENED SEVERAL ENGLISH Lordships. after richard the red earl died in 1324 he was succeeded by his

GRANDSON, WILLIAM, ONLY TO BE MURDERED IN 1333 WHICH LED TO THE COLLAPSE OF THE De burgh lordship of connacht. cousins of the earls took control of the LORDSHIP, DIVIDING IT INTO NORTH CONNACHT UNDER THE MHIC UILLIAM A BURC, AND SOUTH CONNACHT UNDER THE CLANNRIOCAIRD A BURC BASED AT LOUGHREA.

No longer ruled by a semi-resident lord, in Galway the townspeople began to look after their own affairs directly. They were faced with Gaeil and Gaill lords to the east, south, west and north of them, all who coveted the income the merchants made from their trades. It was this often adversarial relationship to the great lineages all around them that made the Galwegians tough in their dealings with such lords and remain independent from them, a tiny republic surrounded by little empires.

Without a resident lord the Hall of the Red Earl gradually fell into disrepair. In the 1600s it was shown on the Pictorial Map as roofless and derelict, eventually demolished sometime in the following century. Only through archaeological excavations in the 1990s were its remains uncovered, now preserved and only display on Druid Lane, previously called Red Earl’s Lane.

title: The Fallons of High Street
summary: The Fallons were never among the Tribes of Galway but unlike so many of them they demonstrated remarkable longevity within the town.
heading: Fallon: Kilkenny Shop, High Street.
paras: The Fallons were never among the Tribes of Galway but unlike so many of them they demonstrated remarkable longevity within the town.

An Ó Fallomháin family resided in Galway since at least the 15th century and in the last year of that century, 1500, Mayor Geoffrey Lynch plus bailiffs James Lynch and Nicholas French, heard a request from Andrew Fallon. On behalf of his daughter Julian Fallon, Andrew asked that her husband, goldsmith DonálÓge Ó hUallacháin (Nolan), be made a freeman of the town, both to support his wife Julian and his father-in-law Andrew, “who is old”. Arms dated 1589 in the Kilkenny shop is intialed A.N. – Andrew Nolan, signifying a descendant of Julian and DonálÓge named after Andrew Nolan. But while Andrew’s family became Nolans, other Uí Fallomháin most certainly continued to live in the town.

A possible brother of Julian was John O’Fallon (alias Seán Ó Fallomháin) who married Joanna Lynch. She was a daughter of Oliver Lynch fitz William, Mayor of Galway 1503-04. Another was Cornell Fallon alias Conchúr Ó Fallamháin, one of four arbitrators of a deed made 27 October 1502. That he was a full
citizen of Galway is demonstrated by him serving as one of the two town bailiffs for the term 1503-04 under Mayor Oliver Lynch.

On 26 February 1539 another Andrew Fallon made a deed of mortgage to a new Galway family, headed by Henry Joyce from Athenry. Edmund O’Fallon owned a stone house in Galway during March 1571 while a twenty-one-year lease made 23 May 1583 concerned the house of Cornelius Falluam on the west. Like Cornell, Cornelius was a Latinised form of Conchúr and with the reoccurrence of Andrew demonstrates lineage continuity among the Fallon families within Galway town. The West refers to what are now the Dominick Street-Henry Street areas and that the Fallons owned their own properties within and without the town shoed they were fully integrated into the town community.

In his 1634 will, Sir Valentine Blake bequeathed twenty shillings to James Fallon of the Society of Jesus. He may be Doctor James Fallon, who along with Father Connor Fallon, were vicars of Saint Nicholas’s Collegiate Church when it was returned to the Catholic denomination in June 1643. He seems to be identical with James Fallon, vicar general imprisoned up to February 1659. When the English Commonwealth army began their siege of Galway in summer 1651, townsmen included Martin Fallon, Andrew Fallon fitz Thomas, Martin Fallon and James Fallon fitz Martin. We know this because they were still alive when the siege ended nine months later in April 1652, with the four of them listed among the majority of townsmen who either refused to sing the Articles of Surrender, or who were absent.

During 1678 Andrew Fallon of Saint Andrew’s parish on Antigua island in the English Caribbean was recorded as owning twenty-six acres and one negro. Bartholomew Fallon of Galway was a goldsmith active in the town from the 1670s to 1718, his initials appearing on surviving examples of his work. During 1690 Father James Fallon performed baptisms in Saint Nicholas’s. Among baptisms recorded in Saint Nicholas’s parish in the 1720s was one held on 11 September 1725 on Agnew, daughter of Martin Fallon and Agnete French, her sponsors Andrew Darcy and Margaret Lynch. Martin was a goldsmith and a son of Bartholomew and in 1728 he leased for thirty-one years a house in Lombard Street from James and Honoria Skerrett, one previously leased by his parents. In another deed of 26 December 1750 the property was mentioned with Martin Fallon still occupying it.

Surprisingly, there were almost no other Fallons in the town in those decades. A hearth roll taken in November 1724 recorded that on Middle Street, Hugh Fallon lived in a house with one chimney. On 11 June 1761 merchant Charles Fallon of Galway leased houses and cabins at Fahybegg. He was dead by October 1786 but survived by his wife Mary who leased Maderia

Island in the west suburbs to Peter Quinn. A presumptive descendant, gentleman John Fallon of West Convent, Galway, was party to a deed of 1807 concerning Maderia island. It was called after the island of Maderia off the coast of Africa where wine was grown and sold. This explains the marriage in May 1791 of Jane daughter of merchant Walter Burke of Galway to merchant Andrew Fallon of Oporto in Portugal.

In 1812 Reverend John Fallon of Galway town was among those who elected Reverend Edmund French of the Dominican Order to the post of Catholic Warden of Galway. During 1845 W. Falon was a paper manufacturer in the town who employed twenty-nine men and intended to employ them all in 1846. In the census of 1901 Fallons were recorded in Bohermore, Newdocks, Williamsgate Street, Abbeygate Street, Spanish Parade, Eyre Square and Market Street. It was a startling demonstration of demographic continuity in one small town from the late 15th to early 20th centuries.

title: The Nolans of High Street
summary: Writing at Galway on 4 April 1616, Nicholas Blake wrote to his son John saying that his letter of 25 February arrived in Galway on 14 March.
heading: Nolan: Kilkenny Shop On High Street.
paras: Writing at Galway on 4 April 1616, Nicholas Blake wrote to his son John saying that his letter of 25 February arrived in Galway on 14 March. He advised John plus his cousins Richard and Andrew Martin to go to Lisbon in Portugal and purchase a cargo of salt. Nicholas’s letter was been carried to John by Charles Nolan, whom Nicholas advised John to go into partnership for half of whatever merchandise he could get. If they failed to get any merchandise then he and Nolan should travel to some other place in Ireland “so as to be sure to be in company with Nolan” seeking indigo, spice, calico and cases of wine. Nicholas prayed for John’s safe return, saying that Charles Nolan would tell of the great losses of men and goods that winter.

Originally surnamed Ó hUallacháin, the Nolans originally came from Manulla civil parish in south County Mayo. In it is a townland called Lios Uí Uallacháin, named after them because it was their home estate. By the 15th century they were goldsmiths responsible for the 1494 Burke-Ó Máille chalice and it was on this basis that they migrated into Galway, becoming freemen.

In 1500 under Mayor Geoffrey French, freeman Andrew Fallon made a request of the Corpration for his daughter, Julie. Her husband was goldsmith DonálÓge Ó hUallacháin “of this same town, goldsmith” and she wished him to be made a freeman in order to better support both her and Andrew. Mayor Lynch and the Corporation granted the request. Almost

certainly their son was a man recording living on High Street in April 1535, Donál Dubh Ó hUallacháin while another descendant was recorded in March 1588. “Dorhan Nollen of Galway, aged about 22” made a legal deposition on 18 March in London, saying he was a factor for a Galway merchant and had freighted goods for him in England and was on the ship “when they were spoiled and carried away by Cook and his company, pirates.”

In the Kilkenny Shop on High Street can be found a Nolan coat of arms. Dated 1589 it bears the initials AN – Andrew Nolan – the arms featuring a circle which denoting a gold ring, an emblem of the Nolan’s profession. His first name was from his maternal ancestor, Andrew Fallon.
The Fallons continued to be documented in the town over the next four hundred years. The 1901 census documented forty-five of them living in the town and its liberties.

title: Ó hAllmhuráin of Quay Lane
summary: As of November 1724, Andrew Holleran was a Catholic living in a cabin with one chimney on Quay Lane in Saint Nicholas’s parish.
heading: Ó Hallmhuráin: Quay Lane
paras: As of November 1724, Andrew Holleran was a Catholic living in a cabin with one chimney on Quay Lane in Saint Nicholas’s parish. He was the only one of his lineage recorded in the town, yet ancestors were once proprietors of the parish. From the early 1100s they were pushed west by successive Ó Flaithberthaighs, Ó Conchobhairs and de Burghs. Even so they remained owners of thousands of acres in the western hinterlands of Galway town well into the 1600s, during which some lived within the town.

ClannFheargail were a dynasty who in the 1090s owned the civil parishes of Rahoon, Saint Nicholas’s, Oranmore and Ballynacourty. Two lesser families were Ó Fearghusa of Ros Cam plus Ó Contuille and Ó Fearghusa, anglicised into Tully and Fergus. Other candidates include Ó Duíolla alias Dooley, whose surname has since at least 1608 been embedded in CeathrúMuintirDhuíolla, modern Ballindooly.

The Ó hAllmhuráins were the most senior family of the dynasty, described in a text of 1092: “Ó hAllmhuráin is taoisech of the twenty-four townlands of ClannFhearghaile and belonging to them are Uí Anntuile and Uí Fhearghusa of Ros Cam.”

Their particular estates were firstly in Saint Nicholas’s and Oranmore parishes. At some point they gained Rahoon parish west of the river Gaillimh. The family were responsible for building a Premonstratian nunnery in or before 1235 on what became the site of Saint Mary’s church in the Claddagh. Aside from some brief references in the 8th and 9th centuries, ClannFheargail were unworthy of mention in the annals. This was because since before the

1090s the dynasty had been suborned by the Ó Flaithbertaigh kings of Iar Connacht. They in turn were suborned by successive Ó Conchobhair Kings of Connacht. One of them, Toirdhealbhach Ó Conchobhair, built a castle and settlement in the heart of their territory during 1124 which became Galway town. Such matters rendered them relatively minor players in political matters. Then in the 1230s Richard de Burgh fitz William invaded the Kingdom of Connacht and captured Dún Gaillimh, garrisoning it with his soldiers and colonising it with English from Leinster and Munster.

Surprisingly MuintirAllmhuráin were left relatively untouched as they continued to reside in and own almost all of Rahoon parish. Ó hAllmhuráin castles were made by them at Barna on the coast and Ohery inland. The townland of Leitir they sold to the French family before the 1520s. At some point between the 13th and 17th centuries the Uí hAllmhuráin sold their lands a mile west of Galway at Poolnarooma to the Skerretts. Pollnarooma West and East plus its adjacent townlands of Acres, Attithomasrevagh, Cappanaveagh and Lenaboy, are all part of Salthill.
